It came under English control in 1152 through the marriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine, and Richard the Lion Heart took it in 1177. Maritime trade made it important commercially. Jean de Dunois, a former companion of Joan of Arc, captured it on 20 August 1451 for the French Crown, at the price of a war indemnity of 40,000 gold écus.

The loss of English trade was followed by the silting of the river. In 1578 dredging under Louis de Foix returned the Adour to its former mouth, and trade revived. Sephardic Jewish refugees fleeing the Spanish expulsions settled in Saint-Esprit and brought skill in chocolate making. In the 17th century Vauban fortified the city, and his works served as models of defence for a hundred years. Activity peaked in the 18th century, with trade with Spain, the Netherlands and the Antilles and the cod fishery off Newfoundland. In 1814 Napoleon's troops fought a Spanish-Anglo-Portuguese coalition led by the Duke of Wellington in and around Bayonne, the last time it was besieged.

The railway from Paris reached Bayonne in 1854, and the city turned to the steel industry while its port declined. The discovery of the Lacq gas field in 1951 gave the port new activity. Bayonne forms a conurbation with Anglet and Biarritz and is the seat of the Communauté d'agglomération du Pays Basque. Its heritage includes the cathedral, the walls, the Basque half-timbered houses along the Nive and the Fêtes de Bayonne.
bayreuth: Bayreuth lies in northern Bavaria on the Red Main, in a valley between the Franconian Jura and the Fichtel Mountains. The town is believed to have been founded by the counts of Andechs, probably around the mid-12th century, and was first mentioned in 1194 as Baierrute, in a document of Bishop Otto II of Bamberg. The syllable rute may mean a clearing, and Baier indicates settlers from the Bavarian region. In December 1457 Margrave Albert Achilles, who was also Elector of Brandenburg, gave the town the coat of arms it still bears, with the black and white of the Hohenzollerns.

Bayreuth was the seat of the margraves, and the New Palace and its court garden served as their residence from 1753. The Margravial Opera House, opened in 1748, is one of the finest Baroque theatres in Europe and a World Heritage Site. From 1701 the Crown Prince and later Margrave George William founded the then independent town of St Georgen am See with a castle, town hall and barracks. In 1705 he founded the Order of Sincerity, renamed the Order of the Red Eagle in 1734, and in 1716 a princely porcelain factory was set up there.

Electric street lights came in 1892, a municipal electricity station in 1908 and the first cinema in the same year. After the First World War a Workers' and Soldiers' Council briefly took power, and on 17 February 1919 a three-day coup, the Speckputsch, interrupted an otherwise staid town.

Bayreuth is the capital of Upper Franconia and is best known for its link with the composer Richard Wagner, who lived there from 1872 until his death in 1883. His villa Wahnfried was built with the sponsorship of King Ludwig II of Bavaria and became a Wagner Museum after the Second World War. The Festival Hall in the north of the town is used only for the annual Bayreuth Festival, at which only his works are performed. The premieres of Siegfried and Götterdämmerung, of the Ring cycle as a whole and of Parsifal took place there.
bazaar: The word bazaar comes from New Persian bazar, from Middle Persian wazar, Old Persian wacar and Proto-Indo-Iranian *waha-carana. It first referred to a town's public market district, and bazaari refers collectively to the merchants, bankers and craftsmen who work in one. The related word souk comes from Arabic and is a loan from Aramaic shuqa, street or market, itself from the Akkadian suqu. The earliest evidence for bazaars dates to around 3000 BCE, and ancient cities in West Asia appear to have had commercial districts, though the lack of archaeological evidence limits detailed study. In Achaemenid Persia documents indicate that crafts were sold in markets close to Persepolis, and bazaars sprang up alongside the ancient caravan routes, linking major cities.

A bazaar is a marketplace of many small stalls or shops, especially in West Asia, North Africa, the Balkans, Central Asia and South Asia. Traditionally it stood in vaulted or covered streets with doors at each end and served as a city's central marketplace. In the Islamic world bazaars shared institutions such as the muhtasib, an official overseeing weights and measures and public morality, and architectural forms such as roofed streets and caravanserais. Bazaars were divided into specialised sections named after their goods, such as the gold, textile, spice or booksellers' souk, which promoted competition and let buyers compare prices. The merchants of each trade were organised into guilds that supported members and clients and negotiated with the government.

Bazaars were also held outside cities where caravans stopped, and they could include festivals and social gatherings as well as trade. According to traditional Muslim narratives, Muhammad established a market in Medina after arriving there in 622 and forbade permanent buildings and taxes in it, but the Umayyad caliphs Mu'awiya I and Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik built structures there and levied taxes. Markets selling the most expensive goods stood near a city's central Friday mosque. In Iran from the 10th century the bazaar became a city's financial centre, often grouped with the citadel and the Friday mosque. In the Mamluk Sultanate and the Ottoman Empire, sultans and ruling elites sponsored commercial buildings in and around the bazaar, whose revenues supported religious complexes through the waqf.

In the 18th and 19th centuries Western interest in oriental culture produced many books on daily life in West Asia, and souks and bazaars feature in paintings, fiction and travel writing. Shopping at a bazaar remains a central part of daily life in many West and South Asian cities. Several bazaar districts are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Medina of Fez, listed in 1981, the Ancient City of Aleppo, in 1986, and the Bazaar complex in Tabriz, in 2010.
bbc: Britain's first live public broadcast was made from the Marconi Company's factory in Chelmsford in June 1920. Sponsored by the Daily Mail's Alfred Harmsworth, 1st Viscount Northcliffe, it featured the Australian soprano Dame Nellie Melba and caught the public imagination. Official circles did not share the enthusiasm, since such broadcasts were held to interfere with military and civil communications, and by late 1920 the General Post Office had secured a ban on further Chelmsford broadcasts. The British Broadcasting Company was formed on 18 October 1922.

Its finances soon proved inadequate, and by mid-1923 talks with the Post Office were deadlocked. The Sykes Committee recommended a simple 10 shilling licence fee to fund broadcasts, and a monopoly without advertising. To avoid competition with newspapers, Fleet Street persuaded the government to ban news bulletins before 7 pm. In September 1923 John Reith launched the Radio Times, the first broadcast listings magazine.

The British Broadcasting Corporation came into existence on 1 January 1927, with the newly knighted Reith as its first director general. It adopted the motto Nation shall speak peace unto Nation, and the World Service was launched in 1932 as the Empire Service. From as early as the 1930s until the 1990s the security service MI5 vetted applicants for BBC jobs without their knowledge, an arrangement that began informally in 1933 and was formalised from 1935; the BBC denied any suggestion of it.

Television broadcasting was suspended from 1 September 1939 to 7 June 1946, and radio kept the nation's spirits up. Most radio operations moved out of London, first to Bristol and then to Bedford, where concerts were broadcast from the Corn Exchange. In 1941 the Archbishops of Canterbury and York broadcast from St Paul's Church there on the National Day of Prayer. George Orwell worked for the BBC for two years during the war.

The BBC is a chartered corporation, independent of direct government intervention. Its royal charter sets out its mission and public purposes, emphasises public service and limited editorial independence, and prohibits advertising on domestic services. It is funded principally by the television licence fee, set by the government and enforced by the criminal law. Its headquarters, Broadcasting House in Portland Place, London, carries statues of Prospero and Ariel by Eric Gill. The BBC has often been criticised over its impartiality, with accusations of bias made from both left and right.
bead: A bead is a small object with a hole for threading or stringing, from under 1 mm to over 1 cm across. The earliest beads were made of natural materials that could be drilled and shaped easily: bone, shell, horn, ivory, seeds, coral and wood. Pearls were for most of human history the most prized natural beads because of their rarity, and amber and jet, both partly fossilised, were also used. Stone beads range from gemstones to common minerals, and precious metals and alloys such as electrum were also worked into beads.

Beads are among the earliest forms of jewellery, and are thought to be one of the earliest goods traded between people. Shell beads from Blombos Cave in South Africa and beads from Ksar Akil in Lebanon, about 45,000 years old, are among the oldest found. The oldest synthetic materials used for beads were ceramics, pottery and glass. Bronze and brass beads were also made in antiquity, but they oxidise more readily and survive less well at archaeological sites. Glass beads were later made in many forms, such as millefiori and chevron beads, the latter sometimes called trade beads.

The English word comes from Old English gebed, meaning prayer, and was transferred to small round objects because of the use of beads for counting prayers, as in the Christian Pater Noster cords and rosaries.

Beads served many purposes. Prayer beads include the rosary, the Muslim misbaha, and the japamala and Rudraksha strings of Hindus, Buddhists and others; Tibetan Dzi beads and Rudraksha beads make the Buddhist and Hindu malas. The Greek komboloi are worry beads, and beads threaded on wires form the counters of the abacus. Aggrey beads from Ghana served as currency, and oware beads are the pieces of a mancala game.

Beads were also traded as goods. In Africa, trade beads were sometimes made in Europe, such as chevron beads, and sometimes made in West Africa by and for Africans, such as Mauritanian Kiffa beads and Ghanaian and Nigerian powder glass beads. Archaeologists have documented that into the late nineteenth century, beads made in Europe still accompanied exploration of Africa along Indigenous routes into the interior. Wampum, made from shells, is a bead of Native American peoples of the north-east, among them the Wampanoag and Shinnecock.
beas: The Beas, from the Hindi Vyas, is the smallest of the five major rivers of the Punjab. It rises at 4,361 metres on the southern face of the Rohtang Pass in Kullu, in Himachal Pradesh, and flows about 470 kilometres to join the Sutlej in Punjab, draining a basin of 20,303 square kilometres. Its chief tributaries are the Bain, Banganga, Luni and Uhal. In its lower course it was crossed by many ferries, several of them inflated skins called darais. The Sutlej carries its waters on to meet the Chenab at Uch, forming the Panjnad, which joins the Indus at Mithankot.

The Rig-veda calls the river Vipāś, meaning unfettered, and later Sanskrit texts call it Vipāśā. The ancient Greeks knew it as the Hyphasis. According to legend the sage Veda Vyasa, author of the Mahabharata, created it from its source lake, the Beas Kund and gave it his name. Another legend tells that the sage Vashishta tried to drown himself in the river, which turned to a sandbed and broke his cords, so that he called it Vipasa, the cord-breaker.

The Beas marks the easternmost limit of the conquests of Alexander the Great. In 326 BCE his troops mutinied at the river and refused to march further east. Alexander shut himself in his tent for three days, and when the mutiny did not cease he gave way and raised twelve colossal altars to mark the limit of his expedition. Their location and fate are unknown, although one historian has suggested that they were later reused in some of the Pillars of Ashoka. According to the Kavyamimansa of Rajasekhara, the lands of the Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Mahipala I reached the upper course of the Beas.

The river has changed its course. It once ran from its present junction with the Sutlej towards Lahore and joined the Chenab near Shujabad, and by 1245 it occupied the old bed of the Chenab that passed Dipalpur. An older channel flowed south of the site of Harappa. Between 1750 and 1800 the Sutlej captured its flow, after many earlier shifts.

In the 20th century the Beas Project developed the river for irrigation and hydroelectric power. The Pandoh Dam diverts water to the Sutlej through tunnels and channels, and the earth-fill Pong Dam in Kangra district was completed in 1974. The Harike Barrage, at the confluence of the Beas and Sutlej, feeds canals that irrigate Punjab and Rajasthan. Under the Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan, the waters of the Beas are allocated to India.
beaune: Beaune stands on a plain beside the hills of the Côte d'Or and is served by a small river, the Bouzaise, whose source lies in a public park on the north-east edge of the town. The name derives from the Latinised Gaulish Belena, the name of a spring around which the settlement grew, itself derived from Belenos, a god of fast-flowing water. The climate is semi-continental with an oceanic influence, with frequent rain in every season.

A Roman fort was built at the site in the first century CE, and the town has features from pre-Roman and Roman times through the medieval and Renaissance periods. The region was already a wine-growing area in the 13th century, and the cellars of producers have stood in the historic centre since Roman times. Beaune is a walled city: much of its battlements, ramparts and moat survives in good condition, and the old town inside the walls is extensive. Historically it is closely connected with the Dukes of Burgundy.

The Hospices de Beaune were founded in the 15th century by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of the Duke of Burgundy, who was encouraged by his wife Guigone de Salins. They are a charity running hospitals and other services for the needy, and through the gifts of benefactors they own vineyards in Burgundy. At the end of the First World War the American Expeditionary Forces University was established in Beaune under Brigadier General Robert I. Rees, with its own chapter of Phi Beta Kappa.

Beaune is a commune and sub-prefecture of the Côte-d'Or department, in the region of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, and is regarded as the wine capital of Burgundy. Many major négociants have their houses there, and the appellation Beaune was created in 1936. An annual charity wine auction is held for the Hospices. Landmarks include the Hospices, the old market, the Beffroi clock tower and the collegiate church of Notre Dame, and the town is the main centre of the polychrome Burgundian tile roofing of the Renaissance. In 2015 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Climats, terroirs of Burgundy.
beauvais: Beauvais is a town and commune in northern France, the prefecture of the Oise département in the Hauts-de-France region, 75 kilometres north of Paris. It lies at the foot of wooded hills on the left bank of the Thérain at its confluence with the Avelon. Its ancient ramparts have been destroyed and it is now surrounded by boulevards. The region around it is called the Beauvaisis.

The Romans knew it by the Gallo-Roman name Caesaromagus, the capital of the Belgic tribe of the Bellovaci. Some hold that it was the fortified town of Bratuspantium that surrendered to Julius Caesar, as De Bello Gallico reports, while others identify that town with Vendeuil-Caply or Bailleul sur Thérain. In the ninth century it became a county, which passed in about 1013 to the bishops of Beauvais, who became peers of France from the twelfth century. At royal coronations the Bishop of Beauvais wore the royal mantle and, with the Bishop of Langres, raised the king from his throne to present him to the people.

The town defended itself against the English in 1346 and was besieged by them again in 1433. The siege by the Duke of Burgundy in 1472 was noted for the heroism of the town's women under Jeanne Hachette, remembered in a procession on 27 June in which women take precedence over men. Beauvais was extensively damaged in World War I and again in June 1940; much of the older part was all but destroyed, and the cathedral was badly damaged before British forces liberated the town on 30 August 1944.

The cathedral of Saint-Pierre, begun in 1247 under Bishop William of Grès, was raised an extra 5 metres to make it the tallest cathedral in Europe, and the vaulting of the interior exceeds 46 metres. Work stopped in 1284 when the vaulting of the choir collapsed, and the fall of a too-ambitious central tower in 1573 halted it again. The building consists only of a transept and choir with an apse and seven apse chapels; a small Romanesque church of the 10th century, the Basse Oeuvre, occupies the site meant for the nave. Its stained glass of the 13th, 14th and 16th centuries includes work by Engrand Le Prince.

The state tapestry manufactory dates from 1664. The church of Saint-Étienne is a Romanesque and Gothic building of the early 12th to late 16th centuries, and a former episcopal palace of the 16th century houses the departmental museum. Beauvais–Tillé Airport, dating from the 1930s, serves as a gateway to Paris.
bede: Almost everything known of Bede's life comes from the last chapter of his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed in about 731. He gives his birthplace as the lands of the twin monastery of Monkwearmouth and Jarrow. Bede says nothing of his origins, but his connections with men of noble ancestry suggest that his family was well-to-do.

At the age of seven he was sent to Monkwearmouth to be educated by Benedict Biscop and later by Ceolfrith. Jarrow was founded by Ceolfrith in 682, and Bede probably moved there with him that year. In 686 a plague broke out at Jarrow, and the Life of Ceolfrith records that only two surviving monks could sing the full office, one of them a young boy, almost certainly Bede. In about 692 he was ordained a deacon by John, Bishop of Hexham, and in about 702 he became a priest.

Bede began writing in about 701 with two classroom works, De Arte Metrica and De Schematibus et Tropis, and eventually completed over 60 books, most of which survive. He wrote on music, metrics, chronology, history and theology, knew some Greek, and read Pliny the Elder, Virgil, Ovid and Horace. In his own time he was as well known for his biblical commentaries as for his history.

The Ecclesiastical History opens with Caesar's invasion and a brief account of Christianity in Roman Britain, then tells of Augustine's mission of 597, the progress of the faith in Kent and Northumbria, the reigns of Oswald and Oswy, and the Council of Whitby. He also studied computus, the calculation of calendar dates, above all the date of Easter, a subject of controversy, and helped to popularise dating forward from the birth of Christ.
His last surviving work is a letter to Ecgbert of York, written in 734. He died on 26 May 735. A cult formed around him by the 10th century and was widespread in England by the fourteenth.

His body was moved to Durham Cathedral in 1020 and placed in the tomb of Saint Cuthbert, then in 1370 to a shrine of its own. The shrine was demolished during the English Reformation, and Bede was reburied in the cathedral. In 1899 Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church, the first native of Great Britain to hold the title.
bedouin: The English word bedouin comes from the Arabic badawī, desert-dweller, traditionally contrasted with ḥāḍir, a sedentary person. The Bedouin originated in the Syrian Desert and Arabian Desert and spread across the rest of the Arab world in West Asia and North Africa after the spread of Islam. They were called Arabaa by the Assyrians. According to tradition, the Arabian Bedouin descend from two groups: the Qahtanis, or Yaman, from south-western Arabia, who claim descent from an ancestral figure, Qahtan, and the Adnanis, from north-central Arabia, who claim descent from Adnan, a descendant of the biblical Ishmael.

The Bedouin are described as having engaged in nomadic herding, agriculture and sometimes fishing in the Syrian steppe since 6000 BCE. By the time the Roman Empire was founded they were recognisable as a single people, though often at war among their families, clans and tribes. A major source of income was taxing caravans and collecting tribute from settlements, and they also carried goods and people across the desert in camel caravans. In 1326 Ibn Battuta reported that Egyptian authorities at Qatya on the Sinai coast used Bedouin to guard the road.

From the 11th to the 15th centuries nomadic Bedouin tribes moved into the Maghreb in great numbers: the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym, from central and north Arabia, moved west in the 11th century and were joined by the Ma'qil, who had roots in south Arabia. In the late 18th century rivalry between the Shammar and Anizah confederations, together with the rise of the Wahhabi movement, led a Shammar faction under the Al Jarba family to migrate across the Euphrates into Upper Mesopotamia. Raiding was still part of Bedouin life in the early 20th century, when Saudi Arabia began a policy of settling the tribes.

The Bedouin are divided into tribes or clans. A widely quoted adage runs, I am against my brother, my brother and I are against my cousin, my cousin and I are against the stranger, which grades loyalties by closeness of kin; disputes are settled by self-help and collective responsibility. Traditional livelihoods were herding goats, sheep and dromedary camels for meat, dairy products and wool. Camels, regarded as a gift from God, were the main food source and means of transport, and were raced at weddings and religious festivals.

Oral poetry is the most popular art form, and a poet in the tribe was highly regarded; it also carried news and served as social control. Raiding, known as ghazw, was a regulated habit. Coffee prepared before the guest is a major part of hospitality. Many Bedouin have since adopted an urban life, while others keep the clan structure, music, poetry and dances.
bedrich-smetana: Smetana was born on 2 March 1824 in Litomyšl, east of Prague near the traditional border between Bohemia and Moravia, then provinces of the Habsburg Empire. He was the third child, and first son, of František Smetana, a brewer in the service of Count Waldstein, and his third wife Barbora Linková. German was the official language of Bohemia, and the children did not learn correct Czech until much later in their lives.

He gave his first public performance at the age of six. He came to Prague in the autumn of 1839 and soon began missing classes at his school in favour of concerts and the opera, convinced after hearing Franz Liszt that he wanted a musical career. His father saw music only as a pastime. Smetana later studied under Josef Proksch, and in 1848 he helped man the barricades on the Charles Bridge as a member of the Citizens' Army, where he met the writer Karel Sabina.

After failing to establish himself in Prague, Smetana left for Gothenburg, where within weeks he gave a recital, opened a music school that was soon overwhelmed by applications and became conductor of the Gothenburg Society for Classical Choral Music. A visit to Liszt at Weimar in the summer of 1857 shaped his later orchestral work and led to the three Gothenburg symphonic poems, Richard III, Wallenstein's Camp and Hakon Jarl.

The announcement in 1861 of a Provisional Theatre for Czech opera drew him back to Prague. The conductorship went to Jan Nepomuk Maýr, because the conservative faction considered Smetana a dangerous modernist in thrall to Liszt and Wagner. His first two operas, The Brandenburgers in Bohemia and The Bartered Bride, were premiered there in 1866, and he then became the theatre's principal conductor, though his years in the post were marked by controversy.

By the winter of 1882–83 Smetana suffered depression, insomnia and hallucinations. By the middle of February 1884 he had ceased to be coherent, and on 23 April his family removed him to the Kateřinky Lunatic Asylum in Prague, where he died on 12 May 1884.

Most commentators agree that he created a canon of Czech opera where none had existed and a musical style matching the emergent Czech national spirit. Relatively few of his works are in the international repertory, and most foreign commentators regard Antonín Dvořák as the more significant Czech composer.
beemster: Around 800 the area was covered in peat. Its name derives from Bamestra, the name of a small river there. Between 1150 and 1250 peat-digging and storm floods enlarged that river into an inland sea, a lake connected with the Zuiderzee. Private investors set about draining the lake. In 1610 the work was almost complete, but the lake filled again after a breach in the Zuiderzee dikes. It was decided to raise the ring-dike to a metre above the surrounding country, and by 1612 the polder was dry and the land was divided among the investors.

In its early days farmers there grew the crops needed for the long sea journeys of the VOC to the East Indies. The farmland was so good that the project was considered an economic success, in contrast to the drainage of Heerhugowaard. In 1901 a co-operative, CONO Kaasmakers, was formed to make cheese from the milk of the polder; it sells the Beemster brand.

The original landscape of fields, roads, canals and dykes survives intact. A grid of canals runs parallel to the grid of roads, with the larger feeder canals offset from the larger roads by about a kilometre. The villages are Middenbeemster, Noordbeemster, Westbeemster and Zuidoostbeemster, and the painters Carel Fabritius and Barent Fabritius were born in Middenbeemster. The former municipality merged into Purmerend on 1 January 2022.

UNESCO inscribed the polder as a World Heritage Site in 1999. It cited the polder as a masterpiece of creative planning that applied the ideals of antiquity and the Renaissance to a reclaimed landscape, with a lasting impact on reclamation projects in Europe and beyond. Five fortresses of the Stelling van Amsterdam, another World Heritage Site, also stand in the Beemster.
beer-hall-putsch: After the Treaty of Versailles, Germany declined as a European power. Hitler, who had fought in the German Army but still held Austrian citizenship, shared the common belief that the country had been stabbed in the back by its own government. He remained in the army in Munich and was sent to infiltrate the small German Workers' Party, which he joined on 12 September 1919 and soon led. He also took the political lead of the Kampfbund, a group of Bavarian patriotic associations, with about 15,000 members of the Sturmabteilung (SA). The coup was inspired by Benito Mussolini's March on Rome.

Hitler came to realise that Gustav Ritter von Kahr, the Minister-President of Bavaria, sought to control him and was not ready to act against Berlin. On the evening of 8 November 1923, 603 SA men surrounded the Bürgerbräukeller, where Kahr was speaking to 3,000 people, and a machine gun was set up in the auditorium. Hitler fired a shot into the ceiling, jumped on a chair and shouted that the national revolution had broken out. He declared the Bavarian government deposed and announced a new government with Erich Ludendorff.

The state police seized the central telegraph office and the telephone exchange and warned Major-General Jakob von Danner, the army's commandant in Munich, who alerted all units. Around 23:00 Danner and other generals compelled Otto von Lossow to repudiate the putsch. The next day Archbishop Michael von Faulhaber and Rupprecht persuaded Kahr to do the same, and a march on the Feldherrnhalle by about 2,000 Nazis met a police cordon.

Hitler escaped immediate arrest but was arrested two days later, and he, Ludendorff, Ernst Röhm and others were charged with high treason. The Nazi newspaper, the Völkischer Beobachter, was banned. The trial lasted 24 days and was widely publicised, giving Hitler a platform. He was sentenced to five years in Landsberg Prison, where he dictated Mein Kampf to Emil Maurice and Rudolf Hess, and was released on 20 December 1924 after about nine months. Afterwards he sought power by legal means. The Nazi dead were later treated as the party's first blood martyrs, and their bloodstained flag became the Blutfahne.
behistun-inscription: The inscription stands on a limestone cliff at Mount Behistun, near Kermanshah, some 100 metres above an ancient road linking Babylon and Ecbatana. The Old Persian text has 414 lines in five columns, the Elamite 260 lines in eight columns and the Babylonian 112 lines; a copy in Aramaic from the reign of Darius II was found in Egypt. It opens with Darius's ancestry from Achaemenes through Teispes, Ariaramnes, Arsames and Hystaspes, and he says that eight of his dynasty were kings before him and he is the ninth. A list of twenty-three subject lands follows.

Later the text tells of the upheaval after the death of Cambyses II, in which Darius says he fought nineteen battles in a year, ending in December 521 BCE. He states that several impostors, each falsely proclaiming himself king, orchestrated the revolts, declares himself victorious in every battle and credits the grace of Ahura Mazda.

A life-sized relief shows Darius holding a bow, his left foot on a figure lying on its back who is reputed to be the pretender Gaumata. Nine one-metre figures with hands tied and ropes round their necks stand for conquered peoples.

The text was composed between Darius's coronation in the summer of 522 BCE and his death in autumn 486 BCE. The Achaemenid inscriptional tradition is thought to derive from those of Elam, Lullubi, Babylon and Assyria, and the relief resembles that of the Lullubi king Anubanini, dated to about 2300 BCE, which its sculptors may have seen. The campaigns are described with formulaic brevity, and, as in earlier inscriptions, victories are tied to divine approval.

After the end of Old Persian cuneiform the nature of the inscription was forgotten and fanciful explanations took its place. Robert Sherley saw it in 1598, and his party wrongly took it for Christian. Carsten Niebuhr published a copy in 1778, which Georg Friedrich Grotefend used to decipher ten of the 37 Old Persian symbols by 1802.

From 1835 Henry Rawlinson, an officer of the East India Company army, scaled the cliff with the help of a local boy and copied the Old Persian text, sending a full and accurate copy to Europe in 1847; the Elamite and Babylonian texts were out of easy reach and left for later. Expeditions in 1904 and 1948 obtained photographs and casts. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006.
beijing: Beijing is situated at the northern edge of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens to the south and east of the city. Mountains to the north, northwest and west shield the city and northern China's agricultural heartland from the encroaching desert steppes. The Great Wall of China across the northern part of the municipality was built on the rugged topography to defend against nomadic incursions from the steppes. The highest point of the municipality is Mount Dongling, at 2,303 metres, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

The name Beijing means 'Northern Capital' and was applied to the city in 1403, during the Ming dynasty, to distinguish it from Nanjing, the 'Southern Capital'. The older English spelling Peking was used by the Jesuit missionary Martino Martini in an atlas published in Amsterdam in 1655. Over the past 3,000 years the city has had numerous other names.

The earliest traces of human habitation in the municipality were found in the caves of Dragon Bone Hill near the village of Zhoukoudian, where Peking Man lived. Homo erectus fossils from the caves date to 230,000 to 250,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens lived there more recently, about 27,000 years ago. Neolithic settlements have been found throughout the municipality, including in Wangfujing in central Beijing.

The first walled city in the area was Ji, the capital of the state of Ji, located around the present Guang'anmen area in the south of Xicheng District. During the early Zhou period the settlement was conquered by the state of Yan, which made it its new capital. Its original capital lay 45 kilometres to the southwest in Fangshan District. Yan eventually became one of the seven major states of China in the Warring States period.

Beijing is the capital of China and is governed as a provincial-level municipality with 16 districts. In 2024 its population was about 21.8 million. Its traditional housing consists of siheyuans, courtyard houses, and the narrow alleys between them called hutongs. It has eight UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace, the Ming Tombs, the Zhoukoudian Peking Man Site and parts of the Great Wall and the Grand Canal. Beijing opera is its best-known traditional form of theatre.
beit-shean: Beit She'an, also called Beth-Shean and, in Arabic, Beisan or Baysan, lies about 120 m below sea level in the Beit She'an Valley. Its position at the junction of the Jordan River Valley and the Jezreel Valley made it strategically important, since it controlled access from Jordan and the interior to the coast and from Jerusalem and Jericho to the Galilee. Its ancient mound holds remains beginning in the Chalcolithic period, and excavations have revealed 18 successive ancient towns.

After Pharaoh Thutmose III conquered it in the 15th century BCE, as an inscription at Karnak records, Beit She'an became the centre of Egyptian administration in the region. Fire destroyed the site around 1150 BCE, and the Egyptians did not rebuild. The Hebrew Bible says the Philistines hung the body of King Saul on its walls, though no archaeological evidence of Philistine occupation has been found. The Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom of Israel burned the city in 732 BCE.

In the Hellenistic period it was reoccupied as Scythopolis, perhaps named for Scythian mercenaries who settled there as veterans. After Pompey made Judea part of the Roman Republic in 63 BCE, Gabinius refounded the town, and it became the leading city of the Decapolis and the only one west of the Jordan. It had a theatre, a hippodrome and a cardo. In 409 Scythopolis became capital of Palaestina Secunda, a mainly Christian city with Jewish and Samaritan communities, which reached about 40,000 people in the 6th century. After the Arab conquest of 634 it took the name Baysan, and an earthquake on 18 January 749 devastated it.

Beit She'an is a city in the Northern District of Israel with about 20,000 people and is the regional centre for the towns of its valley. Its Muslim and Christian inhabitants fled or were expelled between 1948 and 1950, and Jewish immigrants then settled it. The ancient ruins are protected within Beit She'an National Park.
bejaia: Béjaïa owes its existence to its port. It stands in a sickle-shaped bay on the Gulf of Béjaïa, protected from the swell by Cape Carbon, and is backed by Mount Gouraya, with the Babors range behind. It is also the outlet of the Soummam valley. Its position between Grande and Petite Kabylie has not given it a firm hinterland, since both regions turn towards inland centres. The name is a transliteration of the Berber Bgayet, probably from a word meaning wild brambles and blackberries; Ibn Khaldun instead derived it from the tribe called the Bedjaïa.

Prehistoric people lived around Béjaïa, and the Afalou caves hold some of the oldest burials of modern humans, of the Iberomaurusian culture. The Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax mentions the site in the 5th century BCE, and the region belonged to Numidia and later to Rome. Umayyad conquerors from Kairouan called the surrounding mountains el 'adua, the enemy, for the stubborn resistance there; the city seems to have been conquered relatively late, around 708. Its prosperity, tied to trans-Saharan and Mediterranean trade, declined around the turn of the 15th century as world trade moved to new sea routes.

Pedro Navarro took the city for the Spanish from Sultan Abdelaziz in 1510, ending the kingdom of Bougie. The harshness of the Spanish caused the local population to flee, and Abu Bakr, Abdelaziz's brother, failed to retake the city in 1512. The beylerbey Salah Raïs entered it after the Battle of Béjaïa in 1555, with the help of the Kabyles of Koukou, and it became part of the Regency of Algiers. The French took it in 1833 after fierce resistance, but kept to a limited occupation until 1846. In 1959 it was Algeria's most important oil port, at the end of the pipeline from Hassi Messaoud.

Béjaïa is the capital of Béjaïa Province in Algeria, with 177,988 inhabitants at the 2008 census. The old town, nestled against the Gouraya massif, keeps Moorish houses, the Casbah and the Sea Gate, and Roman remains such as a cistern. Spanish and French building removed many medieval structures, among them the Hammadid Palace of the Star. The port exports oil, iron ore, phosphates and wine.
bela-iv-of-hungary: Béla was the eldest son of King Andrew II of Hungary and his first wife, Gertrude of Merania, and was born in the second half of 1206. Noblemen murdered his mother in 1213, and in 1214 a group of lords had the eight-year-old Béla crowned against his father's wishes. Andrew refused him a province until 1220, when he became Duke of Slavonia and married Maria, daughter of Theodore I Laskaris, Emperor of Nicaea. From 1226 he governed Transylvania, where he supported Dominican missions among the Cumans, and in 1233 he adopted the title King of Cumania.

Béla succeeded his father on 21 September 1235 and set out to restore royal authority. Commissions revised the land grants made since 1196 and he reclaimed royal estates, which alienated many nobles and prelates. When the Mongols under Batu Khan reached Hungary in 1241 the lords he had alienated gave poor support, and the Cumans, his most valuable allies, left after a mob in Pest killed their chieftain Köten. His army, of fewer than 60,000, was destroyed at Mohi on 11 April 1241, and the Mongols ravaged the lands east of the Danube until they withdrew in March 1242.

Béla returned in May 1242 to a ruined country, at least half the villages east of the Danube depopulated, and famine followed. He abandoned the royal monopoly on castle-building, and nearly 100 new fortresses were raised by the end of his reign, among them one he founded at Visegrád. He settled colonists from the Holy Roman Empire, Poland and neighbouring lands, and made Buda a royal town. With Ruthenian and Polish princes he formed a defensive alliance against the Mongols, and he held the Duchy of Styria from 1254 to 1258.

From the early 1260s Béla quarrelled with his eldest son and heir, Stephen, who suspected his father of favouring Béla's younger son, also named Béla, and his daughter Anna. A civil war followed in which Stephen routed his father's army at Isaszeg in March 1265, and it ended in 1266 with Hungary divided along the Danube. Béla died on 3 May 1270 on Rabbits' Island and was buried at Esztergom. He died as a Franciscan tertiary, and his daughters Kunigunda, Yolanda and Margaret were later venerated as saints. Posterity called him the second founder of the state. The Illuminated Chronicle called him a man of peace, but the least fortunate in the conduct of armies.
bela-kun: Béla Kun was born Béla Kohn on 20 February 1886 in the village of Lele, in the Kingdom of Hungary, now part of Romania. His father was a lapsed Jewish village notary, and his mother, a Hungarian, had converted to Judaism on marriage. He studied law at Franz Joseph University in Kolozsvár from 1904, the year he began to be called Kun rather than Kohn, and befriended the poet Endre Ady, who introduced him to Budapest's left-wing intelligentsia. He worked as a journalist until the First World War, served in the Austro-Hungarian Army and was captured by the Russian army in 1916.

The Russian Revolution freed him from a prisoner-of-war camp. In March 1918 in Moscow he co-founded the Hungarian Group of the Russian Communist Party and came to know Lenin, though he stood with the ultra-radical left, which wished to continue the war against the Central Powers. He fought for the Bolsheviks in the Russian Civil War and returned to Budapest on 16 November 1918 with Soviet money. On 24 November he founded the Party of Communists from Hungary and campaigned against the government of President Mihály Károlyi.

The Hungarian Soviet Republic was proclaimed on 21 March 1919, after his release from prison. Sándor Garbai was its nominal head, but power rested with Kun, officially People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs and from April also for Defence. Social Democrats held most commissariats but accepted the leadership of the smaller Communist Party. Four months later the regime collapsed before an offensive by the Kingdom of Romania.

Kun went into exile in Vienna, where he was interned until July 1920. In Russia he led the Crimean Revolutionary Committee and took part in the Red Terror in Crimea in 1920-1921. He advised the German Communists in the failed March Action of 1921, which Lenin blamed him for. During the Great Purge he was arrested by the NKVD on 28 June 1937, accused of Trotskyism and sentenced to death after a brief secret trial. He was shot at Kommunarka on 29 August 1938. After his rehabilitation in 1956 the Soviet party told the Hungarians that he had died in prison in 1939; only in 1989 did the Soviet government acknowledge the true date.
belagavi: Belagavi lies in north-western Karnataka, near the borders with Maharashtra and Goa, near the foothills of the Sahyadri range of the Western Ghats. It stands at an average elevation of 770 metres, about 100 kilometres from the Arabian Sea, with the Markandeya river flowing nearby. It is 502 kilometres from Bangalore and 500 kilometres from Mumbai, and is the administrative headquarters of the Belagavi division and district.

The town was founded in the late 12th century by the Ratta dynasty, who moved from nearby Saundatti. A Ratta official named Bichiraja built the Jain temple of Kamal Basadi, dedicated to Neminatha, in 1204. Its original name was Venugram, a Sanskrit name meaning village of bamboo. In the early 13th century it passed to the Yadava kingdom, as an inscription of 1261 attests. The Khalji dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate invaded the region in the 14th century, after which Belgaum came under the Vijayanagara Empire.

The Bahmani Sultanate conquered it in 1474 with an army led by Mahmud Gawan. After the Bahmani state split in 1518 the town became part of the Bijapur Sultanate. In 1686 the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb overthrew Bijapur, and the Mughals called the town Azamnagar. Mughal control collapsed after Aurangzeb's death in 1707, and the Maratha confederacy took the area under the Peshwas. Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan overran it in 1776, but the Peshwa regained it after Tipu was defeated. The British annexed Belgaum in 1818. In 1824 Kitturu Chennamma, queen of Kittur, led an unsuccessful armed rebellion against them.

Belgaum hosted the 39th session of the Indian National Congress in December 1924 under the presidency of Mahatma Gandhi. It was a major British military installation, partly because of its proximity to Portuguese Goa, and in 1961 the Indian government used forces from Belgaum to end Portuguese rule in Goa. In 1956 the States Reorganisation Act transferred Belgaum and ten taluks of Bombay State to Mysore State, which was renamed Karnataka in 1973. Maharashtra claims the city on linguistic grounds, a dispute taken to the Supreme Court. The Maharashtra Ekikaran Samiti, formed in 1948 to campaign for the merger, marks 17 January as martyrs' day for activists shot by police in 1956.

On 1 November 2014 the Karnataka government changed the name from Belgaum to Belagavi. Kannada and Marathi are the predominant languages, with Urdu, Konkani, Hindi and Telugu also spoken. The Suvarna Vidhana Soudha, an administrative building inaugurated in 2012, hosts the annual winter session of the Karnataka Legislative Assembly.
belarus: Belarus is a landlocked country of 207,600 square kilometres, lying between latitudes 51° and 57° N and measuring 560 kilometres from north to south and 650 from west to east. It is relatively flat, with large tracts of marshy land, about 40% forest, and 11,000 lakes.

Three major rivers run through it: the Neman flows west toward the Baltic Sea, the Pripyat flows east to the Dnieper, and the Dnieper flows south toward the Black Sea. The highest point is Dzyarzhynskaya Hara, at 345 metres. About 70% of the radiation from the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in neighbouring Ukraine entered Belarusian territory, and about a fifth of the land was affected by fallout.

Baltic tribes first permanently settled the region in the 3rd century, and around the 5th century the Slavs took it over, and the gradual assimilation of the Baltic settlers into Slavic culture was peaceful. In the 9th century it became part of Kievan Rus', a vast East Slavic state ruled by the Rurikids, which split into independent principalities on the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054.

The Battle on the Nemiga River in 1067 is considered the founding date of Minsk. The lands avoided the brunt of the 13th-century Mongol invasion and joined the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; the annals affirm an alliance and united foreign policy between Polotsk and Lithuania for decades. The duchy fought alongside Poland against the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410.

By the 14th century the lands had come fully under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, a period lasting 500 years until the partitions of 1792–1795 placed Belarus within the Russian Empire for the first time. The Byelorussian SSR, formed after the Russian Revolution, became a founding republic of the Soviet Union in 1922. After the Polish-Soviet War (1918–1921) Belarus lost almost half its territory to Poland, and in the Second World War it lost about a quarter of its population and half of its economic resources. Many prominent Belarusian intellectuals were exiled or killed in Stalinist purges in the 1930s.

Belarus proclaimed its sovereignty on 27 July 1990 and gained independence on 25 August 1991. Belarus and Russia signed a treaty in 2000 forming the Union State. The official languages are Russian and Belarusian. Francysk Skaryna's Bible, published between 1517 and 1525, was the first book printed in Belarus or anywhere in Eastern Europe.
belarusians: Balts historically inhabited most of the territory of present-day Belarus, and many ancient place names there are of Baltic origin. Slavic settlement began around the 6th and 7th centuries, and the Balts were gradually absorbed, a process that ended in eastern and central Belarus around the 12th century. In the 8th and 9th centuries most of the land was held by three tribal unions, the Kryvichs, Dryhavichs and Radzimichs. The Kryvichs were the most important, and Polotsk and Smolensk, which they founded, were the chief cultural and political centres. The principalities formed there belonged to Kievan Rus'.

Beginning with Mindaugas and Gediminas, Lithuania expanded rapidly east and south, and by the mid-14th century most of modern Belarus, including Polotsk, Vitebsk, Minsk, Turov and Pinsk, belonged to the Lithuanian state. These lands kept their Orthodox Christian and East Slavic traditions, and the Ruthenian nobility took full part in Lithuania's political life. Polish influence grew after the Union of Lublin in 1569 and the Union of Brest in 1596, and Polish replaced Ruthenian in official use in the late 17th century. A modern Belarusian national identity did not yet exist.

After the Third Partition of 1795 the Russian Empire took most of these lands. In 1839 Tsar Nicholas I banned the word Belarus and replaced it with Northwestern Krai. A short-lived Belarusian Democratic Republic was declared in March 1918. By the Peace of Riga in 1921 the territory was split between the Second Polish Republic and Soviet Russia, which created the Belarusian Soviet Socialist Republic. More than two million people, about a quarter of the population, were killed in Belarus during the three years of German occupation.

Before 1991 Belarusians were known as Ruthenians, Litvins and White Ruthenians, and in the Soviet era as Byelorussians. The name White Rus' was first used in the Middle Ages for the area of Polotsk. The Republic of Belarus has existed since the Belovezha Accords ended the Soviet Union in 1991. Belarusians form the majority of its population, with minorities in Ukraine, Poland, Russia and Lithuania, and many emigrated to the United States, Brazil and Canada in the early 20th century. Most are Eastern Orthodox.
belem: Belém lies about 100 km upriver from the Atlantic Ocean, on the Pará River, which belongs to the greater Amazon River system and is separated from the larger part of the Amazon delta by Marajó Island. It is the gateway to the Amazon, with a busy port. The climate is tropical rainforest, with more than 60 mm of rain on average in every month and a wetter season from December to May. The city is called the City of Mango Trees because of the many mango trees in it, and it is named after Santa Maria de Belém in Lisbon.

In 1615 the Portuguese captain-general Francisco Caldeira Castelo Branco led a military expedition, sent by the Governor General of Brazil, to check the trading excursions of French, Dutch and English up the Amazon. On 12 January 1616 he anchored in Guajará Bay, where the Pará and Guamá rivers meet. Mistaking the bay for the main channel, he built a wooden fort covered with straw, which he called Presépio, meaning nativity scene, now known as Forte do Castelo. The colony it formed was named Feliz Lusitânia and became the beginning of Belém. The fort failed to suppress Dutch and French trading but did ward off colonisation. Belém was the first European colony on the Amazon, and was given city status in 1655.

Sugar was important in the region until the end of the 17th century, followed by cattle ranching and, in the 18th century, rice, cotton and coffee. Belém then became the main exporting centre of the Amazon rubber industry, and its position was further enhanced in 1866 when the Amazon, Tocantins and Tapajós rivers were opened to navigation, although the Port of Manaus upriver reduced its importance somewhat. The rubber era ended after the boom of 1910–12, but Belém remained the main commercial centre of northern Brazil.

Belém is the capital and largest city of the state of Pará, in northern Brazil. Its colonial quarter keeps tree-filled squares, churches and traditional blue tiles. On the second Sunday in October it holds the Círio of Nazaré, described as the largest religious event in Brazil, a procession that follows a statue of the Virgin and Child and is regarded as the Christmas of the Amazon; its river pilgrimage honours the water men, who regard the Virgin of Nazareth as their patron saint. The Federal University of Pará and the State University of Pará are in the city.
belfast: Belfast stands on the banks of the River Lagan and is connected to the open sea through Belfast Lough and the North Channel. Its name comes from the Irish Béal Feirste, "mouth of the Farset", a river whose name means a sandbar or tidal ford. The Farset flowed into the Lagan, until it was culverted in the late 18th century, along what is now High Street, and the early settlement developed at the low-water crossing near the present Queen's Bridge. The site has been occupied since at least the Neolithic, and the Giant's Ring, a 5,000-year-old henge, lies near the city.

In 1613, under a commission from King James VI, Sir Arthur Chichester undertook the Plantation of Belfast and its surroundings, building a new castle and attracting mainly English and Manx settlers. Scottish Presbyterians followed, and in 1649 an English Parliamentarian army temporarily expelled them in the town's only recorded siege. Their descendants' disaffection with Ireland's Anglican establishment contributed to the rebellion of 1798 and the union with Great Britain in 1801.

From the 1820s Belfast expanded rapidly in industry. After a cotton boom and bust it became the global leader in linen goods, earning the name Linenopolis, and shipbuilding led to heavier industry. When it was granted city status in 1888 it was the world's largest centre of linen manufacture, and by the 1900s its shipyards were building up to a quarter of all United Kingdom tonnage.

New industry drew large numbers of Catholics from rural districts to a largely Protestant town, and sectarian tensions grew. They erupted in sustained violence in 1920–22, as Belfast became the capital of the six north-eastern counties that kept the British connection.

In the spring of 1941 the German Luftwaffe attacked the city four times, damaging or destroying more than half its housing and killing more than a thousand people, the heaviest loss of life in any air raid outside London. The Troubles began in the late 1960s, and the British Army was on the streets from August 1969 in the longest continuous deployment in its history.

Belfast is the capital, largest city and main port of Northern Ireland, the second largest city on the island of Ireland after Dublin, with 345,418 people recorded in 2021. A division of working-class Protestant and Catholic districts by barriers remains a legacy of the conflict. The port still has commercial and industrial docks and a reduced Harland and Wolff shipyard, and the Titanic Quarter has been developed on former dockland. Ulster University and Queen's University Belfast are in the city.
belgian-revolution: After the defeat of Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, the Congress of Vienna combined the United Provinces of the Netherlands with the former Austrian Netherlands under the House of Orange-Nassau, creating a buffer state north of France. The southern provinces were mainly Flemish and Walloon and traditionally Catholic, while the north was dominated by the Dutch Reformed. King William I was a supporter of the German Lutheran tradition and wished to influence the appointment of bishops.

The southerners held about 62% of the population but 50% of the seats in the General Assembly. Only one minister in four was Belgian, and the administration had four times as many Dutch officials as Belgian. Grievances included state control of schools, a language reform of 1823 that favoured Dutch, a free trade policy that hurt southern industry, high unemployment and the limits on freedom of the press and assembly.

On 25 August 1830, at the Théâtre Royal de la Monnaie in Brussels, a performance of Daniel Auber's opera La Muette de Portici was followed by riots, as members of the audience joined a crowd already in the streets. Uprisings spread, factories were occupied and machinery destroyed. The Crown Prince William, sent to Brussels, was persuaded that an administrative separation of north and south was the only solution, but his father rejected it.

About 8,000 Dutch troops under Prince Frederik failed to retake Brussels in street fighting from 23 to 26 September, and many southern recruits deserted. A National Congress was summoned and a Provisional Government formed under Charles Latour Rogier. The London Conference of the five major powers, Austria, the United Kingdom, France, Prussia and Russia, eventually accepted Belgian independence, and none sent troops to aid the Dutch.

The National Congress decided on a constitutional monarchy, and the Belgian Constitution was proclaimed on 7 February 1831. It refused any candidate from the House of Orange-Nassau and eventually offered the throne to Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, who took his oath as king on 21 July 1831, the date now kept as Belgian National Day.

On 2 August 1831 William invaded in the Ten Days' Campaign and defeated the Belgian army at Hasselt, but French troops under Marshal Étienne Maurice Gérard crossed the border on 9 August, and the Dutch agreed to an armistice. The Treaty of London of 19 April 1839 recognised Belgium as independent and neutral, with half of Luxembourg and Limburg. A movement for reunion with the Netherlands, Orangism, was active in Flanders and Brussels and was banned from public expression in 1834.
belgium: Belgium covers 30,689 square kilometres in the Low Countries, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, France and the North Sea. It has three main geographical regions: the coastal plain in the northwest, with sand dunes and polders; the central plateau, a slowly rising landscape of fertile valleys and the sandy plain of the Campine; and the forested, rugged Ardennes in the southeast. The highest point is the Signal de Botrange, at 694 metres. The climate is maritime temperate, with significant precipitation in all seasons.

In his account of the conquest of Gaul, Julius Caesar described the Belgae as inhabiting northern Gaul between the Seine and Marne rivers and the Rhine, and as the bravest of the Gauls. The northernmost tribes, including the Menapii, Nervii and Atuatuci, held most of modern Belgium. After Caesar's conquests the Roman province of Gallia Belgica covered most of northern Gaul, and the eastern part of modern Belgium lay in Germania Inferior. As Roman central government collapsed, the provinces were inhabited by Romanised populations and Germanic-speaking Franks, who came to dominate military and political life.

The region was later part of the Carolingian Empire, the Holy Roman Empire and the Burgundian Netherlands, and was ruled by Habsburg Spain (1556–1714), the Austrian Habsburgs (1714–1794) and Revolutionary France (1794–1815). Most of it joined the United Kingdom of the Netherlands after the Congress of Vienna in 1815. Being contested by so many powers gave Belgium the name the Battlefield of Europe.

An independent Belgium was established in 1830 after the Belgian Revolution. It was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, and mining and steelmaking in Liège Province and around Charleroi made it one of the three most industrialised nations in the world from 1830 to 1910, although Flanders suffered famine from 1846 to 1850.

Belgium is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a federal state of three regions, Flanders, Wallonia and the Brussels-Capital Region, with Dutch-speaking, French-speaking and small German-speaking communities. Tensions between Dutch-speakers and French-speakers rose in the second half of the twentieth century and led to reforms that turned a unitary state into a federal one between 1970 and 1993. After the 2010 federal election the country went a record 589 days without forming a government. Brussels hosts the seats of several European Union institutions, and the country's colonies, the Belgian Congo and Ruanda-Urundi, became independent between 1960 and 1962.
belgrade: Belgrade lies 116.75 m above sea level at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers, at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkan Peninsula. Its historical core, Kalemegdan, stands on the right banks of both rivers. Since the 19th century the city has expanded to the south and east, and after World War II New Belgrade was built on the left bank of the Sava, connecting Belgrade with Zemun. The name in Serbian, Beograd, means White City.

Chipped stone tools found in Zemun show that nomadic foragers lived around Belgrade in the Palaeolithic and Mesolithic eras. The first farmers belonged to the Neolithic Starčevo culture, which flourished between 6200 and 5200 BCE, and the Vinča culture (5500-4500 BCE) grew out of their settlements and is known for very large settlements. In antiquity Thraco-Dacians inhabited the region, and after 279 BCE Celts settled the city and named it Singidūn. The Romans conquered it under Augustus and awarded it city rights in the mid-2nd century.

Slavs settled the city in the 520s. It then changed hands several times between the Byzantine Empire, the Frankish Empire, the Bulgarian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary before becoming the seat of the Serbian king Stefan Dragutin in 1284. It was the capital of the Serbian Despotate under Stefan Lazarević, and his successor Đurađ Branković returned it to the Hungarian king in 1427. Noon bells rung in support of the Hungarian army during the siege of 1456 against the Ottoman Empire remain a widespread church tradition.

After the Serbian Revolution Belgrade was named capital of Serbia again in 1841. Northern Belgrade remained the southernmost Habsburg post until 1918, when former Austro-Hungarian territories joined the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Belgrade was the capital of Yugoslavia from its creation to its dissolution. Placed in a strategic position, it has been battled over in 115 wars and razed 44 times, and has been bombed five times and besieged many times.

Belgrade is the capital and largest city of Serbia and the seat of its central government. The 2022 census counted 1,197,114 people in the city proper and 1,682,720 in its administrative area. The University of Belgrade, founded in 1808 as the Velika škola, is the oldest institution of higher learning in Serbia. The author Ivo Andrić wrote The Bridge on the Drina in the city, and it hosted the first Non-Aligned Movement Summit in 1961.
belisarius: Belisarius was born around 500, probably in Germaneia, a fortified town within the borders of Thrace and Paeonia. His ancestry is unknown. By 526 he was a senior guardsman of Justinian, nephew of Emperor Justin I, though how he reached that post is unrecorded. In the war against Persia over Iberia his early record was mixed: he and Sittas raided Persian territory, but he lost his first independent command, fled with his troops at Tanurin after his colleagues were lured into a trap, and lost at Mindouos. He was promoted soon after, so he was probably not held to blame.

During the Nika riots of 532, in which the Blues and Greens rose against Justinian and declared Hypatius emperor, Belisarius, Mundus and Narses were called in. Belisarius led his troops into the crowd in the Hippodrome while Narses blocked the other exits, and the revolt ended in a massacre in which between 30,000 and 60,000 people died, mostly unarmed civilians.

In June 533 Belisarius sailed for North Africa with about 17,000 soldiers and a fleet, against the Vandal king Gelimer, who had deposed Justinian's guest friend Hilderic in 530. He landed at Caput Vada rather than at Carthage, defeated the Vandals at Ad Decimum and took Carthage, and Gelimer was compelled to surrender after Tricamarum. In 535 Justinian sent him against the Ostrogoths in Italy. He took Sicily, entering Syracuse on 31 December 535, and from March 537 to March 538 held Rome against the far larger army of Vitiges. By late 539 he had surrounded Ravenna.

In 559 Justinian called him from retirement to meet the Kutrigur Bulgars under Khan Zabergan, who had crossed the Danube and approached Constantinople. With 300 veterans and a host of civilians he camped near them, had a trench dug and many torches lit to exaggerate his numbers, and placed his men in a narrow defile where the Kutrigurs could not use their numbers.

In 562 Belisarius was tried in Constantinople on a charge of conspiring against Justinian, found guilty and put under house arrest, but he was soon pardoned and restored to favour. He died in March 565. A later legend that he was blinded and reduced to begging near the Pincian Gate of Rome is thought apocryphal by most modern scholars. Procopius's Secret History, whose reliability is debated, portrays him as a cuckolded husband dependent on his wife Antonina, and recent work reads that portrait as invective. Historians generally rate him highly, chiefly for Dara, Ad Decimum and Tricamarum.
belize-city: Belize City stands at the mouth of Haulover Creek, a distributary of the Belize River, which empties into the Caribbean Sea eight kilometres from the city. The city proper is usually divided into two areas: Northside, bounded by Haulover Creek and ending in the east at the Fort George area, and Southside, which includes downtown and the port. Four bridges, among them the Swing Bridge at Market Square, link the divisions, and the main canals are Haulover Creek, Burdon Canal and Collet Canal. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a long wet season from May through February, and the city is susceptible to flooding in the rainy season.

The city was founded as Belize Town in 1638 by English lumber harvesters, on the site of a small Maya settlement called Holzuz. The place suited the English as a central post because it was on the sea and was a natural outlet for the local rivers and creeks down which they shipped logwood and mahogany. It also became the home of the thousands of African slaves brought in by the English, and later the British from 1707, to work in the forestry industry.

Belize Town was the coordination site for the Battle of St. George's Caye in 1798, which the British won against would-be invaders, and the home of the local courts and government officials until the 1970s. For this reason historians often say that the capital was the colony, since the centre of British control lay there. Antonio Soberanis Gómez, George Price and Evan X Hyde all lobbied to take their movements outside the city, but people continued to look to it for guidance.

Belize City was directly struck by hurricanes in 1931 and 1961, and fires have burnt out stretches of housing at various times. Hurricane Hattie swept ashore in October 1961 and almost entirely destroyed the city. The government was moved to the new capital, Belmopan, in 1970.

Belize City is the largest city in Belize, with a population of 63,999 at the 2022 census, and it is the country's principal port and its financial and industrial hub. It has branches of all the major banks and the Central Bank, and the Supreme Court of Belize still sits there.

St John's Cathedral, begun in 1812 and completed in 1820 of orange bricks that came on British ships as ballast, is the oldest Anglican church in Central America and the only Anglican cathedral outside England where kings have been crowned.
bella-ciao: The origins of the song are unclear. One hypothesis is that it began as Alla mattina appena alzata, sung with different words by the seasonal workers of the rice fields of Italy's Po Valley from the late 19th century to the first half of the 20th. The work, weeding the flooded fields from the end of April to the beginning of June, was done mainly by women called mondine, recruited from the poorest classes, who spent the day barefoot in water up to their knees. Poor conditions, long hours and low pay led to discontent and, at times, riots in the early 20th century. The earliest written version, dated 1906, comes from near Vercelli in Piedmont.
A possible source for the melody is a Yiddish tune, the Koilen song, recorded in 1919 in New York by the klezmer accordionist Mishka Ziganoff, according to the researcher Fausto Giovannardi.

As a partisan song, Bella ciao is dedicated to the fighters of the Italian Resistance against Nazi German occupation and the collaborationist fascist forces. Its place in the war itself is disputed. There is no documentary trace of the partisan version before its text was first published in 1953 in the magazine La Lapa, and then in L'Unità in 1957, and it is absent from important songbooks of the time. The partisan and journalist Giorgio Bocca said he never heard it sung in twenty months of the partisan war, and historians such as Antonio Virgilio Savona and Michele Straniero agree that it became popular only after the war. A few, including Cesare Bermani and Ruggero Giacomini, claim that some version was sung by some brigades.

The song spread after Yves Montand recorded it in 1963 and the group Il Nuovo Canzoniere Italiano presented it at the Festival dei Due Mondi at Spoleto in 1964, as both a song of the mondine and a partisan hymn. Its message was inclusive enough to hold together the currents of the Resistance, Catholic, Communist, Socialist and Liberal, and it was sung at the end of the Christian Democracy congress of 1975. Many singers have recorded it, among them Milva, Quilapayún, Mary Hopkin, Sandie Shaw and Manu Chao, in dozens of languages. It has come to stand for liberation from tyranny in many places.
bellerophon: Bellerophon, a hero of Corinth, was in most accounts the son of Poseidon and the mortal Eurynome and the foster son of Glaukos. His earlier name was Hipponous, or in another version Leophontes. The name Bellerophon is explained as meaning slayer of Belleros: according to the Scholia of Homer, he killed a Corinthian citizen of that name by accident while practising knife-throwing, and was exiled. In another account he murdered his own brother. In the Iliad, however, his grandson Glaucus tells the story and names the hero's father as Glaucus, king of Potniae and son of Sisyphus.

To atone for the killing he sought out Proetus, king of Tiryns, who cleansed him. Proetus's wife, Anteia or Stheneboea, made advances to him, and when he refused her she accused him of making advances to her. Proetus would not kill a guest and instead sent Bellerophon to his father-in-law Iobates in Lycia, carrying a sealed tablet asking that the bearer be put to death.

Iobates feasted Bellerophon for nine days before reading the tablet. Fearing the Erinyes if he killed a guest, he sent him to kill the Chimera, a fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, a goat's body and a serpent's tail. The seer Polyeidos told him that he would need the winged horse Pegasus. Bellerophon slept in the temple of Athena and found a golden bridle beside him on waking. He caught Pegasus as it drank at the spring of Pirene at Corinth. Unable to wound the Chimera, he mounted a block of lead on his spear and thrust it into the creature's throat, where its fiery breath melted the lead and suffocated it.

Iobates then set further tasks. Bellerophon defeated the Amazons by dropping boulders from Pegasus, and in some versions the Solymi before them. He killed the men sent to ambush him. When Poseidon flooded the plain behind him, the women of the palace came out and bared themselves, and he withdrew. Iobates relented, showed him the letter and gave him his daughter Philonoe and half his kingdom. She bore him Isander, Hippolochus and Laodamia. In one version he took revenge on Stheneboea by taking her up on Pegasus and throwing her into the sea off Milos.

As his fame grew, so did his pride, and he sought to fly to Olympus on Pegasus. Zeus sent a gadfly to sting the horse, and Bellerophon fell to earth and died, while Pegasus reached Olympus and carried Zeus's thunderbolts. In other accounts he was blinded by a thorn bush and lived out his life in misery on the Plain of Aleion in Cilicia. Euripides wrote a tragedy, Bellerophon, of which about thirty quotations survive. Its passage doubting the gods' existence apparently led Aristophanes to accuse the poet of atheism.
belmopan: Belmopan stands in Cayo District, 76 metres above sea level, just east of the Belize River and about 80 km inland from the Caribbean coast. It lies near the Belize River Valley with a view of the foothills of the Mountain Pine Ridge. The name joins two words: Belize, the name of the longest river in the country, and Mopan, one of the rivers of the area, which empties into the Belize River.

Hurricane Hattie in 1961 destroyed about 75 per cent of the houses and business premises in low-lying, coastal Belize City. The government proposed a new capital on better terrain, which would need no costly reclamation of land and would have room for an industrial area, and in 1962 a committee chose the site now called Belmopan. In 1964, when Belize was the British colony of British Honduras, Premier George Cadle Price led a delegation to London to seek funds. The British government did not commit itself but saw the logic of a capital on high ground safe from storm surges.

The site was dedicated by Lord Greenwood, the Secretary of State for the Commonwealth and Colonies, on 9 October 1965. The estimated cost was 40 million Belize dollars, but only 20 million were available. Work began in 1967, and the first phase was completed in 1970 at a cost of 24 million. The government moved there in 1970, and until 2000 the Reconstruction and Development Corporation, known as Recondev, ran the city. Foreign governments were at first reluctant to move their embassies, and the British High Commission opened in 1981, when British Honduras became independent as Belize.

Belmopan is the capital of Belize and the second-largest settlement in the country after Belize City, with 20,754 inhabitants in 2022, which makes it the smallest capital city in the continental Americas by population. The city is laid out around the Ring Road, just under 4 km in circumference, with most government buildings within or around it. The National Assembly Building, of grey stone with broad steps, is designed to resemble a Maya temple.
belozersk: Belozersk lies on the southern bank of Lake Beloye, from which it takes its name, 214 kilometres north-west of Vologda. Until 1777 it was known as Beloozero, meaning white lake. On several occasions the settlement was moved from one bank of the lake to the other. The Belozersky Canal, part of the Volga–Baltic Waterway, passes through the town, bypassing the lake to the south.

The Primary Chronicle first mentions Beloozero in 862, among several towns that later became part of Kievan Rus', and says that Rurik's brother Sineus became its prince. Sineus and his brother Truvor most likely never existed. In the 11th century the region was inhabited mainly by Finnic peoples who resisted Christianization. In 1071 local pagan priests rose in rebellion and were put down by the Kievan commander Yan Vyshatich. From the 10th to the 13th century the territory was controlled by the Novgorod Republic.

Beloozero was the seat of a small principality, governed by the Belosselsky-Belozersky princes, between 1238 and the 1370s, and between 1380 and 1384 it became subordinate to the Grand Duchy of Moscow. On 10 July 1612 Polish and Lithuanian raiders known as the Lisowczycy captured the town without a fight and looted it. Under the reform of Peter the Great in 1708 it joined the Ingermanland Governorate, and in 1727 it became the seat of Belozersk Province in the Novgorod Governorate.

In June 1918 Belozersky Uyezd was placed in the new Cherepovets Governorate. In 1927 the uyezds were abolished and Belozersky District was created, and in 1937 the district was transferred to the newly established Vologda Oblast.

Belozersk is the administrative centre of Belozersky District in Vologda Oblast and had 8,464 inhabitants in the census of 2021. Its economy rests on the timber and food industries. The Ministry of Culture of Russia classifies it as a historical town. The monuments of the centre include the Assumption Church of 1552, the Transfiguration Cathedral of 1668 and the wooden shrine of St. Elijah of 1690, and the neighbourhood has old monasteries, among them Kirillo-Belozersky and Ferapontov. Two medieval icons, the Virgin of the White Lake and Saints Peter and Paul, were made in the town in the 13th century.
belvedere-vienna: The Belvedere stands in Vienna's third district, Landstraße, and consists of two Baroque palaces, the Upper and Lower Belvedere, with an Orangery, stables and a formal garden. It was built when Vienna was the imperial capital of the Habsburg monarchy, after Prince Eugene of Savoy's successful campaigns against the Ottoman Empire. On 30 November 1697 Eugene bought a plot south of the Rennweg and chose Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt as chief architect rather than Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach. Dominique Girard, who had trained at Versailles, laid out the gardens in the formal French manner over three terraces, with sculpture linking Eugene to the god Apollo.

The Lower Belvedere served as a Lustschloss, a pleasure palace tied closely to the gardens. Marcantonio Chiarini of Bologna began painting the quadratura in its central hall in 1715. The Upper Belvedere was begun in the late 1710s and finished in 1723, conceived less as a private residence than as a building for ceremonies, receptions and display. Eugene received the Turkish ambassador Ibrahim Pasha there in 1719, while the interior was still being decorated. Carlo Innocenzo Carlone painted the ceiling fresco of the Marble Hall between 1721 and 1723.

Prince Eugene died on 21 April 1736 without a legally binding will, and his niece Maria Anna Victoria of Savoy inherited the estate and soon tried to sell it. Maria Theresa bought it in 1752. In 1776 she and Joseph II decided to move the Imperial Picture Gallery to the Upper Belvedere to make the imperial collection accessible to the public. It is often described as one of the world's first public art museums, with the opening dated to 1777 or 1781. The Moderne Galerie opened in the Lower Belvedere in 1903, and on 15 May 1955 the Austrian State Treaty was signed at the Upper Belvedere. The Upper Belvedere holds a major group of works by Gustav Klimt, including The Kiss.
ben-jonson: Jonson was born in June 1572, possibly on the 11th, in or near London. His father, a Protestant who had lost his property and been imprisoned under Queen Mary, became a clergyman after his release and died a month before his son's birth; what is known of him comes from the poet's own account. His widow married a master bricklayer two years later. A family friend paid for his studies at Westminster School, where the antiquarian William Camden was one of his masters; their friendship and Camden's wide scholarship left a lasting mark on Jonson's style until Camden's death in 1623.

A play he wrote with Thomas Nashe, The Isle of Dogs, was suppressed in 1597 after causing great offence, and Jonson was jailed in Marshalsea Prison. In 1598 he killed the actor Gabriel Spenser in a duel on 22 September and was imprisoned in Newgate; he pleaded guilty to manslaughter but was released by benefit of clergy, forfeiting his goods and being branded on the left thumb.

His public plays were mainly comedies, among them Every Man in His Humour, Volpone, The Alchemist and Bartholomew Fair; his two tragedies, Sejanus and Catiline, largely failed to impress audiences. His comedies show a keen eye for absurdity and hypocrisy. When James VI and I came to the throne in 1603 he quickly adapted to the demand for masques and entertainments encouraged by the king and Anne of Denmark, and enjoyed the patronage of Elizabeth Sidney and Lady Mary Wroth, which led to his country house poem To Penshurst.

According to a contemporary letter, Jonson died in London on 18 August 1637, and his funeral was attended by all or the greater part of the nobility then in town.
