He is buried in the north aisle of the nave of Westminster Abbey, with the inscription O Rare Ben Johnson over his grave; John Aubrey records that a passer-by, John Young, paid a workman eighteen pence to cut it. The upright burial was taken as a sign of his reduced circumstances.

Younger poets such as Robert Herrick, Richard Lovelace and Sir John Suckling called themselves the Sons or Tribe of Ben. After the Restoration his comedies and his theory of humour characters were the blueprint for many Restoration comedies, and his work, with Shakespeare's and Fletcher's, formed the core of the repertory when the theatres reopened. He has been called the first poet laureate, and many critics since the 18th century have ranked him below only Shakespeare among English Renaissance dramatists. Of Shakespeare he wrote in Timber that he was not of an age, but for all time.
benazir-bhutto: Benazir Bhutto was born on 21 June 1953 in Karachi, the eldest of four children of the barrister and politician Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and Begum Nusrat Ispahani, who was born in Isfahan of Persian and Kurdish descent. The Bhuttos were wealthy landlords from Sindh. From 1969 to 1973 she studied at Radcliffe College, entering at sixteen, and graduated cum laude in comparative government. She then studied at the University of Oxford, where she became President of the Oxford Union.

In 1977 her father was ousted in a military coup and later executed. Benazir and her mother took control of the Pakistan People's Party and led the Movement for the Restoration of Democracy. She was repeatedly imprisoned by Zia-ul-Haq's military government and lived in self-exile in Britain from 1984, returning in 1986. She chaired the party from 1982 until her death and moved its platform from socialist to liberal. After Zia died in an air crash in August 1988, she led the party to victory and became Pakistan's first female prime minister.

Her attempts at reform were stifled by conservative and Islamist forces, including President Ghulam Ishaq Khan and the military, and her administration, accused of corruption and nepotism, was dismissed in 1990. She was sworn in again on 19 October 1993, after the party won 86 seats. In this term she established a Ministry of Women's Development and a Women's Development Bank and sought to privatise industries nationalised in the 1970s. Her brother Murtaza was killed, and on 5 November 1996 President Farooq Leghari dismissed her government on grounds of corruption and incompetence.

She lived in exile between Dubai and London from 1998 and was convicted by a Swiss court in 2003. She returned to Pakistan in October 2007, after negotiations with President Pervez Musharraf, to contest the 2008 elections.

On 27 December 2007 she spoke at a party rally in Rawalpindi's Liaquat National Bagh. As she left in a bulletproof vehicle and stood up through its escape hatch to wave, a man fired three shots and detonated a suicide vest. Twenty-two others also died. She was buried beside her father at Garhi Khuda Bakhsh. Al-Qaeda claimed responsibility, though other involvement was also suggested. Opinions of her were deeply divided: critics called her inexperienced and corrupt, and Islamist and conservative forces opposed her secularist, modernising agenda. After her death she came to be regarded as an icon for women's rights.
bendigo: Bendigo, formerly known as Sandhurst, lies in the Bendigo Valley in north-central Victoria, near the geographical centre of the state and about 150 kilometres north-west of Melbourne. The Dja Dja Wurrung (Djaara) people are the traditional owners of the area, which they called Leanganook. They used its rich hunting grounds. The city is surrounded by parts of the Greater Bendigo National Park and by the Bendigo Box-Ironbark Region, an Important Bird Area identified for swift parrots and other woodland birds. Its climate is dry and temperate, with warm, variable summers and cool, cloudy winters.

White settlers established the first of a number of vast sheep runs in 1837 and displaced the Dja Dja Wurrung, who experienced two waves of settlement and dispossession, from the south from 1837 and from the north from 1845. Introduced animals also rooted up the nutritious moon-nar tuber, the yam daisy, which became scarce within a year.

Gold was officially discovered in October 1851, just after the finds at neighbouring Castlemaine, and some diggers moved from there, bringing the population to 40,000 in less than a year. A number of them were Chinese, and their descendants still live in the region. The discovery on Bendigo Creek turned a sheep station into one of colonial Australia's largest boomtowns, intensified the Victorian gold rush and drew migrants from around the world, particularly Europe and China. In 1852 William Swan Urquhart surveyed the goldfields under the Surveyor General of Victoria, Robert Hoddle. From 1853 to 1891 the town was officially named Sandhurst.

Bendigo was declared a city in 1871. Its rapid growth caused a water shortage, partly solved by a viaduct from the Coliban River. The architect William Charles Vahland left a mark on it, designing more than 80 buildings, among them the Alexandra Fountain, and giving his name to a popular cottage design. A tram network existed by 1890. The boom lasted until the early 20th century, and after a temporary decline in population and employment, growth resumed from the 1930s as Bendigo became a manufacturing and regional service centre.

The wealth of the gold rush is reflected in the city's late Victorian colonial architecture. Several buildings are on the Victorian Heritage Register, including the Bendigo Town Hall, the Old Post Office and the Old Bendigo Law Courts, which are in the Second Empire style. Sacred Heart Cathedral, completed in 1977, is the largest church building in provincial Australia. The Bendigo Art Gallery is one of Australia's oldest and largest regional art galleries. Tourism centres on the gold-rush history, with attractions such as the Central Deborah Gold Mine, the Bendigo Tramways and the Golden Dragon Museum. The first women's cricket match in Australia was played in Bendigo in 1871.
benedict-xiv: Prospero Lambertini was born into a noble family of Bologna, the third of five children of Marcello Lambertini and Lucrezia Bulgarini. At thirteen he began attending the Collegio Clementino in Rome, where he studied rhetoric, Latin, philosophy and theology, and he often read the works of Thomas Aquinas, his favourite author. In 1694, at nineteen, he received the degrees of Doctor of Sacred Theology and of both ecclesiastical and civil law.

As Promoter of the Faith from 1708 he secured the canonization of Pope Pius V and wrote a treatise on the process of beatification and canonization of saints. Created a cardinal in 1726, he was named Archbishop of Bologna in 1731 and wrote there a three-volume treatise on the diocesan synod, De synodo dioecesana.

After Clement XII died in February 1740 the conclave lasted six months. Lambertini arrived late and was not among the favourites of any faction; he was put forward as a compromise and is reported to have said, 'If you wish to elect a saint, choose Gotti; a statesman, Aldrovandi; an honest man, me.' He was elected on the 255th ballot on 17 August 1740.

His pontificate began amid disputes with Catholic rulers over their demand to nominate bishops, and he settled the quarrels of the Holy See with Naples, Sardinia, Spain, Venice and Austria. The papal government was heavily in debt, by 56,000,000 scudi, and he cut the army and the pay of its officers and soldiers, though the administration still ran a deficit at his death. He encouraged agriculture and free trade, revived anatomical studies at the University of Bologna and added about 3,300 of his own books to the Vatican Library.

On 22 December 1741 the bull Immensa Pastorum Principis excommunicated anyone who enslaved the indigenous peoples of Brazil, though it went unenforced. In the bulls Ex quo singulari of 1742 and Omnium sollicitudinum of 1744 he condemned the accommodation of Chinese and Indian customs by the Jesuit missions, and many converts left the Church.

Benedict XIV had suffered from kidney problems for years. After a battle with gout he died on 3 May 1758, at the age of 83, lucid to the end, and was buried in Saint Peter's Basilica. He was noted for his modesty and humour and was also an avid gambler who used profane language.

His intellectualism and advocacy of science education earned him the nickname the Enlightenment Pope. Horace Walpole described him as a pope without nepotism and an author without vanity, a man whom neither intellect nor power could corrupt.
benevento: Benevento stands on a hill 130 metres above sea level at the confluence of the Calore and the Sabato rivers in Campania. As Maleventum it was one of the chief cities of Samnium, on the Appian Way 51 kilometres east of Capua. Ancient writers ascribed its foundation to Diomedes after the Trojan War, a legend its inhabitants adopted, and in the time of Procopius they claimed to display the tusks of the Calydonian Boar as proof. Another tradition names Auson, a son of Ulysses and Circe, as founder.

The city first appears in history as a Samnite town, strong enough that the Romans did not attack it in their first two wars with the Samnites. Its theatre, completed under Caracalla between 200 and 210, reflects its growing importance after the Via Appia Traiana opened. After Totila sacked it and razed its walls in 545, Benevento became the seat of a powerful Lombard duchy, whose creation is disputed. Arechis I, who died in 640, captured Capua and Crotone. After his reign the Eastern Roman Empire held only Naples, Amalfi, Gaeta, Sorrento, the tip of Calabria and the maritime cities of Apulia in the south.

Benevento passed peacefully to the papacy when Emperor Henry III ceded it to Leo IX in exchange for the pope's consent to the founding of the Diocese of Bamberg. In 1806 Napoleon gave the principality to Talleyrand, who never ruled it, and in 1815 it returned to the papacy. It was united with Italy in 1860. A Jewish community lived there from at least the fifth century, and was expelled in 1569 under Paul IV.

Benevento is the capital of its province and the seat of an archbishop. Its Lombard church of Santa Sofia, a circular building of about 760, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2011 as one of seven buildings called Longobards in Italy. The Arch of Trajan, the Roman theatre and the castle called the Rocca dei Rettori also survive. Allied bombing in the summer of 1943 killed 2,000 people, destroyed half the town and almost all of the cathedral, which was rebuilt by 1965.
bengaluru: Bengaluru lies in the south-east of Karnataka on the Mysore Plateau, part of the Deccan Plateau, at an average elevation of 900 m. The topography is generally flat, with small hills of granite and gneiss to the south. No major river runs through the city, though six rivers rise at the Nandi Hills about 60 km to the north, and most of its water comes from the Kaveri. Because of its elevation the climate is moderate, with distinct wet and dry seasons. The city is known as India's Garden City because of its parks and greenery.

Stone Age artefacts indicate human settlement around 4000 BCE, and Roman coins of the first century CE show that the region took part in trans-oceanic trade. The earliest known reference to the name Bengaluru is an Old Kannada hero stone of 890 CE at Begur. In 1537 Kempe Gowda I, a local chieftain aligned with the Vijayanagara Empire, built a mud-brick fort that became the centre of the modern city. He divided the town into pētēs and built tanks such as Kempambudhi for water storage. In 1638 an Adil Shahi army defeated Kempe Gowda III, and the Mughals later sold the city to the Maharaja of Mysore. Hyder Ali seized the kingdom after 1759, and the city passed to his son Tipu Sultan.

After the Anglo-Mysore Wars the city returned to the Maharaja of Mysore, and in 1809 the British formed a military garrison and set up the cantonment outside the old city. By the late 19th century Bengaluru was essentially two cities, the Pete and the Cantonment. A plague epidemic in 1898 claimed nearly 3,500 lives and led to better sanitation. The two settlements merged under one urban administration in 1949, and the city became the capital of Mysore State, renamed Karnataka in 1973.

Bengaluru is the capital and largest city of Karnataka, with 8.4 million inhabitants at the 2011 census. Its official name was Bangalore until 1 November 2014. Kannada is the official language of the state and the mother tongue of 42.1 percent of the city's people at that census, and many other languages are spoken. The city was among the first in India to have electric power, in 1905. Lal Bagh, established in the 1760s, is a botanical garden of 97 hectares with a glass house of 1889 modelled on the Crystal Palace in London.
benguela: Benguela was founded in 1617 as São Felipe de Benguela by the Portuguese under Manuel Cerveira Pereira, who had been the eighth governor of Angola from 1604 to 1607. It was long the centre of an important trade, especially in slaves sent to Brazil and Cuba. Ships anchored about 1.6 kilometres off the shore, in depths of 7 to 11 metres, and transferred their loads to smaller boats that used five or six jetties in the town. The nearby sheltered deep-water harbour of Lobito was a much larger port.

Besides the churches of São Felipe and S. António, the hospital and the fortress, there were only a few stone-built houses in 1911. A short way beyond the town is Baía Farta, where salt was made and sulphur extracted.

In the early 20th century Portugal built the Benguela Railway to link the city and Lobito with the interior, and it was highly successful once connected to the Copperbelt of Katanga in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. The sisal and fishing industries expanded, and the financial, construction and service markets boomed until 1974. Angola became independent in 1975, after the Carnation Revolution of April 1974 in Lisbon. The Angolan Civil War, which lasted from 1975 to 2002, closed the railway except for the 30 kilometres between Benguela and Lobito. In 1983 the city had a population of 155,000, and it grew as refugees came in from the countryside. Restoration of the railway between Benguela and Huambo began in the mid-2000s.

Benguela is the capital of Benguela Province in western Angola and has a population of 555,124 in the city, according to the 2014 census. Its Umbundu name is Luombaka. It remains an important commercial link between western and eastern Angola, trading coffee, corn, sisal, sugarcane, tobacco and manganese from the interior. Local industries include fish processing and sugarcane milling, and the city also produces pottery, soap and tools. Foreign trade passes through the deep-water port of Lobito, 29 kilometres to the north. The Universidade Katyavala Bwila was founded in 2009.
benin-city: The indigenous people of Benin City are the Edo, also called the Benin people, who speak the Edo or Bini language. By tradition they were first ruled by kings called the Ogiso, who named the land Igodomigodo, and the elders later asked Oduduwa of Ife to rule. He sent his son Oranmiyan, whose son Eweka I became the first Oba of the present line; Yoruba and Edo traditions differ on details but agree that Oduduwa sent Oranmiyan to found the Oba dynasty. The city was called Ubinu, which the Portuguese took as Benin, and around 1470 Ewuare changed the name of the state to Edo.

The Portuguese reached Benin City about 1485. The city grew rich in the 16th and 17th centuries through trade within southern Nigeria and with Europeans, mostly in pepper and ivory. In the early 16th century the Oba sent an ambassador to Lisbon, and the King of Portugal sent Christian missionaries. A Portuguese captain, Lourenco Pinto, described it in 1691 as larger than Lisbon, with straight streets and a richly decorated royal palace. In a letter of 1701 or 1702 the Dutch East India Company merchant David van Nyendael called it a mere village of half-ruined houses, though he praised the palace with its turreted roofs decorated with brass snakes.

On 17 February 1897 British forces captured, sacked and burnt Benin City. The force of 1,200, under Admiral Sir Harry Rawson, acted after all but two men of a British delegation led by Acting Consul General James Robert Phillips had been ambushed and killed. The capture paved the way for British colonisation, and the monarchy was permitted to return in 1914, with real power in colonial hands. The Benin Bronzes, portrait figures and groups of brass, ivory and iron, were looted from the palace, and some were auctioned to meet the expedition's costs; most are now in museums abroad.

Benin City is the capital and largest city of Edo State in southern Nigeria, and it was the fourth-largest city in Nigeria in the 2006 census. It became capital of the Mid-Western Region in 1963, of Bendel State in 1976 and of Edo State in 1991. Its monarchy is one of the oldest still continuing in the world, and its attractions include the Oba Palace, the National Museum, Igun Street, known for bronze casting, and the remains of the Benin moats.
benito-juarez: Benito Pablo Juárez García was born on 21 March 1806 in the village of San Pablo Guelatao, Oaxaca, in New Spain, a settlement of about two hundred people. He came from a poor rural Indigenous family and was orphaned as a child. At the age of 12 he moved to Oaxaca City, where he worked as a domestic servant.

His employer, a lay Franciscan, sponsored him, and he enrolled for a time in a seminary before switching to law, becoming active in liberal politics. As a lawyer he took cases of Indigenous villagers and was imprisoned after helping villagers of Loxicha accuse a priest of abuses. He sat in the Oaxaca state legislature from 1832, married Margarita Maza on 31 October 1843, and later became governor of Oaxaca.

After the Plan of Ayutla ousted Antonio López de Santa Anna, President Juan Álvarez made Juárez his Minister of Justice. He was instrumental in the Juárez Law, part of the reforms known as La Reforma, which ended the separate courts of clerics and soldiers. As head of the Supreme Court he succeeded to the presidency when Ignacio Comonfort resigned early in the Reform War, and he led the Liberals to victory after three years. Liberal troops entered Mexico City on Christmas Day 1860.

The Second French Intervention followed at once. French troops took Puebla on 17 May 1863 and entered Mexico City on 10 June 1863, and Juárez moved his government north to San Luis Potosí, Monterrey and Chihuahua City. The Second Mexican Empire collapsed after the last French troops left on 12 March 1867. Maximilian and his generals were captured at Querétaro on 14 May 1867, and Juárez re-entered the capital on 15 July.

In his last years Juárez faced opposition from Liberals who thought him autocratic. He stood for re-election in 1871, and when he lacked the required majority, Congress decided for him on 12 October 1871. Porfirio Díaz rebelled against him in the Plan de la Noria. Juárez died of a heart attack in 1872 and was given a state funeral.

He is seen as a symbol of Mexican nationalism and resistance to foreign intervention, and his policies favoured civil liberties, equality before the law and the authority of civilian power over the Church and the army. After his death the city of Oaxaca added "de Juárez" to its name, and his birthday, 21 March, is a national holiday.
benito-mussolini: Benito Amilcare Andrea Mussolini was born on 29 July 1883 in Dovia di Predappio, in Romagna. His father, Alessandro, was a blacksmith and socialist, and his mother, Rosa Maltoni, a devout Catholic schoolteacher. He was named after the Mexican president Benito Juárez, and his middle names honoured the Italian socialists Amilcare Cipriani and Andrea Costa. He became a journalist for the Italian Socialist Party newspaper Avanti! and was expelled for advocating military intervention in the First World War. He served in the army from 1915 until wounded in 1917, and during the war turned to nationalism.

On 23 March 1919 Mussolini founded the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in Milan, often considered the world's first fascist movement. It became the National Fascist Party in 1921, and after fascist militants marched on Rome King Victor Emmanuel III appointed him prime minister in 1922. He founded the secret police OVRA in 1927, outlawed strikes and, through measures such as the Acerbo Law, turned a parliamentary democracy into a one-party state. By the end of 1925 press censorship had tightened and appointed podestàs had replaced elected mayors. He signed the Lateran Treaty in 1929, establishing Vatican City, and ordered the Pacification of Libya, which some scholars characterise as a genocide.

His invasion of Ethiopia brought condemnation from the League of Nations, which isolated Italy and pushed him towards Adolf Hitler and the Rome-Berlin Axis of 1936. The Pact of Steel followed in 1939. In June 1940, believing a German victory imminent, he joined the Second World War on Germany's side.

After defeats and the Allied landing in Sicily, the Grand Council of Fascism voted the Grandi motion, and in July 1943 the king dismissed Mussolini and placed him in custody. After the armistice of September 1943 German forces rescued him, and Hitler made him figurehead of the Italian Social Republic, a collaborationist puppet state in German-occupied northern Italy. In April 1945 he and his mistress Clara Petacci tried to flee to Switzerland, were captured by communist partisans and were summarily executed on 28 April 1945.
benjamin-constant: Henri-Benjamin Constant de Rebecque was born in Lausanne on 25 October 1767, into a family descended from French Huguenots who had fled to Switzerland. His mother died soon after his birth, and his father was a high-ranking officer in the Dutch States Army. He studied at the University of Erlangen and the University of Edinburgh. In Paris he met the Dutch woman of letters Isabelle de Charrière, with whom he wrote an epistolary novel. In September 1794 he met Germaine de Staël, and their collaboration between 1795 and 1811 made them one of the best-known intellectual couples of the time.

A committed republican from 1795, Constant backed the coups of 18 Fructidor and 18 Brumaire. After 18 Brumaire Napoleon Bonaparte, with grave reservations, appointed him to the Tribunat, and in 1802 forced him to withdraw because of his speeches and his connection with Madame de Staël. He became the leader of the Liberal opposition in 1800. In 1814, after the Restoration, he proposed a constitutional monarchy on the Council of State, and during the Hundred Days he helped draft the Charter of 1815.

He was elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1818 and remained a deputy until his death. As head of the parliamentary bloc first called the Independents and later the liberals, he was one of the most eloquent orators of the Chamber and an opponent of Charles X. He supported the accession of Louis Philippe I in the July Revolution, and died in Paris on 8 December 1830.

Constant distinguished the Liberty of the Ancients, the right to take direct part in politics through votes in a public assembly, which rested on slavery and on small, homogenous societies, from the Liberty of the Moderns, based on civil liberties, the rule of law and freedom from excessive state interference. He criticised the French revolutionaries for applying ancient liberties to a modern state, and held that commerce is preferable to war. He opposed imperialism and colonial racism.

He developed a theory of constitutional monarchy in which royal power is a neutral power balancing the executive, legislature and judiciary, while ministers accountable to Parliament hold the executive. This made four powers rather than Montesquieu's three. The theory was applied literally in Brazil in 1824 and in Portugal in 1826, where the monarch was given Moderating Powers. He also wrote on religion for forty years, and published the novella Adolphe in 1816.
benjamin-franklin: Benjamin Franklin was born on Milk Street in Boston on 17 January 1706 and baptised at the Old South Meeting House. His father, Josiah Franklin, born at Ecton in Northamptonshire, was a tallow chandler and soap and candle maker. Benjamin was his fifteenth child and tenth and last son. His mother, Abiah Folger, was born in Nantucket, and both parents were pious Puritans.

His father could afford to send him to school for only two years, and he continued to educate himself by reading. At 12 he became an apprentice to his brother James, a printer. When James founded The New-England Courant, Franklin wrote letters in the name of Silence Dogood, a middle-aged widow, and neither the readers nor his brother knew the author. He later left the apprenticeship without permission and so became a fugitive.

Franklin became a successful printer and editor in Philadelphia, publishing The Pennsylvania Gazette at 23 and Poor Richard's Almanack under the pseudonym Richard Saunders. In 1736 he created the Union Fire Company, and in 1743 he founded the American Philosophical Society. In 1749 he printed Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania and was appointed president of the Academy, which opened in 1751.

His electrical research began in the 1740s. He proposed that vitreous and resinous electricity were one fluid under different pressures, was the first to call them positive and negative, and discovered the principle of conservation of charge. He invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove and bifocal glasses and never patented them. As an agent in London he led the repeal of the Stamp Act, and as the first United States ambassador to France he secured French support for the Revolutionary War. He served as President of Pennsylvania from 1785 to 1788.
Franklin owned at least seven slaves from 1735 and advertised slaves for sale in his newspaper, but by the late 1750s he had begun to argue against slavery and later became an active abolitionist.

Franklin died of a pleuritic attack at his home in Philadelphia on 17 April 1790, aged 84. About 20,000 people attended his funeral, and the assembly of revolutionary France went into mourning for three days. He left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia, to gather interest for 200 years. He is the only person to have signed the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris with Britain and the Constitution.
beowulf: Beowulf is an epic in the tradition of Germanic heroic legend, composed in alliterative verse by an anonymous author called the Beowulf poet. The only certain dating is that of its manuscript, produced between 975 and 1025, and scholars disagree about when the poem was composed. Some place it in the 8th century, J. R. R. Tolkien among them, since he held that it keeps too genuine a memory of Anglo-Saxon paganism to be much later than the Christianisation of England. Others link it with the courts of King Alfred the Great or King Cnut the Great, and some suggest a 7th-century origin at Rendlesham in East Anglia.

The story is set in pagan Scandinavia in the 5th and 6th centuries. Beowulf, a hero of the Geats, helps Hrothgar, king of the Danes, whose mead hall Heorot has been attacked for twelve years by the monster Grendel. He kills Grendel with his bare hands, and then kills Grendel's mother, who has taken revenge by killing Hrothgar's advisor Æschere, with a giant's sword found in her lair.

Beowulf returns home and becomes king of the Geats. Fifty years later a slave steals a golden cup from a dragon's lair, and the dragon burns the land. Beowulf resolves to fight it alone, but only his young Swedish relative Wiglaf stays to help him. They kill the dragon, but Beowulf is mortally wounded, and his body is cremated and a barrow visible from the sea is raised for him. Digressions on the Swedish–Geatish wars, the fight at Finnsburg and biblical tales give the poem historical depth.

The poem survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, now British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.XV, copied by two scribes. It has no title in the manuscript and takes its name from its hero. A fire at Ashburnham House in London in 1731 charred its margins and cost some readings. Grímur Jónsson Thorkelin made the first transcriptions in 1786, which are prized because the manuscript has crumbled since. Some verses were first translated into modern English in 1805, and nine complete translations followed in the 19th century. Tolkien's 1936 lecture argued that its literary value had been overlooked in favour of its historical content.
beqaa-valley: The Beqaa Valley lies about 30 km east of Beirut, between Mount Lebanon to the west and the Anti-Lebanon Mountains to the east. It is the northern continuation of the Jordan Rift Valley, part of the Great Rift Valley, and is about 120 km long and 16 km wide on average. The region broadly corresponds to the Coele-Syria of classical antiquity. Mount Lebanon casts a rain shadow, so rainfall averages 230 mm a year in the north and 750 mm in the central valley. Two rivers rise here: the Orontes, which flows north into Syria and Turkey, and the Litani, which flows south and then west to the Mediterranean.

Baalbek has evidence of habitation going back almost 8,000 to 9,000 years, and Ard Tlaili, dated to around 5780 to 5710 BCE, has the southernmost pottery of the Halaf Culture. In the Middle Bronze Age the valley, known as Amqu, was a highway between Qatna in the north and its vassal Hazor in the south, and belonged to the Amorite kingdoms of Amurru and Qatna. The city of Enišasi, southwest of Baalbek, appears in the Amarna letters of 1350 to 1335 BCE. By the early Iron Age Phoenician and Aramaic speakers dominated the valley, and many scholars place the Aramaean kingdom of Aram-Zobah, mentioned in the Bible, here, though its exact location is debated.

In the time of Alexander the Great the valley was reportedly inhabited by the Itureans, possibly an Arab or Aramaean people. They later broke away from the weakened Seleucid Empire to form the Kingdom of Chalcis, expanded to include the Phoenician coastal cities and came close to Damascus. Their territory was absorbed into Roman Syria. The Roman Empire valued the valley as one of the important agricultural regions of its eastern provinces, and from the 1st century BCE it supplied grain to the Roman provinces of the Levant. It was known for its many temples. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra built the Canalizations of Zenobia, linking the valley with her city.

The valley makes up about 40 percent of Lebanon's arable land and is the country's most important farming region. The north is used mostly for grazing, and farther south the soils support wheat, maize, cotton and vegetables, with vineyards and orchards centred on Zahle, the valley's largest city. The valley accounts for the majority of Lebanon's wine production. Landmarks include the Roman ruins of Baalbek and the Umayyad ruins of Anjar.
berbera: Berbera lies on the coast of northern Somaliland, about 160 km from Hargeisa. It has the only sheltered harbour on the southern side of the Gulf of Aden, and the surrounding coastal lowlands are semi-arid. The climate is hot and arid, with about 52 millimetres of rain a year. The name is traced by one account to the Somali phrase beri-beri, meaning occasionally, because the place was a seasonal settlement occupied in the cooler months; the Royal Asiatic Society suggested instead an Arabic word meaning talking much or shouting.

Berbera is believed to be the port of Malao described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek merchant's guide of the first century CE, which lists exports of myrrh, frankincense and cinnamon. In the Middle Ages it was a harbour for the Adal and Ifat sultanates, and with Zeila one of the two main ports of Adal. Ludovico di Varthema, Duarte Barbosa and Leo Africanus described its trade with Aden and Cambay in the early 16th century, and a Portuguese fleet sacked it and Zeila between 1516 and 1518.

In the 18th and 19th centuries it was the most important port of the Somali Peninsula. An annual fair between October and April drew Isaaq clans, caravans from Harar and the interior, and Indian merchants. In the 1833 season the town swelled to 70,000 people, and in 1848 duties on goods from Berbera supplied 80% of the revenue of Aden. Somali merchants brought coffee grown near Harar to Mokha and Aden as Berbera coffee. After a British ship was attacked in 1825 and a blockade followed, the Habr Awal were defeated in a battle in 1827 and ordered to pay 15,000 Spanish dollars.

After treaties with the clans between 1884 and 1886 the British made Berbera the capital of the protectorate of British Somaliland, until Hargeisa replaced it in 1941. In August 1940 the British evacuated about 7,000 people through the port before Italy occupied the territory, and they recaptured it in March 1941. After independence in 1960 Berbera was the Somali Republic's main livestock port, and the Soviet Union built port facilities and a military base there that were completed in 1969.

Berbera is the capital of the Sahil region of Somaliland and its main sea port, linked by road to Hargeisa and Burco. Its exports have included livestock, gum arabic, frankincense and myrrh, and goods from Ethiopia also pass through it. The port has been expanded under an agreement made in 2016 with DP World, and the city has an airport with a very long runway.
berchtesgaden: Berchtesgaden lies in the Berchtesgaden Alps in Bavaria, near the border with Austria, 30 km south of Salzburg and 180 km south-east of Munich. The Berchtesgaden National Park, established in 1978, stretches south of the town along three parallel valleys. The Kehlstein mountain, 1,835 m high, carries the Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest. The name was recorded in 1121 as Perehtgeresgadem, from a personal name and the word gadem, meaning a one-roomed house.

The first known record of the area, from 1102, mentions its rich salt deposits. Salt mining began in 1517 and produced much of the town's wealth. The town belonged to the Berchtesgaden Provostry, an independent state of the Holy Roman Empire ruled by the prince-provost of the Augustinian monastery, until 1803. In 1805 the Treaty of Pressburg ceded the area to Austria, and in 1810 it passed to the Kingdom of Bavaria. The Wittelsbach royal family often visited the Königssee and kept a hunting residence in the former monastery, and artists came to the area. In the 1760s several anonymous toy symphonies, among them the Toy Symphony often attributed to Haydn or Leopold Mozart, were composed here, when the town manufactured toy instruments.

Adolf Hitler began holidaying here in the 1920s and bought a house on the Obersalzberg, which he renovated as the Berghof. Other leading Nazis frequented the area, and the town became an outpost of the Reich Chancellery. Hitler met Neville Chamberlain there in 1938 before the Munich Agreement. American troops received the town's surrender on 4 May 1945.

Tourism centres on the national park, the Königssee, the salt mine and the Dokumentationszentrum Obersalzberg, a museum of the area's history. The Königssee track has hosted international bobsleigh, luge and skeleton competitions, and the town is home to the International Luge Federation.
bergen: Bergen occupies most of the peninsula of Bergenshalvøyen on the west coast of Norway. The city centre faces the fjord of Byfjorden and is surrounded by mountains, so that Bergen is called the city of seven mountains, though locals debate which seven they are. The highest is Gullfjellet, at 987 metres. The climate is temperate oceanic, with plentiful rain in every season, and the Gulf Stream keeps the winters mild. The Old Norse name Bjǫrgvin combines a word for mountains with vin, a new settlement where a pasture or meadow had been.

The traditional founder of the city was King Olav Kyrre in 1070, but modern research has found that a trading settlement already existed in the 1020s or 1030s. Bergen served as the capital of Norway in the 13th century. It became a bureau city of the Hanseatic League, and until 1789 it had exclusive rights to mediate trade between Northern Norway and abroad. It was the largest city in Norway until the 1830s, when Christiania, now Oslo, overtook it. What remains of the quays, Bryggen, is a World Heritage Site.

Fire marked the city's history. In 1198 the Bagler faction burned it during the civil war with the Birkebeiner. In 1428 the Victual Brothers plundered it, and a drunk trader started the fire that burned down Bryggen in 1476. A fire in 1686 destroyed 231 city blocks. The worst came in 1702, when 90 per cent of the city burned to ashes, and in 1756 a fire at Strandsiden consumed 1,500 buildings.
Bergen became a county of its own in 1831 and a municipality on 1 January 1838. The Norwegian School of Economics was founded there in 1936 and the University of Bergen in 1946.

Bergen is the second-largest city of Norway and the administrative centre of Vestland county. It is an international centre of aquaculture, shipping and the offshore petroleum industry, and its port is the busiest in Norway. Natives speak a distinct dialect known as Bergensk.
bergen-auf-rugen: Bergen auf Rügen lies in the middle of Germany's largest island, Rügen, on the Baltic Sea coast. The town is built on a glacial moraine left when the ice sheets retreated at the end of the last ice age, in hilly country. The Rugard woods rise to 91 metres on its north-eastern edge, and the surrounding land is mostly farmland. Two shallow bays lie near it: the Kleiner Jasmunder Bodden to the north-east and the Greifswalder Bodden to the south-east.

The island was settled in the early Middle Ages by the Rani, a Slavic people who kept a pagan worship site at Cape Arkona, defended by a fort, the Jaromarsburg. A castle stood on the Rugard hill in the area of present-day Bergen. After the Danes subdued the Rani they set up the Principality of Rügen under a local dynasty, and the Rugard became an administrative centre. The principality became Christian and received German settlers in the Ostsiedlung. The town itself was built on the neighbouring hilltop, outside the ramparts of the Rugard. Its name comes from the Slavic word gora, mountain, and is recorded in 1232 as the place Gora.

The Jaromarsburg fell in 1168, and soon afterwards work began on St Mary's as the palace church of Prince Jaromar I. In 1193 it became a Cistercian convent, and the foundation encouraged the first inn, built in 1232. In 1325 the principality passed by inheritance to the Duchy of Pomerania. Fires, such as that of 1445, nearly destroyed the town, the convent and part of the church. The Reformation reached Pomerania in 1534, and the dukes took over the convent. Bergen received Lübeck law town rights in 1613, passed to Sweden in 1648 as part of Swedish Pomerania, and became part of the Prussian Province of Pomerania in 1815.

Bergen auf Rügen is in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and is the administrative seat of its Amt, which has more than 23,000 inhabitants. Railways reached it in 1883. St Mary's, the former convent church, is the oldest surviving brick building in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and has the only complete painting of a church interior in northern Germany. The town museum occupies a restored abbey building and covers the history of Rügen from the Stone Age. The Ernst Moritz Arndt tower, completed in 1877, gives views over much of the island.
bergen-op-zoom: Bergen op Zoom lies in North Brabant, at the border with Zeeland. The city was built where sandy soil meets marine clay. Over centuries the sand pushed against the clay and formed hills, called the Brabantse Wal, literally the ramparts of Brabant. Bergen means hills, and Zoom refers to the border of these ramparts. Marshes and easily flooded polders surrounded the site, which made it a strong natural defensive position, and it could receive reinforcements and supplies by sea.

Bergen op Zoom was probably granted city status in 1212. In 1287 it became a lordship, separated from the lordship of Breda, and in 1559 a margraviate. Several noble families, among them the House of Glymes, ruled it until 1795, though the title was nominal from at least the seventeenth century. During the reign of Jan II van Glymes, who lived from 1417 to 1494, the city grew economically. Large fairs held every spring and autumn drew merchants from all over Europe, and they continued until 1910. A recession in the mid-16th century, caused largely by floods in Zeeland and West-Brabant that harmed the port, left the enlargement of the town church unfinished.

In the early modern period it was a very strong fortress and one of the main armouries of the United Provinces. During the Eighty Years' War Alessandro Farnese besieged it in 1588 and Ambrosio Spinola in 1622; both failed, and the city earned the nickname La Pucelle, the Virgin, because no siege had taken it. In 1747, during the War of the Austrian Succession, the French besieged it. The works built by Menno van Coehoorn had no second line of fortification, and after seventy days the city was taken and thoroughly sacked, and the garrison slaughtered. British forces besieged it unsuccessfully in March 1814.

The municipality has a population of about 70 thousand. The Markiezenhof Palace, built in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, houses a cultural centre and a museum. Hotel De Draak, founded in 1397, is described as the oldest hotel in the Netherlands, and its present building dates from 1500. Among the people born in the town are the composer Jacob Obrecht and the humanist Desiderius Erasmus.
berkshire: Berkshire, officially the Royal County of Berkshire, is a ceremonial county in South East England, with Reading as its county town and largest settlement. The whole county is drained by the Thames. The Berkshire Downs, a chalk upland, lie in the west and are the source of the River Kennet, which flows east through Newbury to meet the Thames at Reading. In the south-east lies Swinley Forest, a remnant of Windsor Forest. The historic county included the parts of Oxfordshire south of the Thames, such as Wantage, where Alfred the Great was born, and the Iron Age Uffington White Horse.

According to Asser's biography of King Alfred, written in 893, the county takes its name from a wood of box trees called Bearroc, a Celtic word meaning hilly, west of Frilsham near Newbury. In the Anglo-Saxon period the region was contested between Mercia and Wessex, and Alfred's campaign against the Danes included the battles of Englefield, Ashdown and Reading. Windsor Castle, built after the Norman Conquest, became the official country residence of the British monarch, since William the Conqueror established Windsor as a royal residence.

The county saw several battles in the First English Civil War, with Reading and Wallingford besieged and two battles fought at Newbury, in 1643 and 1644. A second Battle of Reading, on 9 December 1688, was the only substantial military action in England during the Glorious Revolution. Reading replaced Abingdon as county town in 1867. The county received the title Royal County in 1957 because of Windsor Castle, and its boundaries changed on 1 April 1974, when the northern part passed to Oxfordshire and Slough and Eton came from Buckinghamshire.

Berkshire is divided into six unitary authority areas: Bracknell Forest, Reading, Slough, West Berkshire, Windsor and Maidenhead, and Wokingham. Its population is concentrated in the east, nearest London, while the west is rural and its largest town is Newbury. Proximity to London led to development from the 19th century, when Slough became an industrial centre and Bracknell was designated a new town. Software and high-technology industry dominate the economy in the east, and the west remains agricultural.
berlin: Berlin lies in low-lying marshy woodland on the Northern European Plain, along the Spree, which empties into the Havel in the western borough of Spandau. The Spree follows the Berliner Urstromtal, an ice-age glacial valley between the Barnim Plateau to the north and the Teltow plateau to the south, formed by meltwater at the end of the last glaciation. About a third of the city's area is forests, parks, gardens, rivers, canals and lakes. The name has roots in the language of the West Slavs and may be related to the Old Polabian stem berl-/birl-, 'swamp'. Five of the twelve boroughs bear Slavic-derived names, among them Pankow and Spandau.

The area has been settled for millennia: a deer mask of about 9,000 BCE is attributed to the Maglemosian culture, and dense settlement along the Spree and Havel gave rise to the Lusatian culture around 2,000 BCE. Germanic tribes settled from about 500 BCE, the Burgundians followed the Semnones after about 200 CE, and in the 7th century Slavic tribes, later known as the Hevelli and Sprevane, reached the region.

Berlin was first documented in the 13th century, at the crossing of two important trade routes. It was capital of the Margraviate of Brandenburg from 1417, the Kingdom of Prussia from 1701 and the German Empire from 1871. In 1685 the Edict of Potsdam granted religious freedom and tax-free status to French Huguenot refugees.

The Greater Berlin Act of 1920 raised the population from 1.9 million to 4 million, and in the 1920s Berlin was the third-largest city in the world. It was capital of the Weimar Republic and of Nazi Germany until 1945. After the Second World War it was split into West Berlin and East Berlin, divided by the Berlin Wall, and Bonn became the West German capital. Berlin again became the capital of all Germany after reunification on 3 October 1990.

Berlin covers 891 km2 and is the most populous city proper in the European Union. Since 1990 it has been one of three city-states among the 16 states of Germany, governed by the Senate and the 141-seat Abgeordnetenhaus. The bombing of the Second World War devastated the city, and many surviving buildings were later demolished; after reunification many heritage structures were reconstructed.

Museum Island, designated a district dedicated to art and antiquities by royal decree in 1841, is one of three UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Charité hospital traces its origins to 1710, and Robert Koch and Rudolf Virchow worked in Berlin. The city hosted the 1936 Summer Olympics.
berlin-conference: Until the later 19th century European power in Africa was largely confined to the coast, where traders held posts protected by gunboats. In 1876 King Leopold II of Belgium founded the International African Association and invited Henry Morton Stanley to join him; from 1878 to 1885 Stanley returned to the Congo as Leopold's agent.

France answered in 1881 by sending the naval officer Pierre de Brazza, who raised the French flag over Brazzaville, and Portugal made a treaty with Great Britain on 26 February 1884 to block the Congo Society's access to the Atlantic. Germany began expeditions of its own, which alarmed British and French statesmen. With British support and on Portugal's initiative, Otto von Bismarck called representatives of thirteen European nations and the United States to Berlin.

The conference met on 15 November 1884 and closed on 26 February 1885 with the signing of the General Act of Berlin. Fourteen countries sent plenipotentiaries, each with a single vote; the United States reserved the right to accept or decline its conclusions. No African state took part.

Sultan Barghash bin Seyyid of Zanzibar asked to send a representative, but British pressure from the Anti-Slavery Society, which objected to Zanzibar's part in the slave trade, led to refusal. Six of the fourteen countries, Austria-Hungary, Russia, Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden-Norway and the United States, came home without any zone of interest in Africa.

The General Act confirmed the holdings of Leopold's International Congo Society, and on 1 August 1885 the territory was named the Congo Free State, a name absent from the Act. It decreed free trade among the signatories throughout the Congo Basin and made the Niger and Congo rivers free for shipping. Article 6 called on the powers to strive for the suppression of slavery.

Under the principle of effective occupation a power could acquire rights only if it had treaties with local leaders, flew its flag and set up an administration, and it had to notify the other signatories of any possession or protectorate it took in Africa. The Act concerned lands on the coast, and allowed a state to claim the hinterland after occupying the coast.

The conference is usually seen as formalising the Scramble for Africa, and by 1914 about 90 per cent of the continent was under European control. Some historians, among them Sybil Crowe, Matthew Craven and Simon Katzenellenbogen, caution against overstating its role, pointing to the many bilateral agreements before and after it. The only borders set at the conference were those of the Congo region, and these were later revised.
bermuda: Bermuda is an archipelago of 181 islands, though the most significant are connected by bridges and appear to form one landmass. Its land area is 54 square kilometres. The nearest land is the coast of North Carolina, about 1,035 kilometres to the west-northwest. The islands lie in the west of the Sargasso Sea and have a tropical climate; a coral reef gives them some protection from tropical cyclones. When discovered, they had no human population and were dominated by forests of Bermuda cedar.

Bermuda was discovered in the early 1500s by the Spanish explorer Juan de Bermúdez and appears on Spanish charts of 1511. Spanish and Portuguese ships used it to take on fresh meat and water. Legends of spirits and devils, now thought to stem from the calls of birds and the noises of introduced wild hogs, together with storms and dangerous reefs, gave it the name Isle of Devils, and neither Spain nor Portugal tried to settle it.

In 1609 a flotilla bound for the Jamestown colony was broken up by a storm, and its flagship, the Sea Venture, was driven onto Bermuda's reef to prevent her sinking, so that all aboard survived. Having heard the true conditions in Jamestown, the settlers were unwilling to move on and made several attempts to rebel and stay. The new settlement became a prison labour camp and built two ships, the Deliverance and the Patience. The Somers Isles Company suppressed shipbuilding, wanting the colonists to farm, but the islanders turned to maritime trades, and in 1684 the company's charter was revoked. The House of Assembly dates from 1620.

After the American Revolution the Royal Navy began improving the harbours, and in 1811 work began on the Royal Naval Dockyard on Ireland Island, guarding the western Atlantic shipping lanes. In the War of 1812 the British attacks on Washington, D.C., and the Chesapeake were planned and launched from Bermuda. In the early 20th century it became a popular destination for tourists, and the Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 ended its agricultural export trade to America and encouraged tourism.

Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory and a self-governing parliamentary democracy, with a bicameral parliament in the capital Hamilton; the United Kingdom is responsible for foreign affairs and defence. It is divided into nine parishes. An independence referendum in 1995 produced a large majority against independence. The historic Town of St. George's is a World Heritage Site.
bernard-of-clairvaux: Bernard's parents, Tescelin de Fontaine, lord of Fontaine-lès-Dijon, and Alèthe de Montbard, belonged to the highest nobility of Burgundy. He was the third of seven children, six of them sons. At nine he was sent to a school at Châtillon-sur-Seine run by the secular canons of Saint-Vorles, where he was drawn to literature and rhetoric. After his mother died he decided to go to Cîteaux, the abbey founded near Dijon in 1098 by a group led by Robert of Molesme to live by a literal reading of the Rule of St Benedict.

Three years after entering Cîteaux, Bernard was sent with twelve monks to found a new house at the Vallée d'Absinthe in the diocese of Langres, which he named Clairvaux on 25 June 1115. Its beginnings were austere, but candidates flocked to it, and more than sixty abbeys followed in his lifetime. He defended the Cistercians against criticism from the Benedictines of Cluny in his Apology, and Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, answered with admiration and friendship.

At the Council of Troyes in 1128 he traced the outlines of the Rule of the Knights Templar. When Honorius II died in 1130 and the election of Innocent II and the Antipope Anacletus II split the Church, Bernard was chosen at the council of Étampes to judge between them and decided for Innocent, then spent years winning over rulers and cities; the schism ended with Anacletus's death in 1138. In 1141 he secured the condemnation of Peter Abelard at a council at Sens.

In 1146 Pope Eugene III commissioned him to preach the Second Crusade, and on 31 March, with King Louis VII present, he preached to an enormous crowd at Vézelay. He also opposed attacks on Jews in the Rhineland and silenced the monk Radulf, who was inspiring them.

The failure of the Second Crusade saddened his last years and put the whole responsibility on him; he wrote that the sins of the crusaders had caused it. He died on 20 August 1153, aged sixty-three, and was buried at Clairvaux. After his remains were destroyed in 1792 by the French Revolutionary government, they were transferred to Troyes Cathedral.

He was canonized 21 years after his death and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1830. Against the rational approach of the scholastics he preached poetically and stressed personal friendship with Christ, and he helped spread devotion to Mary. His sermons on the Song of Songs are his best known. Bernard appears as Dante's last guide in the Divine Comedy.
bernardo-houssay: Bernardo Alberto Houssay was born on 10 April 1887 in Buenos Aires, the son of Albert and Clara Houssay, immigrants from France. A precocious youngster, he was admitted to the Pharmacy School of the University of Buenos Aires at 14 and to its Faculty of Medicine at 17, studying there from 1904 to 1910. While a third-year medical student he took a post as research and teaching assistant in the Chair of Physiology.

After graduating he presented a doctoral thesis on the physiological activities of pituitary extracts, published in 1911, a theme he pursued for the rest of his scientific career. He became Professor of Physiology in the university's School of Veterinary Medicine, worked as an assistant physician at the municipal hospital of Buenos Aires, and in 1913 became Chief Physician at the Alvear Hospital. In 1915 he became Chief of the Section of Experimental Pathology at the National Public Health Laboratories. In 1919 he was appointed to the chair of physiology at the university's medical school and held it until 1943, turning the department into a research centre of international standing.

In 1943 the military government deprived him of his university posts because of his liberal political ideas, and he re-established his research and staff at a privately funded Instituto de Biología y Medicina Experimental. The Peronist government dismissed him a second time in 1945. When Perón was ousted in 1955 he was reinstated at the University of Buenos Aires, where he stayed until his death. From 1957 he also directed the National Scientific and Technical Research Council.

Houssay worked in many fields of physiology, but his main contribution was experimental research on the part played by the anterior pituitary gland in the metabolism of carbohydrates, particularly in diabetes mellitus. In the 1930s he demonstrated the diabetogenic effect of anterior pituitary extracts and the lessening of diabetes after removal of the gland. These findings stimulated the study of hormonal feedback control, central to modern endocrinology. The work won him the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, shared with Carl Ferdinand Cori and Gerty Cori.

He published more than 600 scientific papers and several specialised books. With his disciples Eduardo Braun-Menéndez and Miguel Rolando Covian he wrote a textbook of human physiology, published since 1950 in Spanish and Portuguese and used in almost all medical schools of Latin America. Covian became the father of Brazilian neurophysiology at the University of São Paulo's medical faculty in Ribeirão Preto. Houssay was elected to the United States National Academy of Sciences in 1940 and became a Foreign Member of the Royal Society in 1943. He died on 21 September 1971.
bernardo-ohiggins: Bernardo O'Higgins was born on 20 August 1778 in Chillán, the illegitimate son of Ambrosio O'Higgins, a Spanish officer born in County Sligo who became governor of Chile and later viceroy of Peru, and of Isabel Riquelme. His father never acknowledged him, and the two never met in person, though Ambrosio supported him financially. At seventeen he was sent to London, where he met the Venezuelan Francisco de Miranda and joined the Lautaro Lodge, a society dedicated to the independence of Latin America. After his father's death in 1801 he inherited a large estate and returned to Chile in 1802 as a gentleman farmer.

On 18 September 1810 O'Higgins joined the revolt that created the Government Junta of Chile, a date now Chile's Independence Day. The patriots were split between the Carrera family and the circle of O'Higgins in Concepción. In October 1814 O'Higgins garrisoned the main square of Rancagua rather than the gorge he and José Miguel Carrera had agreed on; Carrera did not arrive with reinforcements, and the royalists won. O'Higgins broke out with a few men and spent three years in Argentina, where he met José de San Martín, assembled the Army of the Andes and returned to Chile in 1817 to win at Chacabuco.

He was granted dictatorial powers as Supreme Director on 16 February 1817 after San Martín declined the post, and Chile proclaimed itself independent on 12 February 1818. He founded the Chilean Military Academy and, with Lord Cochrane, the modern Chilean Navy, and sent an expedition to liberate Peru. His proposals to establish democracy and abolish titles of nobility met resistance from landowners, and he offended the Church and then the business community. The government went bankrupt, and Carrera's execution in 1821 damaged his name. A conservative coup deposed him on 28 January 1823.

O'Higgins left Valparaíso in July 1823 and never saw Chile again. Simón Bolívar's government granted him two haciendas in Peru but gave him no command. In 1842 the National Congress of Chile voted to allow his return, but he fell ill with heart trouble at Callao and died in Lima on 24 October 1842. His remains were brought to Chile in 1869 and now lie in the Crypt of the Liberator. A region of Chile, a national park and the main avenue of Santiago bear his name.
bernburg: The town centre lies in the fertile Magdeburg Börde lowland on the Saale river, about 40 km downstream from Halle and 45 km upstream from Magdeburg. It is dominated by the huge Bernburg Castle, which holds a museum and a bear pit in its moat. Bernburg is the capital of the Salzlandkreis district and a stop on the Romanesque Road. Near the town, in Lower Triassic deposits, the type fossil of the amphibian Trematosaurus brauni was found.

Archaeological sites in the area belong to the Walternienburg-Bernburg Culture, a mid-Neolithic funnel-beaker culture of about 3200 to 2800 BCE. Around 150 CE a settlement named Luppia appears in Ptolemy's Geography. In the early Middle Ages the Saale marked the border between the German stem duchies in the west and the lands of the Polabian Slavs in the east. Bernburg itself is first mentioned as civitas Brandanburg in a deed of King Otto I of 961. Enemies set fire to the castle, then held by the Ascanian prince Albert the Bear, in 1138, and in 1252 the rebuilt castle became the residence of his great-grandson Prince Bernhard I of Anhalt-Bernburg.

During the Nazi dictatorship a wing of the town's mental hospital was used for the mass murder of an estimated 15,000 people in Action T4 and Action 14f13. The victims included Jews, people with physical and mental illnesses and concentration camp inmates. The site now holds a memorial to them.
bertolt-brecht: Eugen Berthold Friedrich Brecht was born on 10 February 1898 in Augsburg. His mother was a devout Protestant and his father a Roman Catholic who had been persuaded to have a Protestant wedding; his Pietist grandmother influenced him in childhood, and the Bible shaped his writing for life. At school he met Caspar Neher, who designed many of the sets for his dramas. Brecht had his first successes as a playwright in Munich and moved to Berlin in 1924, where he worked as a dramaturg. His collection of poems Devotions for the Home was completed with the help of the assistant Elisabeth Hauptmann and published in January 1927.

He fled Germany in February 1933, just after Hitler took power. After brief spells in Prague, Zurich and Paris, he and Helene Weigel accepted an invitation from the writer Karin Michaëlis to Denmark, and lived for six years in Svendborg on Funen, where guests included Walter Benjamin and Hanns Eisler.

In April 1939 he moved to Stockholm and then to Helsinki, where he co-wrote Mr Puntila and His Man Matti with Hella Wuolijoki. During the war he settled in Southern California as a screenwriter, under FBI surveillance. In September 1947 the House Un-American Activities Committee subpoenaed him; he testified and returned to Europe the next day, eventually settling in East Berlin, where he co-founded the Berliner Ensemble with Weigel.

Brecht developed his epic theatre by synthesising and extending the experiments of Erwin Piscator and Vsevolod Meyerhold, treating the theatre as a forum for political ideas. An epic play should not make the spectator identify emotionally with the characters; it should provoke rational self-reflection and a critical view of the action. Brecht thought that a climactic catharsis left an audience complacent, and he wanted audiences to recognise social injustice and to act on it outside the theatre.

He used techniques that remind the spectator the play is a representation and not reality, in the hope of showing that the audience's own reality is equally constructed and so changeable. He later preferred to call it dialectical theatre. He also wrote hundreds of poems, the last new collection published in his lifetime being the Svendborger Gedichte of 1939, and worked in collaboration with composers, designers and actors.

Brecht died of a heart attack on 14 August 1956, aged 58, and is buried in the Dorotheenstadt Cemetery in Berlin. According to Stephen Parker, he had had rheumatic fever as a child, which left him with chronic heart failure. Helene Weigel managed the Berliner Ensemble, which was devoted mainly to his plays, until her death in 1971. His aesthetic theories strongly influenced radical cinema of the 1960s and 1970s, in the work of Jean-Luc Godard, Rainer Werner Fassbinder and Nagisa Ōshima among others.
bertrand-russell: Russell was born on 18 May 1872 at Ravenscroft, a country house in Trellech, Monmouthshire, to John Russell, Viscount Amberley, and Katharine, Viscountess Amberley, both early advocates of birth control. His mother died of diphtheria in June 1874, followed shortly by his sister Rachel, and his father died in January 1876. He was raised by his paternal grandparents at Pembroke Lodge in Richmond Park, chiefly by his grandmother, the Countess Russell, whose progressive views on social justice and standing up for principle remained with him all his life.

He began at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1890 on a scholarship to read for the Mathematical Tripos, graduating seventh Wrangler in 1893 and becoming a Fellow in philosophy in 1895. His first major publication was An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry (1897).

Russell started in British idealism, the dominant philosophy of the time, but his friendship with G. E. Moore led him to analytic philosophy, and the two led a revolt against idealism. With Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica, published in 1910–1913. His article On Denoting has been considered a paradigm of philosophy. In 1916 he was convicted under the Defence of the Realm Act 1914 for his pacifist activity in the First World War and dismissed from Trinity. After a campaign by the Fellows, he was offered reinstatement and accepted it in 1920, but he resigned in 1921.

In August 1920 he visited Soviet Russia as part of a delegation and met Vladimir Lenin, whom he found disappointing. The visit ended his tentative support for the revolution, and he wrote The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism. He opposed rearmament against Nazi Germany, but changed his view in 1940 and in 1943 adopted a position he called relative political pacifism, that war may in extreme circumstances be the lesser of two evils. His History of Western Philosophy (1945) was a best-seller.

Russell is credited as one of the founders of analytic philosophy, and Willard Van Orman Quine named his work as a chief influence on his own. He made language a central part of philosophy and influenced Ludwig Wittgenstein, Gilbert Ryle, J. L. Austin and P. F. Strawson. In lectures of 1918 he set out logical atomism, the view that knowledge can be reduced to atomic propositions and their truth-functional compounds.

He argued that religion is largely harmful and was a member of the advisory council of the British Humanist Association. He became the 3rd Earl Russell in 1931 and held the title until his death on 2 February 1970.
berwick-upon-tweed: Berwick-upon-Tweed lies at the mouth of the River Tweed on the east coast, 4 km south of the Anglo-Scottish border, 90 km south-east of Edinburgh and 105 km north of Newcastle upon Tyne. Its name has the same origin as the word berewick, a portion of farmland detached from a manor for the lord's own use, from the Old English berewíc, meaning corn farm. The earliest recorded spelling, Berewich, dates from 1167, and the medieval town seal showed a bear and a wych tree as a pun on the name.

The town was founded as an Anglo-Saxon settlement in the Kingdom of Northumbria. It remained part of the Earldom of Northumbria until control passed to the Scots after the Battle of Carham of 1018. David I of Scotland, who reigned from 1124 to 1153, made it a royal burgh and county town of Berwickshire, and a mint was present by 1153. In 1174, after the defeat of William I of Scotland, the Treaty of Falaise ceded Berwick to Henry II of England, until the treaty was annulled in 1189 when William paid Richard I 10,000 marks.

By the middle of the 13th century Berwick was prosperous. William Edington, a bishop and chancellor of England, wrote that it was so populous and of such commercial importance that it might be called another Alexandria, whose riches were the sea and the water its walls. Its position on the border led to centuries of raids, sieges and changes of ownership. The last came when Richard, Duke of Gloucester, later Richard III, retook it for England in 1482.

The Treaty of Norham of 1551, ending the Rough Wooing, left Berwick in English hands and declared it a free town independent of either kingdom, although in practice England controlled it. Under Elizabeth I large sums, one source giving £128,648, were spent on fortifications in the Italian style, to which Sir Richard Lee and the engineer Giovanni Portinari contributed. After the Act of Union of 1707 Berwick stayed within the legal system of England and Wales.

Berwick is a market town in Northumberland and the northernmost town in England, with 12,043 inhabitants at the census of 2011. Its medieval walls, the Elizabethan ramparts, the Georgian Town Hall and the barracks built by Nicholas Hawksmoor in 1717 to 1721 survive, as do the ruins of the 13th-century castle and the Old Bridge of 1610 to 1624. Berwick Rangers Football Club and Berwick Rugby Football Club play in Scottish leagues.
bes: Bes, also written Bisu, was an ancient Egyptian deity, paired with a female counterpart, Beset, and probably of Nubian or C-Group origin. People in Upper Egypt venerated him long before those in Lower Egypt, which points to a southern origin. In Nubian the word bes means cat, and the god is regularly shown with feline features. The feathered crown he wears was also common dress in ancient Kush. Donald Mackenzie suggested in 1907 that Bes was a Middle Kingdom import from Nubia, whose cult spread widely only at the beginning of the New Kingdom, but figurines resembling Bes, thirteen of them at Tell el-Farkha, have since been found in deposits of the pre-dynastic Naqada period.

Bes is first mentioned in the Pyramid Texts but seems to have been best known and most widely worshipped in the Middle Kingdom. Evidence of his worship continues into Coptic Egypt, the latest being a jug showing Bes from Tell Edfu, dated to the 10th century CE.

Bes protected households and, in particular, mothers, children and childbirth. His tasks included killing snakes, driving off evil spirits and watching over children, and he was present with Taweret at births. Where Egyptian gods were normally shown in profile, Bes appeared in a full-face portrait, ithyphallic and sometimes in a soldier's tunic, ready to attack any approaching evil. Because he drove off evil, he also came to symbolise the good things in life, music, dance and sexual pleasure. Some modern scholars, among them James Romano, hold that in its earliest form Bes represented a lion rearing on its hind legs.

Images of Bes were kept in homes. From the Middle Kingdom he appears on masks, amulets, infant feeding bottles, magic knives, furniture, toiletries and game pieces, and many jugs and storage jars bear his image. In the New Kingdom dancers, musicians and servant girls wore tattoos of him on the thigh, as a wall painting of the 19th Dynasty from Deir el-Medina shows. In the Ptolemaic period chambers at Saqqara were painted with Bes and Beset, which Egyptologists think were used for curing fertility problems or for healing rituals.

His worship spread abroad. Beset was more popular in Minoan Crete, while Bes found favour with the Phoenicians and the ancient Cypriots. From the end of the 6th century BCE his image spread across the Achaemenid Empire, to which Egypt then belonged, and has been found at Susa and as far off as central Asia. Over time he came to be shown in Persian clothes and headdress. His cult reached Syria and the Balearic Islands as well.
besalu: Besalú is a town in the comarca of Garrotxa, in the province of Girona in Catalonia. Its name derives from the Latin Bisuldunum, meaning a fort on a mountain between two rivers. It was designated a historical national property, a conjunt historicoartístic, in 1966, and its urban layout is almost identical to the original one.

The town was most important in the early Middle Ages, as capital of the county of Besalú. The county had roughly the territory of the present Garrotxa, but sometimes extended as far as Corbières in the Aude, in France. In 894 Besalú became a county with its own dynasty. Wilfred the Hairy, credited with the unification of Catalonia, was Count of Besalú, and the troubadour Raimon Vidal was born in the town.
In 1111 Besalú lost its independence to the county of Barcelona. Centuries later the town entered a period of decline, made worse by wars with the French and the Carlist wars.

The emblem of Besalú is its 12th-century Romanesque bridge over the Fluvià, which has seven uneven arches and two towers, with a gateway at its midpoint. Parts of the old walls survive. The narrow streets nearest the bridge belong to the former Jewish quarter, where a mikveh, a ritual bath dating from the 11th or 12th century, is the only Romanesque one remaining in Spain, and the remains of a medieval synagogue lie near the river.

The church of Sant Pere was consecrated in 1003, and of the Benedictine monastery of Sant Pere only a three-nave church and one apse remain. Other monuments include the Royal Curia, the apse of Santa Maria and a tower of the old counts' castle, and the parish church of Sant Vicenç. Industry and tourism are now the main sources of income.
bessarabia: Bessarabia is bounded by the Dniester to the north and east, the Prut to the west, and the lower Danube and the Black Sea to the south, and has an area of 45,630 square kilometres. It is mostly hilly plains and flat steppe, very fertile. About two thirds of it lies in modern Moldova, with the Budjak in the south and a small part of the Chernivtsi Oblast in the north in Ukraine. According to the traditional explanation the name derives from the Wallachian Basarab dynasty, who allegedly ruled the south in the 14th century; some scholars argue that it began as an exonym used by Western cartographers and was first used in local sources only in the late 17th century.

In antiquity the region was inhabited by Thracians and, for shorter periods, by Cimmerians, Scythians, Sarmatians and Celts. Greek settlers founded the colony of Tyras in the 6th century BCE, and the Roman Empire defeated the Dacian kingdom in 106 CE. From the 3rd to the 11th century it was invaded in turn by Goths, Huns, Avars, Bulgars, Magyars, Pechenegs, Cumans and Mongols. After the 1360s it was gradually included in the Principality of Moldavia, which by 1392 controlled Akkerman and Chilia. Stephen the Great ruled from 1457 to 1504 and built churches and monasteries near his battlefields, many along the Dniester. In 1484 the Ottomans captured Chilia and Akkerman, and in 1538 more land in the south.

By the Treaty of Bucharest of 28 May 1812 the Ottoman Empire ceded the land between the Prut and the Dniester to Russia, and the whole of it was then called Bessarabia. German settlers arrived from 1814, and Bulgarians and Gagauz settled in the south. The south returned to Moldavia in 1856, and Russian rule over the whole region was restored in 1878, when Romania exchanged it for the Dobruja. On 9 April 1918 its assembly, the Sfatul Țării, voted for union with Romania; the Soviet Union never recognised this. In 1940, under an ultimatum, Romania withdrew; it retook the region in 1941 and lost it in 1944, and the Treaty of Paris of 1947 recognised the border along the Prut.

When the Soviet Union dissolved, the Moldavian and Ukrainian republics declared independence in 1991 and kept the existing division of Bessarabia, so that most of it forms the core of Moldova and its northern and southern fringes lie in Ukraine. Chișinău, the former capital of the Russian Bessarabia Governorate, is the capital of Moldova.
bethlehem: Bethlehem stands in the Judean Mountains at about 775 metres above sea level, some 30 metres higher than Jerusalem, which lies about ten kilometres to the north. The Arabic name Bēt laḥm means house of meat, while the Hebrew Bet Leḥem means house of bread or house of food. Beit Jala and Beit Sahour form an urban cluster with the city, and the refugee camps of Aida and Azza lie within its limits.

A possible earliest reference is in the Amarna correspondence of ancient Egypt, where Abdi-Heba, the Egyptian-appointed governor of Jerusalem, appeals for help in retaking a town near Jerusalem called Bit-Lahmi after attacks by Apiru mercenaries. The reading is uncertain and has met with objections. The Hebrew Bible names Bethlehem as the birthplace of David. In 2012 excavators in the City of David found a clay seal impression reading From the town of Bethlehem to the King, which they date to the 8th or 7th century BCE and take to have sealed a tax shipment.

The Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke place the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, though scholars regard the two accounts as contradictory and are divided on his actual birthplace. Under the Roman Empire Hadrian destroyed the city, and Constantine the Great later commissioned the Church of the Nativity in 327 CE. It was heavily damaged in 529 by Samaritans in revolt and rebuilt by Justinian I. In 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ordered it demolished, but local Muslims, who were permitted to worship in its southern transept, spared it.

Crusaders took Bethlehem in 1099 and replaced the Greek Orthodox clergy with Catholic ones. The Mamluk Sultanate demolished its walls in the mid-13th century, and the Ottoman Empire rebuilt them in the 16th. From 1517 the Catholic and Greek Orthodox churches bitterly disputed custody of the basilica. Bethlehem was part of Mandatory Palestine from 1920 to 1948, was held by Jordan after the 1948 Arab–Israeli War and was captured by Israel in 1967. Refugees from the 1947–48 war settled near the city and helped turn its Christian majority into a Muslim one.

Bethlehem is the capital of the Bethlehem Governorate and had 28,591 inhabitants in 2017. Its economy is closely tied to tourism and to pilgrimage to the Church of the Nativity at Christmas, and it is known for olive wood and mother-of-pearl carving, a craft said to have been introduced by Franciscan friars from Italy in the 15th century. Bethlehem University, founded in 1973, was the first university established in the West Bank.
betty-friedan: Betty Friedan was born on 4 February 1921 to Harry and Miriam Goldstein, whose secular Jewish families came from Russia and Hungary. Her father owned a jewelry store in Peoria, and her mother wrote for a newspaper's society page when he fell ill, a life outside the home that seemed much more gratifying. As a girl she was active in both Marxist and Jewish circles, and later wrote that her passion against injustice originated in the injustice of anti-Semitism. At Peoria High School, after her application to write a column was turned down, she and six friends launched a literary magazine, Tide.

After leaving Berkeley she became a journalist for leftist and labour union publications. She wrote for Federated Press from 1943 to 1946 and for the United Electrical Workers' UE News from 1946 to 1952, where she reported on the House Un-American Activities Committee. She married Carl Friedan in 1947, and was dismissed from UE News in 1952 because she was pregnant with her second child. She then wrote freelance for magazines including Cosmopolitan. Her biographer Daniel Horowitz argues that her feminism began in the 1940s, though she disputed this.

NOW grew from the failure of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. At a conference of state commissions on the status of women, delegates were not allowed to pass a resolution urging it to act, and they met in Friedan's hotel room, where she wrote the acronym NOW on a paper napkin. With Pauli Murray she wrote its statement of purpose. In 1970 she helped defeat the Supreme Court nomination of G. Harrold Carswell, and she supported the Equal Rights Amendment, which passed the House by 354 to 24 and the Senate by 84 to 8.

Friedan pushed the movement to concentrate on economic issues, such as equality in employment and business and provision for child care, and wished to lessen its emphasis on abortion and on rape and pornography. She opposed equating feminism with lesbianism and coined the term lavender menace at a NOW meeting in 1969. Her later books included It Changed My Life, The Second Stage, The Fountain of Age and Beyond Gender, and her autobiography, Life So Far, appeared in 2000.
