She died of congestive heart failure at her home in Washington, D.C., on 4 February 2006, her 85th birthday.
bevagna: Bevagna lies in the flood plain of the Topino river, in the western part of the Umbrian valley and about 225 metres above sea level. It is 25 km south-east of Perugia, 8 km west of Foligno and 16 km south of Assisi. The Clitunno runs close to its ancient walls, and the Timia waters a fertile, well-cultivated plain. In antiquity Classical authors, among them Columella, Silius Italicus and Lucan, refer to the fertility of this valley.

As Mevania the town was an important Umbrian city on the Via Flaminia, between Carsulae and Fulginium. It was already a significant centre before the Roman conquest, and Umbrian forces were stationed there in 308 BCE when the consul Fabius advanced against them. Strabo lists it among the strongest Umbrian cities, and Pliny records that it was enclosed by brick walls and that its territory produced a prized wine called Irtia. Inscriptions show that it belonged to the tribus Aemilia and had quattuorviri among its magistrates.

The city suffered serious damage in barbarian incursions in the 6th century. After the 11th century it became a free municipality governed by consuls, and in 1249 Pope Innocent IV granted it the right to choose its chief magistrate. In November of that year the imperial vicar Thomas I of Aquino besieged and badly damaged it, in the context of Frederick II's claim to the Duchy of Spoleto.

It was under the Trinci family of Foligno from 1371 to 1439, when Cardinal Giovanni Vitelleschi returned it to the direct rule of the Holy See. From 1562 to 1566 its governor was Cardinal Charles Borromeo.

Under the Roman Republic of 1798 Bevagna was assigned to the Canton of Spello. The papal government was restored on 14 May 1814, Pope Leo XII granted the town the title of city in 1825, and in 1860 it joined the Kingdom of Italy.

Roman remains include a temple of the 2nd century, converted into the church of the Madonna della Neve, and the arcaded substructures of a theatre of the 2nd century, which shaped the later streets. A bath building preserves a floor mosaic in black and white of the same century, showing tritons, hippocamps, octopuses, dolphins and lobsters.

The medieval square holds the church of San Michele Arcangelo, with a façade of the early 13th century, the Romanesque church of San Silvestro, built by the architect Binello, whose plaque is dated 1195, and the Palazzo dei Consoli of the later 13th century, which has housed the Teatro Torti since 1886. Medieval festivals are held each year, including the Mercato delle Gaite in June, in which four quarters of the town compete.
beziers: Béziers stands on a small bluff above the River Orb, about ten kilometres from the Mediterranean coast and 75 kilometres south-west of Montpellier. It is a subprefecture of the Hérault department. The Canal du Midi crosses the Orb here by the Pont-canal de l'Orb, an aqueduct claimed to be the first of its kind. Its inhabitants are called Biterrois, after Baeterrae, the Roman name of the town.

Béziers is one of the oldest cities in France. Research published in March 2013 dates its ancient Greek colony to 575 BCE. The Romans refounded it as a colony for veterans in 36–35 BCE, as Colonia Julia Baeterrae Septimanorum, and it exported wine to Rome. It was conquered by Muslims and remained part of Islamic Iberia between 720 and 752. From the 10th to the 12th centuries it was the centre of a viscounty, whose rulers controlled the coastal plain and the main east–west route through Languedoc. The Trencavels ruled for 142 years, until the Albigensian Crusade.

Béziers was a stronghold of Catharism, which the Catholic Church condemned as heretical. The crusaders arrived on 21 July 1209 and offered the Catholics of the town the choice of handing over the heretics or leaving; many refused. The town was sacked the next day, and no one was spared, not even priests or those sheltering in the churches. The papal legate Arnaud-Amaury reported to Pope Innocent III that almost 20,000 people were put to the sword. The Cathedral of Saint Nazaire burned and collapsed on those inside. Other accounts give a handful of survivors.

The city was repopulated, and repairs to the cathedral began in 1215. Béziers joined the royal domain in 1247. In 1632 the Edict of Béziers abolished the privileges of Languedoc, restored in 1649. In the 18th century it prospered through vine growing. On 12 May 1907, 150,000 people gathered in Béziers to defend southern winegrowing, and in June soldiers of the 17th regiment, sent to Agde, mutinied and returned to the town.

The Gothic Cathedral of Saint-Nazaire, rebuilt in the 14th century, rises above the town; its nave is 32 metres high. The park of the Plateau des Poètes dates from 1867, and the allées Paul Riquet carry a statue of the creator of the Canal du Midi. Every August the town holds the Feria de Béziers, centred on bullfighting.
bhagalpur: Bhagalpur, historically known as Champa Nagari, stands on the southern bank of the Ganges in Bihar, at the convergence of Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal. It is the headquarters of Bhagalpur district and division. The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary lies near the town, and the Kosi and Chanan rivers also cross the district.

The city is historically the capital of Anga, an ancient region. Jain tradition holds that all five auspicious events in the life of Vasupujya, the twelfth Teerthankar, took place at Champapur, and that Mahavira spent three rainy-season retreats there. Its main Jain temple is said to be about 2,500 years old. Champa is also the setting of the story of Behula and Lakhinder, told in medieval Bengali works such as the Mansamangal, many of which were produced between the thirteenth and the eighteenth centuries.

At Antichak village lie the excavated ruins of the Vikramshila Mahavihara. Emperor Dharmapala of the Pala Empire established it as an international centre of learning, with Tantric studies among its fields, and it was considered on a par with Nalanda. Bhaktiyar Khilji destroyed it. The Khanqah-e-Shahbazia, founded in 1577, holds the grave of the saint Maulana Shahbaz Muhammad, and its library includes a Qur'an copied by Murshid Quli Khan, the Nawab of Murshidabad.

Bhagalpur is known as the Silk City, after the silk trade of ancient Champanagari. The 2011 census gave its urban agglomeration 410,210 people, making it the third largest city of Bihar. Hinduism is the majority religion, followed by Islam, and Angika is the main language of the district, with Hindi, Bengali, Urdu and Santhali also spoken. Its festivals include a Kali Puja procession so long that one phase of immersing the images takes 36 hours, and the Manasa or Bishari Puja.
bhagat-singh: Bhagat Singh was born into a Punjabi Jat Sikh family in the village of Banga, in the Lyallpur district of the Punjab, then in British India and now in Pakistan. He was the second of seven children of Vidyavati and Kishan Singh Sandhu. His father and his uncle Ajit Singh took part in progressive politics, including the agitation of 1907 around the Canal Colonisation Bill and later the Ghadar Movement. After the village school he attended the Dayanand Anglo-Vedic School in Lahore, and in 1923 he joined the National College there, which Lala Lajpat Rai had founded two years earlier in response to Mahatma Gandhi's non-cooperation movement.

When the Simon Commission visited Lahore on 30 October 1928, Lajpat Rai led a march against it. The superintendent of police, James A. Scott, ordered a lathi charge and personally assaulted Rai, who died of a heart attack on 17 November. Singh, a prominent member of the Hindustan Republican Association, probably did much to change its name to the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. On 17 December 1928 he and Shivaram Rajguru shot John P. Saunders, who had left the District Police Headquarters; the postmortem found eight bullet wounds. Chandra Shekhar Azad shot dead Head Constable Channan Singh, who had given chase. Bhagat Singh escaped by train, with his hair cut and wearing Western dress, passing as a married couple with Durgawati Devi.

In 1929 he proposed a dramatic act to gain publicity: a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly, nominally against the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Dispute Act. After it was thrown on 8 April, he and Batukeshwar Dutt dropped leaflets and were arrested. In the jail he joined Jatin Das in a hunger strike for better conditions, and Das died of starvation in September 1929.

Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were sentenced to death in the Lahore conspiracy case and hanged in the Lahore jail on 23 March 1931, 11 hours ahead of the schedule of 24 March. Their bodies were cremated in secret near Ganda Singh Wala village and the ashes thrown into the Sutlej. He had written that he held human life sacred, but that force used for a legitimate cause was morally justified, and he declined to sign a draft letter for clemency.

An atheist, he read Bakunin, Marx, Lenin and Trotsky, and in his last testament named a Marxist basis for social reconstruction. Jawaharlal Nehru wrote that he became popular because he seemed to vindicate the honour of Lajpat Rai, and that the act was forgotten while the symbol remained. A bronze statue of him was installed in the Parliament of India on 15 August 2008. Communists, Hindu nationalists and others have each claimed his memory.
bhagavata-purana: Bhagavata means follower or worshipper of Vishnu, and Purana means ancient or old traditional history. The text calls Krishna Bhagavan, the Blessed One. Many Indologists give no precise date for the Puranas, because their material was passed on orally, and a date applies only to the text as it now stands. Sheridan, in a study of 1986, dated its composition between 500 and 1000 CE and argued that a version must have existed by 1030, when al-Biruni mentions it. Many scholars, Hardy among them, date its final redaction to the 9th or early 10th century. The oldest surviving manuscript dates to c. 1124-25 and is held in Varanasi.

The twelve books consist of interwoven dialogues. The main reciter is Suka, who speaks to King Pariksit and quotes an earlier speaker, Narada, addressing King Yudhisthira; the text says that the first speaker was its composer, Vyasa, whose son Suka is. The first book opens at the onset of the Kali Yuga with sages performing a thousand-year sacrifice in the forest of Naimisaranya. Later books cover creation, genealogies, avatars of Vishnu such as Rama and Parashurama, and the destruction of the Yadu dynasty. The tenth book, of 90 chapters, tells of Krishna's life.

Its theology uses Vedanta and Samkhya in the service of bhakti. Traditions of Vedanta, among them the Advaita of Adi Shankara, the qualified monism of Rāmānujachārya, the dualism of Madhavacharya and the Bhedābheda of Vallabha and Caitanya, have each read its verses through their own commentaries.

The Bhagavata Purana is widely recognised as the best known and most influential of the Puranas and is called the Fifth Veda. It is among the most commented texts in Indian literature: over eighty medieval commentaries in Sanskrit alone are known, and a version exists in almost every Indian language. Its legends are retold in festivals such as Holi and Diwali, it inspired Ras Leela, dramatic enactments of Krishna's pastimes, and it played a significant part in the Krishna-bhakti movement of Chaitanya in Bengal.

A French translation of a Tamil version appeared in 1788, and the Bhagavata was the first Purana translated into a European language. In the 20th century it spread beyond India and was translated into over twenty languages.
bhaktapur: Bhaktapur lies in the eastern corner of the Kathmandu Valley and is a major Newar settlement. Locally it is called Khwopa, and it was historically known as Bhadgaon. The name Bhaktapur, first attested in an inscription of 928, is widely held to be a Sanskrit rendering of the older Newar name Khōpring, from words meaning cooked rice and village, which appears in a Licchavi inscription of 594. Folklore says the valley was once a lake, drained when the Bodhisattva Manjushri cut a gorge with his sword; the Swiss geologist Toni Hagen showed that it was indeed a lake, which began to drain about thirty thousand years ago.

The 14th-century Gopal Raj Vamshavali credits Ananda Deva, who ruled from 1146 to 1167, with founding the city, probably by joining earlier settlements, and with making it the capital with a royal court, Tripura Rājkula. Shrines of eight Matrikas around the city and that of Tripura Sundari at the centre make the whole town a sacred mandala. As seat of government Bhaktapur attracted invasions, because divisions in the royal family brought in Tirhut and the Khasa Kingdom. Rudra Malla married his sister to the king of Tirhut in the 1310s to end its attacks.

After Nepal Mandala divided into three kingdoms, Bhaktapur stayed a wealthy and powerful Newar kingdom, helped by its place on the India-Tibet trade route. Queen Ganga Devi, the only queen regnant, ruled jointly with her two sons, and under her it reached its territorial zenith. In 1769 the Gorkha Kingdom annexed Bhaktapur, which lost importance to Kathmandu and Lalitpur and stayed isolated. After 1846 Dhir Shumsher Rana, as mayor, had many old palaces demolished and replaced with buildings in British style.

Bhaktapur is predominantly Hindu, and about 90 per cent of its people are Newar. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979. The Nyatapola, a five-roofed pagoda completed in 1702 and commissioned by King Bhupatindra Malla, stands in Taumadhi Square, and Durbar Square holds the palace complex and the stone temples of Vatsala Devi and Siddhi Lakshmi. The city has about 104 hitis, carved water spouts, and 50 artificial ponds, the two oldest built in 1118 and 1168.
bharatiya-janata-party: The party's origins lie in the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, founded in 1951 by Shyama Prasad Mukherjee in collaboration with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and widely regarded as its political arm. Its aims included protecting India's Hindu cultural identity and countering what it saw as the appeasement of Muslims and of Pakistan by the Congress party under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. The RSS lent it several full-time workers, among them Deendayal Upadhyaya, who became General Secretary. The Jana Sangh won three Lok Sabha seats in 1952 and kept a minor presence in parliament until 1967.

After Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a state of emergency in 1975, thousands of Jana Sangh members were imprisoned in the protests. In 1977 the party merged with the Socialist Party, the Congress (O) and the Bharatiya Lok Dal to form the Janata Party, which won a majority and formed a government under Morarji Desai. The former Jana Sangh supplied 93 of its seats, and Atal Bihari Vajpayee became Minister of External Affairs.

The Janata Party dissolved in 1980, and the former Jana Sangh members formed the Bharatiya Janata Party, with Vajpayee as its first president. It first softened the Hindutva stance of its predecessor and stressed Gandhian socialism, and won only two Lok Sabha seats in 1984, an election held soon after Indira Gandhi's assassination, when the Congress won 414 seats. The party then grew through the Ram Rath Yatra in Uttar Pradesh and victories in several state elections, and in 1996 became the largest party in parliament; its government under Vajpayee lasted 13 days.

After the 1998 election the BJP led a coalition, the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), and Vajpayee returned as Prime Minister. The coalition broke up in May 1999 when J. Jayalalithaa withdrew her support, and fresh elections followed. The next NDA government under Vajpayee served a full term, the first non-Congress government to do so, and lost the 2004 election. In the 2014 general election the BJP won 282 seats, the NDA 336 of 543, and Narendra Modi was sworn in as Prime Minister on 26 May 2014.

The party's official philosophy is integral humanism, first formulated by Deendayal Upadhyaya in 1965. It follows Hindutva, a Hindu nationalist ideology, and keeps organisational and ideological links with the RSS. During its first period in national government it set its Hindutva priorities aside and concentrated on economic growth.

The name means Indian People's Party. Its symbol is the lotus, the national flower of India, which has cultural significance in Hinduism and was used by Indian nationalists during the independence movement. Its flag is mostly saffron with a green stripe, and the lotus is set within the saffron part.
bhaskara-ii: Bhāskara II, commonly called Bhāskarāchārya, belonged to a Deśastha Brahmin family of court scholars, mostly astronomer-astrologers, in western India. Verses in his main work place his birth in 1114 at Vijjadavida, in the Sahyadri ranges of the Western Ghats. Scholars disagree about the exact location; many place it near Patan in Chalisgaon, in present-day Maharashtra, while others have suggested Beed, Bijapur, Bidar or Basar. His father Maheśvara was a mathematician, astronomer and astrologer who taught him, and he in turn taught his son Lokasamudra. He is said to have headed the astronomical observatory at Ujjain, the leading centre of mathematical astronomy in medieval India. He died in 1185.

Bhāskara wrote the Siddhānta Śiromaṇi in 1150, at the age of 36. It is an orthodox work of the Brāhmapakṣa school and did not displace the canonical texts of other astronomical traditions. Its two astronomical parts are the Grahagaṇita, on the motions of the planets, eclipses and related phenomena, and the Golādhyāya, on the celestial sphere, the Earth, instruments and the seasons. The Līlāvatī, on arithmetic, and the Bījagaṇita, on algebra, are sometimes counted as parts of it but were usually copied separately. He also wrote a treatise called Karaṇā Kautūhala.

The Līlāvatī has 13 chapters and covers interest, progressions, plane and solid geometry, the shadow of the gnomon, indeterminate equations and combinations. It is written in compact verse for memorising, and its problems are addressed playfully to an inquisitive young learner, using images such as swans, bees and peacocks. A popular story that it was named after Bhāskara's widowed daughter was first recorded in 1587 and has no contemporary support. The Bījagaṇita, in twelve chapters, is regarded as the earliest surviving Indian treatise wholly devoted to algebra. It sets out rules for positive and negative numbers, zero and surds, and methods for linear, quadratic and indeterminate equations.

His chakravala, or cyclic, method gave the first general solution of equations of the type known in the West as Pell's equation. Bhāskara solved a case that Pierre de Fermat posed as a challenge in 1657, which was not solved in Europe until the time of Leonhard Euler. In the Grahagaṇita he also gave a result that can be read as a forerunner of the idea that the cosine is the derivative of the sine, though he did not develop the notion of a derivative.
bhubaneswar: Bhubaneswar lies in the Khordha district of Odisha, in the eastern coastal plains along the axis of the Eastern Ghats, in the Mahanadi River Delta, at an average altitude of 45 metres. The Daya River is 4 kilometres to the south and the Kuakhai 4 kilometres to the east. The name is the anglicisation of the Odia Bhubanēśwara, from Tribhubanēśwara, the Lord of the Three Worlds, which in this context refers to Shiva. The old town was historically often called Chakra Khetra and Ekamra Khetra, the area adorned with a mango tree.

Bhubaneswar stands near the ruins of Sisupalgarh. At Dhauli, near the city, the Kalinga War of about 262 to 261 BCE took place, in which the Mauryan emperor Ashoka invaded and annexed Kalinga. One of the most complete edicts of Ashoka, dating from between 272 and 236 BCE, remains carved in rock 8 kilometres southwest of the modern city. After the decline of the Mauryan empire the area came under the Mahameghavahana dynasty, whose best-known ruler is Kharavela; his Hathigumpha inscription is at the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves near the city. Several dynasties followed, including the Satavahanas, Guptas, Matharas and Shailodbhavas.

Cuttack, the capital of British-ruled and independent Orissa, was vulnerable to floods and short of space, and in September 1946 a proposal to build a new capital was introduced in the Legislative Assembly of the Odisha Province. The German architect Otto Königsberger designed the modern city in 1946, and with Jamshedpur and Chandigarh it was one of modern India's first planned cities. The foundation of the new capital was laid on 13 April 1948 and the Legislative Assembly moved from Cuttack in 1949. The first census of independent India, in 1951, counted just 16,000 people. A municipality was established on 12 March 1979, and the Bhubaneswar Municipal Corporation on 14 August 1994.

Bhubaneswar is the capital and largest city of Odisha and is called the Temple City. Its temples are built in the Kalinga architectural style, with a curving spire over the sanctum housing the presiding deity and a pyramid-roofed hall where people sit and pray. They include the Lingaraja, Muktesvara, Rajarani and Ananta Vasudeva temples, and the small Kukutesvara Siva Temple, a shrine to Shiva about a thousand years old. At the festival of Ashokashtami the image of Lingaraja is taken in procession to the Mausima Temple. The area formed by Bhubaneswar and Cuttack, often called the twin cities of Odisha, had a population of 1.7 million in 2011. The main language is Odia, and Utkal University is the oldest university in Odisha.
bhumibol-adulyadej: Bhumibol was born on 5 December 1927 at Cambridge Hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the youngest son of Prince Mahidol Adulyadej and his commoner wife Mom Sangwan, later Princess Srinagarindra. His father was enrolled in the public health programme at Harvard University, which made Bhumibol the only hereditary monarch born in the United States. He had an older sister, Princess Galyani Vadhana, and an older brother, Prince Ananda Mahidol. He spent his early life in Switzerland, growing up after the 1932 Siamese revolution that toppled the absolute monarchy of his uncle, King Prajadhipok.

Bhumibol became king on 9 June 1946, when Ananda Mahidol died of a gunshot wound in circumstances that remain unclear. An early government statement called it an accident, but an investigation committee judged that virtually impossible. Three palace aides were convicted of regicide and executed by firing squad on 17 February 1955, after Bhumibol rejected their appeals for clemency. He was crowned on 5 May 1950 in the Grand Palace, the first coronation of a Thai sovereign under constitutional monarchy, pledging to reign with righteousness for the benefit and happiness of the Siamese people.

In his early years, under the military government of Plaek Phibunsongkhram, he held little real political power. In September 1957 he advised the field marshal to resign to avoid a coup; Phibunsongkhram refused, and General Sarit Thanarat seized power that evening. Under Sarit the monarchy was revitalised: the king toured the provinces, patronised development projects and visited the United States and Europe in 1960. In 1973 he announced the resignation and departure of General Thanom Kittikachorn after police killed dozens of students. In 1992 he played a key role in ending the Black May crisis, when the military killed many protesters. He was also a jazz saxophonist and composer, a sailor and a painter, and held patents for a waste water aerator and for rainmaking.

Bhumibol died aged 88 at Siriraj Hospital in Bangkok on 13 October 2016, after a period of declining health. Thousands lined the route as his body was taken to the Grand Palace. His reign of 70 years and 126 days was the longest of any Thai monarch. He was widely revered, and protected by strict lese-majeste laws, under which critics could be jailed for three to fifteen years. His son, Crown Prince Maha Vajiralongkorn, succeeded him as Rama X, and the cremation took place in 2017 at Sanam Luang.
bias-of-priene: Bias was born at Priene in Ionia and was active in the sixth century BCE. He was the son of Teautames and a younger contemporary of Solon. He is said to have descended from the Thebans who founded Priene, a claim common among the Ionian aristocracy. His dates are unclear, since he is described in connection with the Second Messenian War, the reign of the Lydian king Alyattes and the conquests of the Akkadian Empire. Diogenes Laertius reports that Duris of Samos called him a labourer, while others described him as wealthy. Plato and Diogenes Laertius, among others, name him as one of the Seven Sages of Greece.

Bias worked as an advocate, offering legal services without payment to those who had been wronged. He went to Samos as an envoy for Priene in a territorial dispute, arguing that the Batinetis belonged to Priene because the Cimmerians had taken it before Samos captured it. The mediator ruled for Samos. This episode is the best attested of the stories about him and is the earliest known case of mediation, as opposed to arbitration, ending a conflict in ancient Greece.

According to Herodotus, Bias proposed that the Ionians migrate together to Sardinia and found one settlement safe from Persia, and he is among the earliest to discuss the Ionians as a single group. Herodotus also says that either Bias or Pittacus of Mytilene persuaded King Croesus of Lydia not to build a fleet. Tradition adds that he ransomed kidnapped Messenian girls and tricked Alyattes into abandoning a siege of Priene by showing fattened mules and corn laid over sand. He is said to have died while arguing a case, with his head in his grandson's lap.

His best-known saying, translated as most men are bad, won the praise of Heraclitus, who made him an exception to his scorn of earlier figures. Diogenes Laertius reports that he held persuasion preferable to force, that one should treat friends as possible enemies and enemies as possible friends, and that the inability to bear misfortune is itself a misfortune. He is said to have treated possessions as unimportant, leaving Priene under attack without them because his letters and wisdom were all he owned, and to have counselled piety in fear of the gods.

Priene established a heroic cult for him with a heroon and in the second century BCE minted coins showing him with his tripod. Most of what is known of him comes from Diogenes Laertius, and for figures of this period history and legend are not always distinct.
biberach-an-der-riss: Biberach an der Riß, often called simply Biberach, is the capital of the Biberach district in the Upper Swabia region of Baden-Württemberg, between the river Danube and Lake Constance. It takes its full name from the small river Riß that flows through it, to tell it apart from other towns of similar names. The town has about 32,000 inhabitants.

For many centuries Biberach was an Imperial Free City of the Holy Roman Empire, and in that role it took part in the Reichstag of 1792. During the Reformation it was notable as one of a few mixed imperial cities, with Ravensburg, Augsburg and Dinkelsbühl, where the Peace of Westphalia established a joint Catholic and Protestant government, with posts divided exactly equally between the two confessions.

This status ended in 1803, when the Margraviate of Baden, soon to become a grand duchy, annexed the town. In 1806 it was traded to the Kingdom of Württemberg in exchange for the town of Villingen, and in 1871 it became part of the German Empire on its creation. During the French Revolutionary Wars the town and its surroundings were the site of two sizeable battles, in 1796 and 1800. In World War II two large prisoner-of-war camps stood here: Oflag V-B for officers and the internment camp Ilag V-B for Allied civilians, mainly from the Channel Islands.

Biberach is a significant industrial location in south-west Germany, home to firms such as Liebherr, which began making cranes there in 1954, and Boehringer Ingelheim. The Braith-Mali-Museum, in a building of the 16th century, presents archaeology, history, art and natural history, and the Wieland-Museum, founded in 1907 in the summer house of the writer Christoph Martin Wieland, explores his life and work. The Biberacher Schützenfest is a historic festival for children and the town, held each July for nine days.
biblical-hebrew: Hebrew developed in the latter half of the second millennium BCE in Canaan, between the Jordan and the Mediterranean. In its earliest stages it was not highly differentiated from Ugaritic and the Canaanite of the Amarna letters, and the Northwest Semitic languages formed a dialect continuum in the Iron Age, with Phoenician and Aramaic at either extreme. Hebrew belongs with Phoenician in the Canaanite subgroup, which also includes Ammonite, Edomite and Moabite. The oldest layer, Archaic Hebrew, appears in the poetry of the Bible, such as the Song of the Sea and the Song of Deborah, and in inscriptions of about 1000 BCE.

Biblical Hebrew has the typically Semitic system of roots, usually of three consonants, arranged in patterns to form words. It distinguishes masculine and feminine genders and singular, plural and the uncommon dual numbers. Verbs have two main conjugations, the suffix and the prefix forms, whose meaning for tense and aspect is debated and depends much on context. The usual word order is verb, subject, object. The language of the Bible had other names: the Hebrew Bible calls it the language of Canaan or Judean, and the term Hebrew comes from Greek and Mishnaic Hebrew texts, its origin obscure.

The consonantal text of the Hebrew Bible reflects several stages of the language, with evidence of regional dialects, including differences between the northern Kingdom of Israel and the southern Kingdom of Judah. In the biblical story of Jephthah, his forces from Gilead identified fleeing Ephraimites by their pronunciation of the word shibboleth.

Spoken Hebrew persisted as a first language through the Second Temple period and eventually developed into Mishnaic Hebrew, which was used as a second language until the 5th century. The Samaritans kept the Paleo-Hebrew script, and still use a descendant of it. After the Babylonian captivity the Imperial Aramaic alphabet gradually displaced it and became the source of the present Hebrew alphabet. The early writing systems marked consonants only, and certain letters called matres lectionis came increasingly to mark vowels.

The earliest Hebrew writing yet found, an ink text of five lines on a potsherd from Khirbet Qeiyafa, dates to the 10th century BCE. The consonantal text of the Bible was transmitted in manuscript and revised during the Second Temple period. The Masoretes added the Tiberian vowel marks in the Middle Ages, after 600 CE, and this is the system still widely used.
bibliotheque-nationale-de-france: The library traces its origin to the royal library founded at the Louvre Palace by Charles V in 1368, from manuscripts he had received from his predecessor John II. The first librarian of record was Claude Mallet, the king's valet de chambre, who made a catalogue of the books. After the death of Charles VI the collection was bought by the English regent of France, the Duke of Bedford, who took it to England in 1424, and it was apparently dispersed at his death in 1435.

The invention of printing led to a new collection at the Louvre, inherited by Louis XI in 1461. Later kings added to it: Charles VIII seized part of the collection of the kings of Aragon, Louis XII brought in the library at Blois, and Francis I merged it with his private library at Fontainebleau in 1534.

The collection moved several times in Paris, and many treasures were lost. Under the librarian Jacques Auguste de Thou it became the largest and richest collection of books in the world, and it grew rapidly under Louis XIII and Louis XIV, in great part through the interest of the minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert. The library moved in 1666 to two houses in the Rue Vivienne and opened to the public in 1692. Jean-Paul Bignon reformed its system, and from 1721 the Richelieu site, the main location for 275 years, began to take shape.

After the French First Republic was established in September 1792 the Assembly declared the Bibliothèque du Roi national property and it became the Bibliothèque Nationale. Its collections passed 300,000 volumes as the private libraries of aristocrats and clergy were seized. Napoleon ordered provincial libraries to send it any book it lacked and added spoil from his conquests, some of it returned after his fall. In 1868 it moved into new buildings on the Rue de Richelieu designed by Henri Labrouste, and in 1896 it was still the largest repository of books in the world.

The library is a public establishment under the Ministry of Culture and the national repository of all that is published in France, which by law must be deposited there. President François Mitterrand announced a new library on 14 July 1988; the architect Dominique Perrault designed it, and after cost overruns that earned it the nickname Très Grande Bibliothèque it was inaugurated on 15 December 1996.

Its Manuscripts department houses the largest collection of medieval and modern manuscripts worldwide, including about 5,000 Ancient Greek manuscripts. Gallica, its digital library established in October 1997, makes freely available millions of books, manuscripts, newspapers, images, maps and recordings.
bicycle: The dandy horse, also called the Draisienne or Laufmaschine, was invented by the German Baron Karl von Drais, who introduced it to the public in Mannheim in 1817 and in Paris in 1818. It was the first means of human transport to use only two wheels in tandem and is regarded as the first bicycle, though it had no pedals: the rider sat astride a wooden frame and pushed it along with their feet while steering the front wheel. A Scottish blacksmith, Kirkpatrick MacMillan, may have built the first mechanically propelled two-wheeled vehicle in 1839, although the claim is often disputed.

In the early 1860s the Frenchmen Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added a mechanical crank drive with pedals to an enlarged front wheel, the velocipede, which was the first to be mass-produced. In 1869 the Scotsman Thomas McCall built a rod-driven velocipede with rear-wheel drive, and Eugène Meyer of Paris patented a method of tensioning wire spokes that allowed stronger, lighter wheels. The velocipede developed into the penny-farthing, with a metal frame, wire-spoked wheels and solid rubber tyres. Britain's first cycle factory grew from the Coventry Sewing Machine Company's order for a Michaux cycle in 1868, which led to the Coventry Model.

A bicycle is a human-powered or motor-assisted, pedal-driven, single-track vehicle with two wheels attached to a frame, one behind the other. The basic shape of the upright or safety bicycle has changed little since the first chain-driven model was developed around 1885. Most have a diamond frame, a truss of two triangles. Historically, women's frames had a top tube joined lower on the seat tube, so that a rider could mount and dismount in a skirt or dress; this is called a step-through or open frame.

It is the most efficient human-powered means of transport in terms of the energy a person must spend to cover a distance. Up to 99 per cent of the energy the rider puts into the pedals reaches the wheels, though gearing may reduce this by 10 to 15 per cent. Cycling takes about four-fifths less energy than walking the same distance.

The bicycle had a considerable effect on society, in both culture and industry. Around the turn of the 20th century it reduced crowding in inner-city tenements by letting workers commute from more spacious suburban homes, and it reduced dependence on horses. It also allowed people to travel into the country for leisure, being three times as energy efficient as walking and three to four times as fast.

Several components that played a key role in the development of the car were first invented for the bicycle: ball bearings, pneumatic tyres, chain-driven sprockets and tension-spoked wheels. The first bicycle sharing scheme was the White Bicycle plan in Amsterdam in 1965.
biella: Biella is the capital of the province of the same name in Piedmont, about 80 kilometres north-east of Turin and at about the same distance west-north-west of Milan. It lies in the foothills of the Alps, in an area of springs and lakes fed by glaciers and watered by the streams Elvo, Oropa and Cervo. The first inhabitants were Ligurians and Celts. A Ligurian people, the Victimuli, exploited gold veins near the Elvo on the plain of the Bessa, an activity that continued into the early Middle Ages.

The name appears for the first time as Bugella in a document of 826, recording the donation of Bugella to Count Busone by Louis the Pious. On 12 April 1160 Uguccione, bishop of Vercelli, granted trade privileges to anyone living on the Piazzo hill as a refuge from the warfare between Guelphs and Ghibellines of Vercelli, which was the birth of the Borgo del Piazzo. A revolt destroyed the bishop's castle in the 14th century, and Biella and its dependent communes came under the House of Savoy.

In the 14th and 15th centuries the Visconti family competed with Savoy for the region. The French occupied Biella in 1704, and in 1706 the Biellese soldier Pietro Micca saved nearby Turin from a siege, but died doing so. The French occupied the town again in 1798 and annexed it after the Battle of Marengo, and the Congress of Vienna returned it to Savoy. In 1859 Biella was besieged by the Austrians until Garibaldi ended the siege.

The statutes of Biella already refer to the guilds of wool workers and weavers in 1245, and the region's high pastures and abundant water suited the trade. A silk factory built in 1695 was converted in 1835 into a wool factory with mechanical looms, putting Biella at the forefront of the industry.

Biella remains an important wool processing and textile centre; Ermenegildo Zegna and Cerruti 1881 are among its firms. Its cathedral grew around the Romanesque baptistery of the 10th and 11th centuries, which houses 13th-century frescoes. Nearby, the Sanctuary of Oropa, a site of pilgrimage, became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.
bihac: Bihać stands on the banks of the river Una in northwestern Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Bosanska Krajina region close to the border with Croatia. It is the administrative centre of Una-Sana Canton in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The town was first built on the river's Island of St. Ladislav, and it was the centre of the Pounje, the lands along the Una. Its municipality includes many villages, among them Ripač, Kulen Vakuf and Brekovica.

Medieval towns around the Una began to appear in the middle of the 13th century. Bihać is first mentioned on 26 February 1260 in a charter of King Béla IV, which describes it as a town on the Island of St. Ladislav owned by the Benedictine abbey of Topusko. Two years later, in 1262, Béla proclaimed it a royal free city under the direct authority of the throne, with rights that let it develop independently of local lords. A charter of 1271 confirms the status. At the head of the municipality stood a town elder, often called a judge, and the town had a curia of magistrates and notaries who kept court and civil records.

In 1530 Austria sent troops to defend seven key strongholds in Croatia, among them Bihać. The Ottomans occupied it in 1592 after a siege of ten days, and until the 19th century it was one of the most important forts in Bosnia. Auguste Marmont, governor-general of the Illyrian Provinces, briefly interrupted Ottoman rule on 5 May 1810 and then withdrew. Ottoman rule ended de facto after the Congress of Berlin.

During World War II the town was occupied by Axis troops and included in the Independent State of Croatia. The Ustaše regime committed the genocide of the Serbs and the Holocaust; from July to September 1941 the Ustaše killed some 15,000 Serbs, along with some Jews and Roma, at Garavice, near Bihać. For two months in late 1942 and early 1943 Bihać was the capital of a short-lived territory, the Bihać Republic, until German forces recaptured it. It returned to Bosnian territory on 28 March 1945. The town was besieged for three years from 1992 to 1995 during the Bosnian War.

At the 2013 census the city had 56,261 inhabitants, of whom 88 per cent were recorded as followers of Islam. The 1991 census recorded 46,737 Bosniaks, 12,689 Serbs, 5,580 Croats and 4,356 Yugoslavs in the municipality. The fertile soil makes agriculture significant for its economy.
bihar: Bihar borders Uttar Pradesh to the west, Nepal to the north, the northern part of West Bengal to the east and Jharkhand to the south, and covers 94,163 square kilometres. The Ganges flows west to east through the state and divides its fertile plain into North Bihar and South Bihar. Along with its tributaries, the Gandak and Koshi from the Nepalese Himalayas and the Bagmati, it regularly floods parts of the plain. The name is generally believed to derive from the Sanskrit and Pali vihāra, a monastery or religious dwelling, and medieval Persian and Turkic writers applied it to the area.

Chirand, on the northern bank of the Ganges in Saran district, has an archaeological record from the Neolithic, about 2500 to 1345 BCE. Regions of Bihar such as Magadha, Mithila and Anga are mentioned in the religious texts and epics of ancient India. According to Buddhist tradition the Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, at the Mahabodhi Temple. Early Buddhist centres of learning such as Nalanda and Vikramashila arose in Bihar and drew students and scholars from across Asia, and under dynasties including the Mauryas and Guptas Buddhism received royal patronage and spread from the region to other parts of Asia.

Buddhism in Magadha declined after the invasion of Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji, when many viharas were destroyed together with the universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila. Some historians believe thousands of Buddhist monks were massacred in the 12th century, while D. N. Jha suggests that these incidents resulted from Buddhist and Brahmin skirmishes in a fight for supremacy. After the Pala Empire the Karnat dynasty came to power in Mithila in the 11th century, and the Oiniwar dynasty succeeded it in the 14th.

After the Battle of Buxar in 1764 the British East India Company obtained the diwani rights, the right to administer and collect revenue, for Bihar, Bengal and Odisha. Bihar remained part of the Bengal Presidency until 1912, when Bihar and Orissa were carved out as a new province. In April 1917 Mahatma Gandhi visited Champaran, where Raj Kumar Shukla had drawn his attention to the exploitation of the peasants by European indigo planters, and the Champaran Satyagraha that followed drew support from Bihari nationalists such as Rajendra Prasad.

Bihar is a state of eastern India. The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its official languages are Hindi and Urdu, and the main native languages are Maithili, Magahi and Bhojpuri.
bijapur: Bijapur lies in the interior of the Deccan peninsula in northern Karnataka, some 519 km north-west of Bengaluru. The Krishna is the most important river of the district, which has deep black soil good for jowar, wheat, pulses and sugarcane. Evidence shows the area was inhabited from the Stone Age.

The city was established in the 10th and 11th centuries under the Kalyani Chalukyas and was known as Vijayapura, the city of victory. It passed to the Yadavas, came under the influence of Alauddin Khalji of Delhi towards the end of the 13th century, and was conquered by the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347. When Bahmani authority over its provinces ceased by 1490, the Adil Shahi dynasty arose, and the sultans of the Bijapur Sultanate ruled from 1490 to 1686.

The city owes much of its greatness to Yusuf Adil Shah, the founder of the independent state, to Ali Adil Shah I, who fortified it, and to Ibrahim Adil Shah II. At its peak in the early 17th century it is estimated to have held half a million to a million people. The fort, completed in 1566, has a wall with ninety-six bastions and a moat, and outside the walls lie the remains of a vast city of tombs and mosques.

The Mughal emperor Aurangazeb conquered Bijapur in 1686, having made it a subah two years earlier, and disease and other disasters afterwards greatly reduced its population. Mughal rule lasted until 1723; the Nizam of Hyderabad held it briefly, and in 1760 it passed to the Maratha Confederacy. After 1818 it came under the British, and in 1956 it joined Karnataka.

Bijapur is the headquarters of Bijapur district and is known for the monuments of the Adil Shahi period, among them the Bijapur Fort, the Bara Kaman, the Jama Masjid and the Gol Gumbaz. Its name was changed officially to Vijayapura in November 2014.
bikini-atoll: Bikini Atoll consists of 23 low islands of coral limestone and sand around a central lagoon of about 594 square kilometres, at the northern end of the Ralik Chain, some 850 kilometres north-west of Majuro. The average elevation is only about 2.1 metres above low tide. Its Marshallese name is Pikinni; the English form comes from the name given to it when it was part of German New Guinea. Between the 19th century and 1946 it was also known as Eschscholtz Atoll.

Bikini islanders lived by cultivating plants and fishing, and built double-hulled proas to sail between the atolls. Land was held by clans under chiefs. Japan took the Marshall Islands in 1914 and held them under a League of Nations mandate from 1920, and American forces captured nearby Kwajalein in February 1944.

The United States Navy wanted to learn what a nuclear weapon would do to ships, and chose Bikini. In 1946 the 167 islanders were moved to Rongerik, which could not feed them; by early 1948 they were close to starvation and were taken to Kwajalein, where they lived in tents beside a runway for six months before settling on Kili Island. From 1946 to 1958 the United States detonated 23 nuclear devices there, with a combined yield of about 77 megatons. Three islands were destroyed.
About 100 residents returned in 1972. In 1978 tests found dangerously high strontium-90 in well water and abnormal caesium-137 in the islanders' bodies, and they were removed again in September 1978.

UNESCO named the atoll a World Heritage Site on 3 August 2010, citing the sunken ships, among them the aircraft carrier USS Saratoga and the Japanese battleship Nagato, and the large crater left by the Bravo test. In 1998 an advisory group of the International Atomic Energy Agency recommended that Bikini Island not be permanently resettled. The islanders and their descendants live on other Marshallese islands and in the United States.
biladi-biladi-biladi: The anthem's words were written by Muhammad Yunis al-Qady and its music composed by Sayed Darwish, who kept close ties with early leaders of Egypt's national movement for independence, such as Mustafa Kamel. The chorus derives from one of Kamel's best-known nationalist speeches, delivered in 1907, in which he told his country that his love, his heart, his life and his blood were for it, and that there was no life except with Egypt. The anthem was officially adopted in 1979, and the musician Mohamed Abdel Wahab was involved in preparing it at the direction of President Anwar El-Sadat.

Egypt's first national anthem was an instrumental royal piece with no official lyrics, associated with the reign of Khedive Ismail and played at the opening of the Suez Canal. It was adopted as the first national anthem in 1871, and its melody is most likely the work of Giuseppe Pugioli, an Italian cornetist who stayed in Egypt. It did not become popular inside Egypt, and Ahmad Shawqi won a competition in 1920 to write words for it, but his entry failed to gain traction with the bureaucracy.

Eslami ya Misr, by Mustafa Sadiq Al-Rafei with music by Safar Ali, served from 1923 to 1936. King Farouk restored the royal anthem in 1936, and it continued, renamed the republican anthem, after the monarchy ended in 1953. In 1960 a decree adopted a wordless melody by Kamal El-Tawil as the anthem, and it served until 1979.

Republican Decree No. 149 of 1979 made Bilady, Bilady, Bilady the national anthem. A decree of December 1982 laid down that the words of the first verse accompany the music at popular and national celebrations, while only the instrumental music is played when welcoming presidents and foreign delegations. An unofficial Coptic version, not codified in law, circulates widely online.
bilbao: Bilbao lies in the north-central part of Spain, about 16 kilometres south of the Bay of Biscay. Its urban core is surrounded by two small mountain ranges, and the Nervión and the Ibaizabal join at Basauri to form an estuary some 15 kilometres long. The climate is oceanic, with rain through the year. Basque has two names for the city, Bilbao and Bilbo, and Bilbo is held to be the historical one.

Diego López V de Haro, lord of Biscay, founded the town by a charter dated at Valladolid on 15 June 1300, which King Ferdinand IV of Castile confirmed at Burgos on 4 January 1301. It stood on the right bank of the Nervión and received the fuero of Logroño, a body of rights that proved central to its growth. At first it had three streets inside walls; four more formed the Seven Streets, and the walls were pulled down in 1571 after floods and a great fire in 1569.

The Catholic Monarchs gave Bilbao the title of Noble Town on 20 September 1475. On 21 June 1511 Queen Joanna of Castile ordered the creation of its Consulate of the Sea, which long controlled the estuary and made the port one of the most important of the kingdom. Wool and iron from the Biscayan quarries were exported across Europe. The first printing press arrived in 1577, and in 1596 the first book in Basque was published there. After the siege of the First Carlist War the city received the added title of Unbeaten on 25 December 1836.

In the nineteenth century iron mines, ironworks and shipbuilding brought heavy industrialisation and a population explosion that led the city to annex neighbouring municipalities. The Bank of Bilbao was founded in 1857, the stock exchange opened on 21 July 1890, and an outer port was built at Santurtzi in 1902.

Bilbao is the largest city of the Basque Country and the capital of the province of Biscay, with 347,342 inhabitants and a metropolitan area of 1,037,847. Its renewal as a city of services began with the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. The football club Athletic Club, which fields only Basque players, is a symbol of Basque nationalism.
bilhorod-dnistrovskyi: Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi lies on the right bank of the Dniester Estuary, which leads to the Black Sea, in the historical region of Budjak. Its names almost all mean white castle or white city: Asprokastron in Greek, Album Castrum in Latin, Cetatea Albă in Romanian, Akkerman in Ottoman Turkish and Weißenburg in German. The Genoese, who ruled it in the 14th and 15th centuries, used Moncastro. Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi has been the official name since 1944; Dnistrovskyi was added to tell it apart from Belgorod in Russia.

Milesian colonists founded a settlement named Tyras here in the 6th century BCE, which later came under Roman and Byzantine rule. In the 13th century the Cumans held the site, and from about 1290 it was a centre of Genoese commerce. Saint John the New, patron saint of Moldavia, was martyred in the city in 1330 during a Tatar incursion. Cetatea Albă was the last city on the right bank of the Dniester to join the Principality of Moldavia, for which it was a major port and fortress. The fortress was rebuilt in 1407 under Alexander the Good and in 1440 under Stephen II of Moldavia.

The Ottomans took the city in the 15th century. The citadel surrendered on a promise of safe passage, but most of the inhabitants were slaughtered. As Akkerman it became an Ottoman fortress against Poland-Lithuania and later Russia, and a centre of the Black Sea slave trade. Russia annexed it in 1812 with the rest of Bessarabia. On 25 September 1826 Russia and the Ottomans signed the Akkerman Convention here. The city belonged to Romania from 1918 to 1940 and again from 1941 to 1944, and has been in Ukraine since the Soviet period.

Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi is a port city in Odesa Oblast with a large freight seaport. In 1897 Jews formed 19.9 per cent of its population; in 1905 a pogrom killed eight of them, and during World War II about 800 who remained in the city were shot, and others were deported to Transnistria, where most died.
bill-of-rights-1689: Interest in Magna Carta revived in the 17th century, and Parliament passed the Petition of Right in 1628 and the Habeas Corpus Act in 1679. After the English Civil War and the years of the Protectorate and the Restoration, Parliamentarians who objected to the policies of James II invited the Dutch stadtholder William III of Orange-Nassau to overthrow him. William's invasion led James to flee to France, and in December 1688 the peers appointed William provisional governor. A Convention Parliament convened on 22 January 1689.

On 29 January the House of Commons proposed a statement of the rights James had violated. On 13 February the Marquess of Halifax offered the throne to William and Mary, who accepted, and they were crowned on 11 April under a new oath promising to govern according to the statutes agreed in Parliament.

The Declaration of Right was enacted as the Bill of Rights, which received royal assent on 16 December 1689. It declared illegal the suspension of laws or dispensing with them without Parliament's consent, the commission for ecclesiastical causes, and the levying of taxes without a grant of Parliament. It affirmed the right to petition the king, free elections, freedom of speech in Parliament, and frequent parliaments. It held that a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent was against the law, and that Protestants might have arms for their defence as allowed by law. It also forbade excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments.

The Act listed twelve policies of James II said to subvert the Protestant religion and the laws of the kingdom, including the prosecution of the Seven Bishops, and declared that he had abdicated. It barred Roman Catholics from the throne, and named William and Mary as successors to James, with the crown passing then to Mary's heirs and to her sister, Princess Anne.

The Act of Settlement of 1701 later altered the line of succession. A separate Claim of Right Act of 1689 applies in Scotland. Together they contributed to parliamentary sovereignty and a constitutional monarchy, and William Blackstone described such acts as fundamental laws of England. The Bill influenced the Virginia Declaration of Rights of 1776, and the Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution reproduces almost verbatim its ban on excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishment. It was also a model for the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen and the European Convention on Human Rights.

The Bill of Rights remains in statute in the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms, and Article 9 on freedom of speech in Parliament is still cited. It restates in statutory form the Declaration of Right that the Convention Parliament presented in February 1689, inviting William III and Mary II to become joint sovereigns.
biloxi: Biloxi lies on the Gulf Coast of southern Mississippi in Harrison County, on the Mississippi Sound, with barrier islands off the shore. It is bordered partly on the northeast by Biloxi Bay, across which lie Ocean Springs and St. Martin, and Gulfport adjoins it on the west. The climate is humid subtropical, and tropical storms strike in late summer and autumn. The French name Bilocci transliterates the name of the local Native American tribe in their own language.

In 1699 French colonists under Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville formed the first permanent European settlement in French Louisiana at Fort Maurepas, now in Ocean Springs and called Old Biloxi. The present city's site was first settled in 1720 around Fort Louis, and the capital of French Louisiana moved there from Mobile. In 1722, fearing tides and hurricanes, Governor Bienville moved it to New Orleans. France ceded its colonies east of the Mississippi to Great Britain in 1763; British rule lasted until 1779 and Spanish rule until 1810, yet Biloxi remained mostly French in character. The United States took over the area in 1811, and Mississippi became a state in 1817.

In the 19th century Biloxi became a summer resort. The Biloxi Lighthouse was built in Baltimore and finished on the site in May 1848. Union forces took Ship Island early in the Civil War and with it control of Biloxi, which suffered no direct damage. The first seafood cannery opened in 1881 and drew immigrants from Europe. Keesler Field, built during World War II, became a major training site. In 1959 the physician Gilbert R. Mason led the Biloxi Wade-Ins against the exclusion of black people from the beach; a riot in 1960 killed ten people, and the protests led to desegregation of the beaches. Legal gambling in the 1990s made the city a centre of resort casinos.

Biloxi had a population of 49,449 at the 2020 census and is one of the two principal cities of the Gulfport–Biloxi metropolitan area. It has six historic districts on the National Register of Historic Places, and its Blessing of the Fleet, begun in 1929, takes place each year before the shrimp season. Katrina's storm surge of 30 feet on 29 August 2005 caused massive damage, and the most destructive earlier hurricanes struck in 1855, 1906, 1909, 1947 and 1969.
bindusara: Bindusara's life is not documented as well as those of his father Chandragupta and his son Ashoka. Much of what is known comes from Jain and Buddhist legends written hundreds of years after his death, such as the 12th-century Parishishta-Parvan of Hemachandra, the Mahavamsa and the Ashokavadana. Most sources, including the Puranas and the Mahavamsa, make him the son of Chandragupta, though the Dipavamsa and the Ashokavadana give other parentage. Hemachandra names his mother as Durdhara.

Greek writers called him Amitrochates or Allitrochades, probably from the Sanskrit title Amitraghāta, slayer of enemies, and like Ashoka he bore the title Devanampriya, Beloved of the Gods. Buddhist and Jain texts tell that the minister Chanakya fed Chandragupta small doses of poison to build his immunity, and that when the pregnant queen ate some, Chanakya cut open her body to save the child. The name Bindusara is explained by drops of goat's blood in the Buddhist version and by a drop of poison in the Jain one.

The historian Upinder Singh estimates that he came to the throne around 297 BCE. The 16th-century Tibetan author Taranatha says that Chanakya destroyed the nobles and kings of 16 towns and made Bindusara master of the land between the eastern and western seas. Some historians take this to mean a conquest of the Deccan, while others think it refers only to the suppression of revolts. Sailendra Nath Sen concludes that he kept the territory he inherited, and Alain Daniélou that his achievement was to organise and consolidate it.

The Ashokavadana says he sent Ashoka to besiege Takshashila, whose people said they opposed only his oppressive ministers. Bindusara kept friendly relations with the Greeks: Deimachos of Plateia was the ambassador of the Seleucid king Antiochus I at his court. According to Athenaeus, Bindusara asked Antiochus for sweet wine, dried figs and a sophist, and was told that Greek law forbade the sale of a sophist. Buddhist texts call him a follower of Brahmanism, while the Ajivika sect appears to have enjoyed his patronage.

He died in the 270s BCE, around 273 BCE according to Singh. The Mahavamsa gives him a reign of 28 years and the Puranas 25. All the sources agree that Ashoka succeeded him, but they differ on how. According to the Mahavamsa, Ashoka hurried from Ujjain to Pataliputra and killed his 99 brothers, sparing only Tishya. The Brahmanda Purana says that Bindusara crowned Ashoka himself. Sen believes that a four-year struggle over the succession followed, ending with Ashoka's accession in 269-268 BCE.
bingen-am-rhein: Bingen am Rhein lies in the Mainz-Bingen district of Rhineland-Palatinate. The river Nahe empties into the Rhine here, where the Rhine Gorge begins, and the town forms the southern limit of the UNESCO Rhine Gorge World Heritage Site. The original name was Bingium, a Celtic word that may have meant a hole in the rock, a description of the shoal behind the Mouse Tower, known as the Binger Loch.

The first settlement seems to have been Celtic. In the early first century CE Roman troops were stationed here, building a wooden bridge across the Nahe and a bridgehead fort, and Bingen was the starting point of the Via Ausonia, a military road to Trier. The presbyter Aetherius founded a Christian community between 335 and 360. After the fall of the Limes the town became a Frankish royal estate, and in 983 Otto II gave it to Archbishop Willigis of Mainz.

The inhabitants repeatedly sought independence, and in 1165 disputes between the archbishop and the emperor led to the town's destruction. It belonged to the Rhenish League of Towns in the 13th century and took an unsuccessful part in the German Peasants' War in 1525. The Cathedral Chapter of Mainz acquired it in two halves, in 1424 and 1438. From 1792 to 1813 it was French, and in 1816, after the Congress of Vienna, it passed to the Grand Duchy of Hesse-Darmstadt. A Jewish community is mentioned in the mid-12th century, was expelled in 1507, and was ended by deportations in 1942, after which only four returned.

The Mouse Tower is associated with a legend in which Hatto II, Archbishop of Mainz, was eaten by mice, a tale attributed since the 19th century increasingly to his predecessor Hatto I. Other sights are the Basilica of St. Martin, Klopp Castle and the Drususbrücke. The poet Stefan George was born in Bingen, and the abbess Hildegard of Bingen was born 40 km away at Bermersheim. Three winegrowing areas meet at the town.
biobio-river: The Biobío is the second-longest river in Chile, after the Loa, and flows 380 kilometres from Galletué and Icalma lakes in the Andes to the Gulf of Arauco on the Pacific. Its basin is the third largest in Chile, after those of the Loa and the Baker, and with an average width of one kilometre it is the widest river in the country. Its major tributaries are the Malleco and the Laja, the Laja being the larger in volume of water.

From the east shore of Galletué Lake it flows a few kilometres east, receives the waters of Icalma Lake, and then turns north-west through a broad Andean valley. Its upper course, known as Alto Bío Bío, runs fast through a narrow valley. After reaching the Intermediate Depression it crosses a flat area, widening to between 60 and 120 metres, and the Vergara River joins it near Nacimiento. Near San Rosendo and La Laja it is joined by the Laja, and at its mouth near San Pedro de la Paz in Gran Concepción it is 2 kilometres wide. Four bridges cross it in the Concepción metropolitan area, the oldest the railway bridge of 1889.

The name Biobío comes from Mapudungun, the language of the Mapuche. During the later part of the Arauco War the river was the traditional borderline, La Frontera, between La Araucanía, the self-ruled Mapuche lands to the south, and the Spanish-ruled Captaincy General of Chile to the north. The territory south of the river was not incorporated into the Chilean state until the later 19th century, after the campaigns known as the Pacification of Araucanía.

In colonial times the river was navigable up and down, and the river island of Diego Díaz, near Colonia Santa Fe, was the scene of an attack in 1610, during the Arauco War, in which Mapuches killed 13 Spanish soldiers. It was once navigable by ship as far as Nacimiento, but deforestation in the 1900s caused erosion that choked it with silt and closed it to boats. In the early 1980s it was regarded as one of the world's best whitewater rafting rivers; the Pangue Dam, built by the state power company Endesa despite protests, ended that, and the Pehuenche people, who had lived in the area for centuries, were displaced.
bioko: Bioko lies in the Bight of Biafra on the Gulf of Guinea, 32 km south of the coast of Cameroon and about 160 km northwest of the mainland part of Equatorial Guinea. It covers 2,017 km2 and is about 70 km long. The island is volcanic and mountainous, mostly basalt, and its highest peak, Pico Basilé, rises to about 3,012 m. Only 60 metres of water over the continental shelf separate it from the mainland, to which it was joined until about 10,000 years ago. Rainfall is very heavy in the south, and tropical rainforest covers most of the island.

Bioko had an indigenous population when Europeans arrived: Bantu-speaking ancestors of the Bubi probably settled there before the 7th century BCE. The Portuguese navigator Fernão do Pó sighted the island in 1472, and in 1494 it was renamed Fernando Pó in his honour. The Portuguese planted sugarcane, and in 1642 the Dutch East India Company used the island to centralise its slave trade in the Gulf of Guinea. Bubi clans withdrew from the coast to the safer interior and began to build a new kingdom under chiefs such as Molambo. Under the Treaty of El Pardo of 1778, Portugal ceded Fernando Po to Spain.

After the British abolished their Atlantic slave trade, they leased bases at Port Clarence, now Malabo, and San Carlos from 1827 to 1843 for the Preventive Squadron. Under William Fitzwilliam Owen their forces detained 20 ships and freed 2,500 enslaved people. Spain raised its flag at Port Clarence in March 1843 and revoked the British lease in 1855. Late in the 19th century Krio planters turned from palm oil to cocoa; dependent on migrant labour, they failed to pay contracts, producing de facto slavery. A League of Nations investigation between 1923 and 1930 into the shipment of contract labour from Liberia found that the abuses arose from conditions on the island.

Bioko is part of Equatorial Guinea, and Malabo, on its north coast, is its largest city. The 2015 census counted 335,048 inhabitants. The Bubi, the historic indigenous people, make up 58 per cent. Spanish, official since 1844, is the language of education and administration; Bube is spoken by about 50,000 people, and the creole Pichi also developed on the island. Two protected areas, Pico Basilé National Park and the Luba Crater Scientific Reserve, cover about 40 per cent of Bioko.
birendra-of-nepal: Birendra was born on 29 December 1945 at the Narayanhiti Royal Palace in Kathmandu, the son of Crown Prince Mahendra and Crown Princess Indra. An earlier son of Mahendra, Rabindra Shah, was born to an unmarried Gurung woman and counted as illegitimate, so Birendra became heir apparent. He studied at St Joseph's School, a Jesuit school in Darjeeling, then at Eton College from 1959 to 1964, and later at the University of Tokyo and Harvard University. On 27 February 1970 he married Aishwarya Rajya Lakshmi Devi, his second cousin.

Birendra came to the throne on 31 January 1972 after Mahendra's death, and was crowned on 24 February 1975 after a mourning year and a year astrologers judged inauspicious. He inherited a country where political parties were banned and rule ran through panchayat councils, so that he was effectively an absolute monarch. Growing pro-democracy demands led him to call a referendum between a party-less and a multi-party system in May 1980. The party-less system won by 55 per cent to 45, a result that democracy campaigners later claimed was rigged.

In 1990 strikes and pro-democracy riots led him to lift the ban on parties and agree to become a constitutional monarch. He promulgated a new constitution on 9 November 1990, making Nepal a constitutional monarchy with multiparty democracy. A civil war between Maoist rebels and government forces began in 1996 and lasted until 2006. His government set up national parks, among them Chitwan and Sagarmatha, and he promoted Nepal as a zone of peace at the United Nations, a proposal 116 countries supported.

On 1 June 2001 Birendra and his immediate family were shot dead at dinner at the Narayanhiti Palace by his son, Crown Prince Dipendra. Dipendra shot himself and, in a coma, was proclaimed king, but died a few days later. Birendra's younger brother Gyanendra then became king. Monuments named for Birendra were renamed after the political changes of 2006 and the end of the monarchy in 2008.
biscay: Biscay lies on the south shore of the Bay of Biscay and is bordered by Cantabria and the province of Burgos to the west, Gipuzkoa to the east and Álava to the south. The southern ranges of the Basque Mountains form a continuous barrier, with passes no lower than 600 metres, and the water divide between the Atlantic and Mediterranean basins. The middle section is occupied by the valleys of the Nervión, the Ibaizabal and the Kadagua. The coast is usually high, with cliffs and small inlets, and its main features are the estuary of Bilbao and the estuary of Gernika. The climate is oceanic, with high precipitation all year.

Biscay has been inhabited since the Middle Paleolithic, and its caves hold cave paintings, those of Santimamiñe showing bison, horses, goats and deer. Roman geographers placed two tribes there, the Caristii and the Autrigones, who are thought to have spoken Basque. The Roman presence had little impact, and the Basque language and traditions survived. The name Biscay first appears in the Chronicle of Alfonso III in the late 9th century, and the territory was then controlled by the Kingdom of Navarre.

The house of Haro, leaders of the pro-Castilian lords, was granted the rule of the newly created Biscay, and tradition names Iñigo López as its first Lord in 1043. The lordship later passed by inheritance to John I of Castile and became one of the titles of the king of Castile. Each lord had to swear to defend the fuero, the Biscayan laws derived from Navarrese and Basque customary rights, which held that sovereignty lay with the Biscayans. Lords and later kings swore the statutes to the oak of Gernika, where the assembly of the lordship sits.

In 1511 the kings granted the port of Bilbao privileges for trade with the ports of the Spanish Empire, and it was already the main Castilian harbour, shipping wool to Flanders. The Carlist Wars of the 19th century grew in part from the desire to keep foral rights, and the victory of the anti-Carlists brought successive cuts to Biscay's autonomy. Iron ore discovered in the 1850s brought foreign investment and rapid industrialization. In 1937 German aircraft under Franco's control destroyed the town of Gernika, and Bilbao fell some months later. The 1979 Statute of Guernica created the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country.

Biscay is a province of the Basque Autonomous Community with its capital and largest city at Bilbao. Its name is Bizkaia in Basque and Vizcaya in Spanish, and its institutions are the Juntas Generales and the Foral Diputation. Its population is 1,167,233.
bishkek: Bishkek stands at an altitude of about 800 metres, just off the northern fringe of the Kyrgyz Ala-Too Range, an extension of the Tian Shan whose peaks rise to 4,895 metres. North of the city a fertile, gently undulating steppe stretches far into Kazakhstan, and the river Chüy drains most of the area. The central city is laid out on a rectangular grid, with wide boulevards, marble-faced public buildings and many Soviet-style apartment blocks, and narrow irrigation channels line most streets to water the shade trees.

The site began as a caravan rest stop on a branch of the Silk Road through the Tian Shan, possibly founded by the Sogdians. In 1825 the khan of Kokand fortified it with a mud fort, Pishpek, to control the caravan routes and collect tribute from the Kyrgyz. Russian forces under Colonel Apollon Zimmermann later took and razed the fort, and a Russian settlement with the original name Pishpek was established on the site in 1868, within the General Governorship of Russian Turkestan.

In 1925 the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast was created and Pishpek became its capital. In 1926 the city was renamed Frunze after Mikhail Frunze, a Bolshevik military leader and associate of Lenin who was born there. It became capital of the Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic in 1936. Until the mid-1990s Russians and other people of European descent were the majority of the population; in the 1970 census the Kyrgyz were only 12.3 per cent. The city was renamed Bishkek on 5 February 1991, and Kyrgyzstan became independent later that year. One tradition derives the name Bishkek from the paddle used to churn fermenting milk.

Bishkek is the capital and largest city of Kyrgyzstan and of the Chüy Region, with about 1.2 million people, near the border with Kazakhstan. It is the country's financial centre and its most important cultural city, with the National Library, the Kyrgyz State Historical Museum on Ala-Too Square and the Frunze House Museum. Most residents are ethnic Kyrgyz, with a sizeable Russian minority. The Dordoy Bazaar on the north-eastern edge is a major wholesale and retail market.
biskra: Biskra is the main city of the Ziban region and the capital of Biskra Province in north-eastern Algeria, about 399 km from Algiers. It stands at the start of the Sahara, at an altitude of 87 metres, and is nicknamed the Queen of the Zibans and the Door of the Desert. Because of its position and its farming, especially its date oases, it has always been a crossroads between the cities of the north and the south.

In Roman times the city was known as Vescera. The Arab commander Uqba ibn Nafi al-Fihri was killed on his return from Morocco in an ambush by the Berber prince Koceila at Tahouda, a small village about 5 km from the oasis now called Sidi Okba, and was buried in the mosque of the town that bears his name. In the early 10th century Biskra and the Ziban area were conquered by the Beni Hammad. A book of the late 12th century describes a large city surrounded by fortresses and thriving villages, with a vast forest of palms and olives, and a centre of jurisprudence and learning.

In the 14th century Biskra became an important hub for the Hafsids of Tunisia, and in 1541 the Ottoman Turks began to conquer it. The French conquered it in 1844 and fortified it as a garrison, and it saw fighting during rebellions in 1849 and 1871. The local chief Bou Zian rallied people against the palm tax and seized the fortification of Zaatcha, 20 km away; a French force of 7,000 took it after fifty-three days of attack, and Bou Zian was killed.

Biskra had a recorded population of 307,987 in 2007. In the late 19th century it became a popular winter resort and gateway to the Sahara and a centre for artists and photographers. André Gide set key sections of The Immoralist there, Henri Matisse painted Blue Nude (Souvenir de Biskra) in 1907, and Béla Bartók collected traditional music in the town in 1913.
bismarck-archipelago: The Bismarck Archipelago lies just off the north-eastern coast of New Guinea in the western Pacific and is part of the Islands Region of Papua New Guinea. Its islands are mostly volcanic and have a total land area of about 49,700 square kilometres, around the Bismarck Sea.

They are grouped by province: Manus Province has the Admiralty Islands, a group of 18 islands including Manus, Los Negros and Lou, and the Western Islands; New Ireland Province has New Ireland, New Hanover, the St Matthias Islands and the Tabar, Lihir, Tanga and Feni groups; East and West New Britain provinces share New Britain and the Duke of York Islands; and others lie off Morobe, Madang and East Sepik provinces, among them Umboi, Ritter, Karkar and the Schouten Islands. The passage between New Britain and New Ireland is St George's Channel.

The first inhabitants arrived around 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. They may have come from New Guinea by boat across the Bismarck Sea or over a temporary land bridge created by an uplift of the crust. Later arrivals included the Lapita people, the direct ancestors of the Austronesian peoples of Polynesia, eastern Micronesia and Island Melanesia.

The first European to visit was the Dutch explorer Jacob le Maire in 1616, and the islands remained unsettled by western Europeans until they were annexed in 1884 as part of the German protectorate of German New Guinea. They were named in honour of Chancellor Otto von Bismarck.

On 13 March 1888 a volcano on Ritter Island erupted and caused a megatsunami; almost the whole volcano fell into the sea, leaving a small rim on the east side of the original island. After the outbreak of the First World War the Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force seized the islands in 1914, and Australia later received a League of Nations mandate for them. They stayed under Australian administration, interrupted only by Japanese occupation in World War II, until Papua New Guinea became independent in September 1975.
bismarck-battleship: Bismarck was the first of two Bismarck-class battleships built for the German Kriegsmarine, the second being Tirpitz. They were designed in the mid-1930s as a counter to the two Richelieu-class battleships that France began in 1935. Ordered as Ersatz Hannover, she was laid down at the Blohm & Voss yard in Hamburg on 1 July 1936, launched on 14 February 1939 with Adolf Hitler making the christening speech, and commissioned on 24 August 1940. She was nominally within the 35,000-ton limit of the Washington Naval Treaty but secretly exceeded it by a wide margin. Her main battery was eight 38 cm guns, and she reached just over 30 knots on trials.

Her only offensive operation, Rheinübung, lasted eight days in May 1941. Bismarck and the heavy cruiser Prinz Eugen were to break into the Atlantic and raid Allied shipping. In the Battle of the Denmark Strait the battlecruiser HMS Hood was destroyed by their combined fire, and HMS Prince of Wales was damaged and forced to retire; three hits from Prince of Wales damaged Bismarck enough to end the raid.

The loss of Hood set off a pursuit by dozens of Royal Navy ships. Heading for occupied France for repairs, Bismarck was attacked by fifteen Fairey Swordfish torpedo bombers from the carrier HMS Ark Royal, and one hit left her steering gear inoperable. In the final battle two British battleships and two heavy cruisers crippled her with heavy loss of life. She was scuttled to prevent boarding, although most experts agree that her damage would have sunk her in the end.

Robert Ballard, who had found the wreck of the Titanic, located Bismarck on 8 June 1989, upright on her keel at about 4,791 metres, some 650 km west of Brest. She had slid down the side of an extinct underwater volcano. Ballard's survey found no penetration of the armoured citadel. The 2002 expedition filmed by James Cameron concluded that the most extensive damage, including long gashes in the hull, came from her impact with the seabed.
bissau: Bissau lies on the estuary of the Geba River, off the Atlantic Ocean. The land around the city is extremely low-lying, and the river is accessible to ocean-going vessels for about 80 kilometres beyond it despite its modest discharge.
