The climate is tropical savanna, with almost no rain from November to May. The name may come from the name of a clan, N'nssassun, in its plural form Bôssassun.

From well before the arrival of Europeans until the early 20th century the island of Bissau was a kingdom of the Papel people. By oral tradition Mecau, a son of the king of Quinara, founded it and moved to the area with his pregnant sister, six wives and subjects of his father's kingdom. The kingdom had seven clans and was highly stratified, and the throne passed to the Bossassun clan, descended from the sister. When the Portuguese began to trade there in the 16th century the king of Bissau was among the most supportive monarchs of the region.

The city was founded in 1687 as a Portuguese trading post. The French were also active, and although King Bacompolco refused them leave to build a fort he granted them a trading factory, from which they shipped thousands of slaves. By 1696 the town had a fort, a church and a hospital. When the Portuguese tried to enforce a monopoly against the Papel policy of free trade, King Incinhate surrounded the unfinished fort, and they soon abandoned it. The Grão Pará and Maranhão Company rebuilt it in 1775 to store more slaves for shipment to Brazil, though real control stayed with the Papel kings.

Around the turn of the 20th century the Papels fiercely resisted Portuguese pacification campaigns. In 1915, after 30 years of war, the Portuguese under Teixeira Pinto and the warlord Abdul Injai defeated the Kingdom of Bissau and incorporated it into Portuguese Guinea. In 1941 the capital was moved from Bolama to Bissau. A dockworkers' strike was bloodily repressed in 1959 and pushed the nationalists towards armed resistance. After the military coup in Lisbon on 25 April, Bissau became the capital of the newly independent state.

Bissau is the capital and largest city of Guinea-Bissau, its main port and its administrative and military centre. Its attractions include the Fortaleza de São José da Amura, built by the Portuguese in the 18th century and containing the mausoleum of Amílcar Cabral, and the Pidjiguiti Memorial to the dockers killed in the strike of 3 August 1959.
bithynia: Bithynia occupied northwestern Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey, adjoining the Sea of Marmara, the Bosporus and the Black Sea. It bordered Mysia to the southwest, Paphlagonia to the northeast and Phrygia to the southeast. Ancient writers placed its eastern limit differently: Strabo at the river Sangarius, others at the Billaeus. Mountains and forests filled much of the land, above all the Bithynian Olympus, about 2,400 m high, above Prusa (modern Bursa), but the valleys and coasts were very fertile. Major cities stood on the shores of the Sea of Marmara: Nicomedia, Chalcedon, Cius and Apamea. Nicaea, the birthplace of the Nicene Creed, also lay in Bithynia.

The region is named for the Thracian tribe of the Bithyni, mentioned by Herodotus beside the Thyni. They probably migrated from the Balkans after the Bronze Age collapse or in the early Iron Age. King Croesus brought the Bithynians into the Lydian monarchy, which Persia conquered in 546 BCE. The Bithynians then asserted their independence under native princes, and Zipoites took the title of king in 297 BCE. His son Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia, which soon grew prosperous. The last king, Nicomedes IV, could not hold his throne against Mithridates VI of Pontus, and after the Roman Senate restored him he bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman Republic in 74 BCE.

As a Roman province Bithynia was usually joined with Pontus; Pliny the Younger governed the two together under Emperor Trajan, and his letters give historians valuable information on provincial administration. Under the Byzantine Empire the region was again divided at the Sangarius, and only the western part kept the name. Nicomedia and Nicaea long rivalled each other for the rank of capital. The Ottoman Turks conquered it between 1325 and 1333.
bitlis: Bitlis stands at an elevation of 1,545 metres in the steep-sided valley of the Bitlis River, a tributary of the Tigris, 15 kilometres from Lake Van. The origin of its name is not known. To Armenians it was Baghesh, one of the most important cities of the province of Aghdznik' in the Kingdom of Armenia, and the main fortress of the canton of Salnodzor. The fortress guarded the Baghesh Pass, which linked the southern edge of the Armenian plateau with northern Mesopotamia.

Under the Byzantine Empire the town was Balaleison. The Arabs conquered it at the end of the seventh century, and it became capital of the Zurārid emirs of Arzan, prospering on an important trade route. Later it passed to the Shaybanid and Kaysite emirs, and the Byzantine general John Curcuas captured it in the tenth century. Many Kurds settled there, and the Marwanid dynasty took the city. After Manzikert it came under Togan Arslan of Akhlat, after brief Dilmachoglu rule, and then Ayyubid rule, the Sultanate of Rûm and the Ilkhanate.

Bitlis was a Kurdish emirate, often subordinate to larger powers but keeping a measure of independence. In the 14th century its emirs, the Rusaki family, were vassals of the Karakoyunlu, and the emir submitted to Timur in 1394. In the 15th century the town flourished as a centre of Armenian manuscript production, the Kurdish emirs permitting monasteries to be built. An Ottoman army besieged it for three months and withdrew; the emir Sheref was killed in 1533 and his son submitted to the Ottoman Empire. The Ruzakid dynasty lasted until 1849, when an Ottoman governor evicted the last emir. Persian was the language of administration and scholarship, in the works of Idris-i Bidlisi and Sharaf Khan among others.

In 1915, during the Armenian genocide, Turks and Kurds led by Jevdet Bey massacred some 15,000 Armenians in Bitlis and its surroundings. Russian forces took the town in March 1916 and abandoned it in August.

Bitlis keeps more medieval and traditional architecture than any other town in eastern Turkey, much of it in the light-brown local stone called Ahlat stone. It has the 12th-century Ulu Mosque with a 15th-century minaret and large stone houses. Only one 19th-century Armenian church survives of the five monasteries and several churches that stood until 1915. Its population was 53,023 in 2021.
bitola: Bitola lies in the southwestern part of North Macedonia, in the southern part of the Pelagonia valley, surrounded by the Baba, Nidže and Kajmakčalan mountain ranges and 14 kilometres north of the Medžitlija-Níki border crossing with Greece. The Dragor River flows through the city, which stands at 615 metres above sea level at the foot of Baba Mountain. It stands at an important junction connecting the south of the Adriatic region with the Aegean Sea and Central Europe.

The earliest organised settlements nearby are early Neolithic tells near the village of Porodin, first inhabited around 6000 BCE. In antiquity the region was Lynkestis, part of Upper Macedonia, and Heraclea Lyncestis was founded by Philip II of Macedon by the middle of the 4th century BCE. Slavic tribes settled the area in the 6th and 7th centuries and built a fortress around their settlement. Bitola was part of the First Bulgarian Empire from the middle of the 8th to the early 11th centuries and was its last capital, in 1015 to 1018; the Bitola inscription is related to the fortress built in 1015. It then returned to the Byzantine Empire and was briefly part of the Serbian Empire in the 14th century.

The Ottomans conquered the city in the mid-1380s, and it was part of the Ottoman Empire as Monastir until 1912. It was the last capital of Ottoman Rumelia, from 1836 to 1867, and the many European consulates earned it the name City of Consuls. The region was a stronghold of the Ilinden Uprising of 1903, planned in Smilevo in May. In the First Balkan War the Battle of Monastir, from 16 to 19 November 1912, led to Serbian occupation, and the Treaty of Bucharest in 1913 ceded Monastir to Serbia, when its official name became Bitola.
In World War II the Germans took control on 9 April 1941, and on 11 March 1943 Bulgarian forces deported the vast majority of its Jewish community, 3,276 people, to Treblinka extermination camp.

Bitola is an administrative, cultural, industrial, commercial and educational centre of southwestern North Macedonia. Its population was historically diverse: about 37,500 at the end of the 19th century, including Aromanians, a Muslim population, a Jewish community of Sephardic origin and Slavic speakers divided between the Bulgarian Exarchate and the Greek Patriarchate.

The ruins of Heraclea Lyncestis lie 2 kilometres from the centre. Ottoman monuments include the covered bazaar, the Gazi Hajdar Kadi Mosque of the early 1560s, ascribed to the architect Mimar Sinan, and the Deboj Bath. The Church of Saint Demetrius was built in 1830 with contributions from local merchants and craftsmen. The St. Clement of Ohrid University of Bitola was founded in 1979.
black-forest: The Black Forest is a large forested mountain range in Baden-Württemberg, bounded by the Rhine Valley to the west and south and close to the borders with France and Switzerland. It is the source of the Danube and the Neckar. It is about 160 kilometres long and up to 50 kilometres wide, with an area of about 6,009 square kilometres, and its highest peak is the Feldberg at 1,493 metres. The gentle eastern slopes contrast with the steeply falling terrain in the west that drops into the Upper Rhine Graben. It consists of a cover of sandstone on a core of gneiss and granite, and it was covered by glaciers in the last glacial period, which left tarns such as the Mummelsee.

In ancient times the range was known as Abnoba mons, after the Celtic deity Abnoba, and in Roman times as Silva Marciana, from the Germanic marka, border; it probably marked the border area of the Marcomanni, a part of the Suebi. Apart from Roman settlements on the perimeter, such as the baths at Badenweiler, mines near Badenweiler and Sulzburg and the Roman road of the Kinzig valley, the colonization was carried out not by the Romans but by the Alemanni. They settled the valleys first and then increasingly higher areas, so that by the end of the 10th century the first settlements stood in the red sandstone region. Rötenbach, for example, was first mentioned in 819.

The ore deposits supported mining, and for several centuries logs were rafted down the Enz, Kinzig, Murg, Nagold and Rhine. This trade boomed in the 18th century and led to large-scale clearances. Most of the long, straight pine logs went to the Netherlands for shipbuilding and were called Dutchmen; used there as piles for houses, they support many historic buildings in Amsterdam. Rafting largely ended in the late 19th century with the railways and roads.

Charcoal burners, potash boilers and glassmakers also lived from the timber. Because the valleys were relatively inaccessible, industrialization arrived late. In winter many farmers made wooden cuckoo clocks, which developed in the 19th century into a precision engineering and watch industry, and the Baden state government founded a clockmaking school at Furtwangen in 1850.

The Black Forest is mainly rural, with many scattered villages and a few large towns, and the main dialect is Alemannic. It is known for its farmhouses with sweeping half-hipped roofs, the Bollenhut headdress worn in villages of the Kinzig valley, wood carving, the cuckoo clock, Black Forest ham and the Black Forest gâteau. In the 19th and early 20th centuries its rural beauty attracted artists such as Hans Thoma. Tourism is now the primary industry, and several ruined military fortifications date back to the 17th century.
black-hills: The Black Hills are an outlying subrange of the Rocky Mountain system, rising from the Great Plains in western South Dakota and eastern Wyoming. The highest summit, Black Elk Peak, rises to 2,207 metres. The range takes its name from its dark appearance from a distance, since it is covered in evergreen trees, and the Lakota call it Pahá Sápa. Its core is granite dated to 1.8 billion years, ringed by metamorphic and sedimentary rocks, and its limestone holds more than 200 caves, among them Jewel Cave and Wind Cave. Most of the hills are covered by ponderosa pine forest.

Tools show a human presence going back as far as 11,500 BCE, with the Clovis culture. The Ponca, Arikara and Mandan were among the earliest recorded inhabitants, later displaced by the Kiowa, Plains Apache and Shoshone, and then by the Cheyenne and Arapaho. After the Lakota conquered the Cheyenne in 1776 the hills became central to Lakota culture. By 1850 the Lakota were the majority, and they call the hills wamakaognaka e'cante, the heart of everything that is. The Cheyenne, Arapaho and other peoples also hold particular sites there to be sacred.

The First Treaty of Fort Laramie of 1851 recognised the Black Hills as exclusive Lakota territory. The Second Treaty of Fort Laramie of 1868 created the Great Sioux Reservation west of the Missouri and protected the hills from settlers forever. In 1874 an expedition under George Armstrong Custer found gold in French Creek, and the reporters with it announced the discovery. Thousands of miners came during the gold rush of 1875 to 1878, and the towns of Deadwood, Central City and Lead grew up in the Northern Hills.

The conflict led to the Great Sioux War of 1876. After the defeat of the Lakota and their Cheyenne and Arapaho allies, the United States occupied the hills in disregard of past treaties, relocated the Lakota to five smaller reservations and sold off 9 million acres. On 23 July 1980, in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, the Supreme Court ruled that the hills had been illegally seized and ordered payment of the original offering price plus interest. The Lakota refused the money because acceptance would end their demand for the return of the land.

The region holds Mount Rushmore National Memorial, Wind Cave National Park, Jewel Cave National Monument, Custer State Park, the Crazy Horse Memorial and, in Wyoming, Devils Tower National Monument, the first national monument of the United States. The economy has moved from mining and timber towards tourism. Rapid City is the largest city, and the former mining town of Deadwood is preserved as a historic place.
black-stone: The Black Stone was venerated at the Kaaba long before Islam, and aniconic stones called baetyls were known across the eastern Mediterranean. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad set it in the Kaaba's wall in 605, five years before his first revelation. In the account of ibn Ishaq, the clans of Mecca could not agree which should replace the stone after the Kaaba was rebuilt, so Muhammad laid it on a cloth and had each clan leader hold a corner as they carried it to the spot.

Muslim tradition gives it a longer past. One account holds that Adam placed it in the first Kaaba, and that the angel Gabriel showed Abraham where it lay so that his son Ishmael could build it into a new temple. Another holds that it was once an angel set to guard Adam.

The stone is set in the eastern corner of the Kaaba in a silver frame fastened with silver nails. It was once a single rock but now consists of several pieces cemented together, and its exposed face measures about 20 by 16 centimetres. It has never been analysed with modern techniques. It has been called basalt, natural glass or a stony meteorite, but geologists regard the meteoritic idea as doubtful.

Pilgrims circling the Kaaba seven times in the tawaf try to kiss the stone, touch it, or raise their hands towards it, following what tradition records of Muhammad. Because of the crowds, it is now acceptable to point towards it. Theologians stress that it has no divine significance; the caliph Umar is reported to have said that it could neither harm nor benefit anyone and that he kissed it only because he had seen Muhammad do so.

It is said to have been smashed by a catapult stone during the Umayyad siege of Mecca in 683, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr rejoined the pieces with a silver band. In January 930 the Qarmatians stole it and took it to Hajar in eastern Arabia, and held it for more than two decades before returning it. The custodians then had a silver frame made, and it has been enclosed in such a frame since.
blackbeard: Little is known of his early life. It is commonly believed that he was between 35 and 40 when he died, and so born around 1680. Contemporary records give his name most often as Blackbeard, Edward Thatch or Edward Teach. People who actually met him wrote Thatch or variants of it, but Teach is the form most often used, because it appears in The Boston News-Letter, North America's only newspaper at the time. He was most likely raised in Bristol, then the second-largest city in England, and could almost certainly read and write. Charles Johnson, an 18th-century author, claimed that he sailed on privateers from Jamaica in the War of the Spanish Succession.

Probably after the Treaty of Utrecht, Teach moved from Jamaica to the island of New Providence, whose harbour too shallow for the Royal Navy's larger vessels. Possibly about 1716 he joined the crew of Captain Benjamin Hornigold, who gave him command of a captured sloop. On 28 November 1717 his ships took the French slave ship La Concorde off Saint Vincent. He renamed her Queen Anne's Revenge and equipped her with 40 guns. His nickname came from his thick black beard and menacing appearance, and he was reported to tie lit slow matches under his hat to frighten his enemies.

By May 1718 he had styled himself Commodore, and his flotilla blockaded the port of Charles Town, South Carolina. About nine vessels were stopped and ransacked. Prominent citizens aboard the Crowley were held, and he demanded medical supplies from the colonial government, threatening to kill the prisoners if none came. On 10 June 1718 Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground on a sandbar at Beaufort Inlet. Teach learned of a royal pardon open to pirates who surrendered by 5 September 1718 and accepted it from Governor Charles Eden at Bath, North Carolina, but he soon returned to the sea.

Alexander Spotswood, the governor of Virginia, feared that Teach and his men would disrupt Virginian commerce and arranged for soldiers and sailors to capture him. On 22 November 1718 (3 December in the modern calendar), after a battle at Ocracoke Inlet, Teach and several of his crew were killed by a small force of sailors led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard. His loot was sold at auction for 2,238 pounds, and Spotswood used part of it to pay for the operation.

A shrewd leader, he relied on his fearsome image more than on violence. He was romanticised after his death and became the model of the archetypal pirate in fiction. Divers found the wreck of Queen Anne's Revenge in Beaufort Inlet in November 1996.
blantyre: Blantyre lies in the Shire Highlands, at the geographical centre of Malawi's Southern Region, and covers an area of 228 km2. The city stands in hilly country at elevations from about 780 to 1,612 metres. Mount Soche, Ndirande mountain, Chiradzulu mountain and Michiru Mountain surround it, and rivers and streams rise in these hills and radiate from the city. The rainy season runs from November to April, and the dry season from May to October.

The mission was founded in 1876 by the Church of Scotland. The site was chosen by the British missionary Henry Henderson, who was joined there on 23 October 1876 by Dr T. T. Macklin and others. Macklin took over the leadership and began building. The first ordained minister, Rev. Duff MacDonald, arrived in 1878. The first missionaries faced local opposition, and three of them were recalled. From 1881 to 1898 the mission was run by David Clement Scott, who built the Church of St Michael and All Angels between 1888 and 1891 with a team of local workmen who had no knowledge of European building techniques. Scott also compiled an Encyclopaedic Dictionary of the Mang'anja Language, later edited by his successor Alexander Hetherwick.

A trading company grew up beside the mission. The Livingstonia Central Africa Trading Company, founded in Glasgow in 1877 and renamed the African Lakes Corporation in 1878, moved in 1881 to Mandala, across the River Mudi. Its Mandala House survives as a National Monument and is the oldest building in Malawi. Blantyre became a British consular station in 1883 and a municipality by 1895, Malawi's oldest. Its commerce began with the colonial trade in ivory, and by the First World War its people included Africans from neighbouring districts and South Asian traders.

Until 1905 the town's growth was confined to three areas within 2 km of each other: the mission, Mandala, and the government and commercial triangle. Limbe began to develop in 1906, after the Shire Highlands Railways Company set up its headquarters and workshops there and the Imperial Tobacco Group built a packaging and grading factory nearby. Indian wholesale and retail shops multiplied, and by 1910 Limbe had surpassed Blantyre. The two towns were merged into one city in 1956.

Blantyre is Malawi's centre of finance and commerce and its second largest city, with 800,264 people at the 2018 census. It is the capital of the Southern Region and of Blantyre District. The Malawi Stock Exchange, opened in November 1996, stands on Victoria Avenue. The city holds eight National Monuments, mostly historic buildings, and the Michiru Mountain Conservation Area lies among its hills.
blekinge: Blekinge is one of the traditional Swedish provinces, on the coast of the Baltic Sea in Götaland, bordering Småland and Scania. It is the second-smallest province by area, after Öland, and the smallest on the mainland. Its name comes from a dialect adjective, bleke, which corresponds to the nautical term for dead calm. The relief is an uneven valley terrain with a scenic archipelago, the bedrock is mostly granite and gneiss, and oak forests characterise its nature. It has warm summers and mild winters by Swedish standards and is sometimes called Sweden's garden.

Evidence of human habitation in western Blekinge dates to about 9700 BCE in the Vesan area, then a small island surrounded by open grassland. A settlement at nearby Ljungaviken, dated to 6500 BCE, contains the remains of at least 50 wooden houses and a buried dog. A survey in 2021 of a pile barrier in the bay of Lyckeby showed that its wood was felled in 1113-14.

Blekinge belonged to Sweden until the early 13th century, when it became part of Denmark; the Danish Census Book is the first secure written evidence of Danish control. With Skåne and Halland it formed Skåneland, the eastern part of the Danish kingdom, where Scanian Law prevailed. As a border province it was often raided and looted by Swedish troops during the Danish-Swedish wars. Sölvesborg was the seat of administration in the west and Kristianopel in the east, and Ronneby (1387), Sölvesborg (1445), Elleholm and Kristianopel had city privileges.

In 1658 Blekinge was ceded to Sweden by the Treaty of Roskilde and has remained Swedish since. Two new towns were built, Karlshamn, chartered in 1664, and Karlskrona, in 1680, to which the populations of Ronneby and Kristianopel were forcibly relocated. Karlskrona has been the principal naval base of Sweden for more than 300 years. The province was granted its arms in 1660, based on a 15th-century seal, with the three crowns of Sweden placed on an oak trunk to mark the change in its status.
blida: Blida lies 190 metres above sea level at the base of the Tell Atlas, on the southern edge of the fertile Mitidja Plain and the right bank of the Oued el Kebir, which flows out of the Chiffa gorge. The stream's abundant water powered large corn mills and several factories and fed the town's fountains and irrigated gardens. Orchards and gardens surround the town, which is known as the city of roses. Its name is a diminutive of the Arabic belda, city. Chréa National Park, one of the largest in the country, lies within Blida, and the nearby Chiffa gorge is one of the few habitats of the endangered Barbary macaque.

No ancient centre preceded the city. It was identified with a medieval town of Mitidja, which was ruined during the campaigns of the Beni Ghania. The present town was founded by Moors, principally Sidi Ahmed El-Kebir, in the 16th century. A mosque was built by order of Khair-ed-din Barbarossa, and under the Turks the town was of some importance. Its gates no longer exist, but their names, such as Bab Er-Rahba and Bab Es-Sebt, are still used as reference points for streets and businesses.

After an earthquake in March 1825 the town was rebuilt on a grid plan, on a site about a mile from the ruins. In 1839 French troops occupied the city and built a military base, an airbase, a communications centre and a military hospital. Life was racially segregated: Muslims were confined to a crowded ghetto, and boarding schools kept separate dormitories. The occupation lasted until Algeria won independence in the Algerian War. Another earthquake damaged the town in 1867.

Blida is the capital of Blida Province, about 45 km south-west of Algiers. The Berbers of the province, the Djebailia, speak Taqbaylit, a Berber language close to the Kabyle varieties spoken east of Algiers. The Stade Mustapha Tchaker, opened in 2002, is the home ground of the Algeria national football team.
bloemfontein: Bloemfontein lies in central South Africa, on the southern edge of the Highveld at an elevation of about 1,400 metres, bordering the semi-arid region of the Karoo. The area is generally flat, with occasional hills, called koppies in Afrikaans, and the vegetation is Highveld grassland. Summers are hot and rainfall comes mainly as short afternoon thunderstorms, while winters are cool and dry with frosty nights. The city is also known as Mangaung in Sesotho, meaning place of cheetahs, and as the city of roses, for its abundance of the flowers and an annual rose festival.

Bloemfontein was historically a settlement of the Orana and the Barolong, and then of Boers. It was officially founded in 1846 as a fort by the British Army major Henry Douglas Warden, as a British outpost in the Transoranje region. That region was occupied by various groups, among them the Orana, Cape Colony Trekboers, the Griqua and the Barolong. The Orange River Sovereignty was proclaimed in 1848 with a British Resident at Bloemfontein, and the Orange Free State, an independent Boer republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers, existed from 1854 to 1902.

On 31 May 1910, exactly eight years after the Boers signed the Peace Treaty of Vereeniging that ended the Anglo-Boer War, South Africa became a Union. Disagreement over where the capital should be ended in a compromise that allowed Bloemfontein to host the Appellate Division and become the Union's judicial capital, and it was also given financial compensation.

Residential segregation in the town began in the 19th century. Ordinance 1 of 1860 decreed that no non-white person, without written permission from the landlord, which was the British government, had the right to occupy urban land in towns that had no municipality. On 3 June 1861 the council marked out separate locations for the black population and for Coloured people, whose inhabitants had to pay a hut tax and a grazing rights tax. This laid the foundation for the residential segregation later planned by the architects of apartheid, which the National Party began to implement after winning the 1948 election.

Bloemfontein is the capital and largest city of the Free State province, with 256,185 residents at the 2011 census within the Mangaung municipality of 747,431. It remains the seat of the Supreme Court of Appeal, formerly the Appellate Division, and the Constitutional Court has been in Johannesburg since 1994. The city has the Anglo-Boer War Museum, the National Women's Monument, the National Museum and the Oliewenhuis Art Museum, as well as Boyden Observatory.
blood-transfusion: Recorded research into blood transfusion began in the 17th century, after William Harvey's experiments on the circulation of the blood, with successful experiments in transfusion between animals. Working at the Royal Society in the 1660s, the physician Richard Lower devised methods of cross-circulation in animals, using closed arteriovenous connections to prevent clotting. In his own account, towards the end of February 1665 he drew blood from a medium-sized dog until its strength was nearly gone, then introduced blood from a larger mastiff fastened alongside it. The animal recovered with no sign of discomfort. Attempts to transfuse animal blood into humans gave variable and often fatal results.

Blood transfusion is the intravenous transfer of blood products into a human or other animal. Except in major trauma, whole blood is rarely used in modern practice, and instead components such as red blood cells, plasma and platelets are transfused. Donated blood is separated by centrifugation into red cells, plasma and platelets, and plasma can be processed further into albumin, clotting factor concentrates and immunoglobulins. Red cells are typically stored at 1 to 6 °C, platelets at 20 to 24 °C with continuous agitation, and plasma frozen at −18 °C or lower.

Only in 1901, when the Austrian Karl Landsteiner discovered three human blood groups, O, A and B, did transfusion gain a scientific basis and become safer. He found that mixing incompatible blood provokes an immune response in which the red cells clump. He won the Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine in 1930. George Washington Crile is credited with the first surgery using a direct transfusion, in 1906 at St. Alexis Hospital in Cleveland.

Before a transfusion the recipient's blood is typed for its ABO and Rh status and screened for antibodies. Most acute haemolytic reactions come from clerical errors or mistaken typing. Blood type O negative is compatible with anyone and is kept for emergencies.
blue-nile: The Blue Nile rises at Gish Abay in Ethiopia, where it is called the Abay, and flows through Lake Tana and out into a canyon about 400 kilometres long. The canyon, cut in the Ethiopian Highlands to a depth of some 1,500 metres, is a tremendous obstacle to travel between northern and southern Ethiopia. The Blue Nile Falls, called Tis Abay, meaning great smoke, lie at its start. The river then runs about 650 kilometres through Sudan and joins the White Nile at Khartoum. It supplies 80 to 86 percent of the Nile's water in the rainy season, and its floods contributed to the fertility of the Nile Valley and so to the rise of ancient Egypt.

The Egyptian fear that Ethiopia might block the river shaped the long relationship between the two countries. Ethiopia depended on the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria for its metropolitan, and from the 11th century the threat to block the river helped secure the appointment of Egyptian metropolitans, though neither diversion nor large-scale use of the water was ever attempted. Emperor Amda Seyon I first occupied the basin and began spreading Christianity there. Later Solomonic emperors, among them Dawit II, Yeshaq I and Zara Yaqob, used their control of the river as a diplomatic tool and identified it with the biblical Gihon.

The Spanish Jesuit Pedro Páez reached the source on 21 April 1618, and the Scottish explorer James Bruce reached the source of the Nile in 1770. The canyon defeated outsiders' attempts to follow the river, from Frédéric Cailliaud in 1821 to W. W. Macmillan in 1902. In 1968 a team of 60 British and Ethiopian servicemen and scientists, led by John Blashford-Snell at the request of Haile Selassie, made the first full descent from Lake Tana to a point near the Sudanese border.

The Blue Nile is vital to Egypt, which receives over 85 percent of its Nile streamflow from it. Its floods in lower Egypt ended with the completion of the Aswan Dam in 1970. In Sudan the Roseires and Sennar dams supply hydroelectric power and irrigate the Gezira Scheme, noted for its cotton. The river's summer floods carry a great amount of silt, which turns its water dark brown or almost black.
bob-hawke: Robert James Lee Hawke was born on 9 December 1929 in Border Town, South Australia, the second child of Arthur Clem Hawke, a Congregationalist minister, and Edith Emily Hawke, a schoolteacher. He was educated at Perth Modern School and the University of Western Australia, graduating in 1952, and then won a Rhodes Scholarship to University College, Oxford, where he wrote a thesis on wage-fixing in Australia. In 1956 he joined the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) as a research officer. He became its advocate in the national wages case, won a fifteen-shilling increase in 1959, and in 1969 was elected ACTU president although he had never held elected office in a union.

Hawke became president of the Labor Party in 1973. In 1980 he stood down from both presidencies and was elected to the House of Representatives for Wills. Three years later he was elected unopposed to replace Bill Hayden as Labor leader and, within five weeks, led it to a landslide victory at the 1983 election. He was sworn in as prime minister on 11 March 1983 and won again in 1984, 1987 and 1990, which made him the most electorally successful prime minister in Labor's history.

With the ACTU Secretary, Bill Kelty, he negotiated the Prices and Incomes Accord of 1983, under which unions limited wage demands in return for a government guarantee to minimise inflation and raise the social wage. The government floated the Australian dollar, deregulated the financial system, cut tariffs and subsidies, privatised enterprises such as Qantas, and established Medicare. In 1989 Hawke proposed a regional forum that became Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, whose first meeting was held in Canberra in November 1989.

In June 1991 Hawke faced a leadership challenge from the Treasurer, Paul Keating, and kept power; Keating challenged again six months later, won narrowly and replaced him. Hawke retired from parliament and worked in business and for charitable causes. He died on 16 May 2019 aged 89 and remains his party's longest-serving prime minister.
bob-marley: Robert Nesta Marley was born on 6 February 1945 at the farm of his maternal grandfather in Nine Mile, in Saint Ann Parish, then the Colony of Jamaica. His father, Norval Sinclair Marley, was a white Englishman who supervised a subdivision of land for war veteran housing. His mother, Cedella Malcolm, was an Afro-Jamaican aged 18 when they married. Norval gave little financial support and died when Marley was 10. Marley began to play music with Neville Livingston, later known as Bunny Wailer, at school in Nine Mile.

In 1963 Marley, Bunny Wailer, Peter Tosh and others formed a group called the Teenagers, which became the Wailing Rudeboys, the Wailing Wailers and finally the Wailers. Their single Simmer Down for Coxsone Dodd's label became a Jamaican number one in February 1964, and they recorded regularly at Studio One. By 1966 the core of the group was the trio of Marley, Wailer and Tosh.

In 1972 Chris Blackwell of Island Records offered the Wailers an advance of £4,000 to record an album, seeing in Marley the rebel image needed to reach a rock audience. They recorded Catch a Fire at Harry J's studio in Kingston, and with Burnin', both 1973, it brought them international attention. Marley then carried on as Bob Marley and the Wailers, with the I Threes, Judy Mowatt, Marcia Griffiths and his wife Rita, as backing singers. A live version of No Woman, No Cry was his first hit outside Jamaica, in 1975.

Marley survived an assassination attempt at his home in Jamaica in 1976, believed to have been politically motivated. He left Jamaica at the end of that year and spent two years in England, where he recorded Exodus. His album Survival in 1979 reflected his support for African struggles, and in April 1980 he was invited to perform at Zimbabwe's independence celebration.

In July 1977 Marley was diagnosed with acral lentiginous melanoma, a skin cancer beneath the nail of his right big toe. He declined to have the toe amputated, citing religious beliefs, and continued to tour. A longtime follower of Rastafari, he was baptised into the Ethiopian Orthodox Church on 4 November 1980 and died on 11 May 1981. He received a state funeral in Jamaica.
bobo-dioulasso: Bobo-Dioulasso lies in the south-west of Burkina Faso, in Houet Province, some 350 km from Ouagadougou. Its name means home of the Bobo-Dioula, and the local Bobo-speaking people, who are related to the Mande, call the city simply Sia. In the late 19th century Sia consisted of two large villages, Tunuma and Sia proper, bounded by ravines cut by the We river and its tributary the Sanyo.

According to local tradition Sia was founded in the 15th century. It became an important market, particularly for the export of horses southwards, and a link in trade routes joining Djenne and the Inner Niger Delta to Kong, Begho and the Gold Coast. Seku Watara founded the Kong Empire in 1710, and members of his family conquered Sia in the late 1730s; after his death the descendants of his brother Famagan ruled the region, known as Gwiriko, with near-autonomy from Kong.

The French occupied Sia on 25 September 1897 after a brief but bloody confrontation, having been asked for help by the local Watara leader Pintyeba, and set up a military post that became the seat of a district of the same name. In 1927 they razed Tunuma and moved its people, and between 1926 and 1929 they laid out a European grid of avenues that formed the framework of the modern centre. The Abidjan railway reached the city in 1934, and after the Second World War it grew again as a commercial and early industrial centre.

Bobo-Dioulasso is the second-largest city of Burkina Faso after Ouagadougou and a major centre of culture and music. Jula is the lingua franca of the region, with French the official language. Its Grand Mosque, possibly the largest example of Sudano-Sahelian architecture in the country, was built in 1880 according to some and 1893 according to others. The city also has colonial buildings in the neo-Sudanic style, such as the museum and the railway station.
bodh-gaya: Bodh Gaya is a place of pilgrimage in the Gaya district of the Indian state of Bihar, about 110 km from Patna. It is associated with the Mahabodhi Temple complex, which contains the Vajrasana or diamond throne and the Bodhi tree. In the time of the Buddha it was known as Uruvela, on the bank of the Lilājan River, and the name Bodh Gaya itself came into use in the 18th century. For Buddhists it is the most important of the four main pilgrimage sites of the Buddha's life, the others being Kushinagar, Lumbini and Sarnath.

Tradition holds that the Buddha practised self-mortification for six years at Uruvela, gave it up because it did not bring liberation, and reached enlightenment after finding the Middle Way. His five former companions abandoned him, then became his first disciples at Sarnath. Archaeological finds show that Buddhists have used the site since the Maurya period. The first temple is credited to the Maurya emperor Ashoka, who visited in about 250 BCE to establish a monastery and shrine. Early representations of it appear at Sanchi and Bhārhut. Kittisirimegha of Sri Lanka, a contemporary of Samudragupta, built a monastery nearby for Sri Lankan pilgrims, and the Chinese pilgrims Faxian in the 5th century and Xuanzang in the 7th left accounts of the site.

For centuries the area lay at the heart of a Buddhist civilisation, until Turkic armies conquered it. From the 11th to 13th centuries local chieftains known as the Pithipatis of Magadha controlled it. Muslim Turk armies led by Qutb al-Din Aibak and Bakhtiyar Khilji of the Delhi Sultanate invaded and destroyed Bodh Gaya and nearby regions.

The Mahabodhi Temple became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002. The present Bodhi tree was originally a sapling of the Sri Maha Bodhi tree in Sri Lanka, itself said to grow from a sapling of the original tree. Buddhists from many countries, among them Tibet, Japan, Thailand, Myanmar and China, have built temples and monasteries around the complex in their own styles. An 80-foot statue of the Buddha was consecrated on 18 November 1989.
bodhisattva: Bodhisattva combines the Sanskrit words bodhi, awakening or enlightenment, and sattva, being. The etymology of the Indic terms is not fully understood, but many modern scholars read the compound as a being seeking or destined for awakening. In the early Buddhist discourses the Buddha regularly speaks of himself as an unawakened bodhisatta, and the term refers to Gautama Buddha in his previous lives and as a young man working towards liberation.

By the time the tradition had divided into competing schools, the idea of a bodhisattva vehicle as a distinct path, separate from that of the arhat and the solitary buddha, was widespread among the Theravāda, Sarvāstivāda and Mahāsāṃghika schools. It appears in sources of the 2nd century CE such as the Avadānaśataka and the Divyāvadāna. The Theravāda Buddhavaṃsa, from the 1st or 2nd century BCE, tells how Gautama received from the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara a prediction of his future Buddhahood.

In the early schools and in modern Theravāda Buddhism a bodhisattva is someone who has resolved to become a Buddha and has been confirmed in this by a living Buddha, and such people are seen as rare. In Mahāyāna Buddhism the term refers to anyone who has generated bodhicitta, the compassionate wish to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. The path is open to everyone, and Mahāyāna Buddhists encourage all to follow it.

The bodhisattva practises the perfections (pāramitās), including the perfection of wisdom and skilful means, and the four divine abodes of loving-kindness, compassion, empathetic joy and equanimity. The Mahāyāna sutras generally depict the path as lasting many lifetimes across many aeons. Some texts say a bodhisattva must postpone final nirvana until all beings are liberated, and the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra gives the vow: I shall not enter into final nirvana before all beings have been liberated. Mahāyāna writers held this path to be higher than that of the arhat.

Mahāyāna Buddhists venerate advanced bodhisattvas, among them Avalokiteshvara, Maitreya and Manjushri. Guanyin, a female form of Avalokiteshvara, is the most widely revered bodhisattva in East Asian Buddhism, and Tara is the most important female bodhisattva in Tibetan Buddhism. Followers of Tibetan Buddhism consider the Dalai Lamas and the Karmapas to be emanations of Chenrezig, and several Japanese schools regard their founders, such as Kukai and Nichiren, as bodhisattvas.

Four mountains in Chinese Buddhism are held to be places of awakening for bodhisattvas: Mount Putuo for Guanyin, Mount Emei for Samantabhadra, Mount Wutai for Mañjuśrī and Mount Jiuhua for Kṣitigarbha. Bodhisattvas are also venerated in Theravāda lands, and the recounting of the Jataka tales of Gautama's past lives remains popular there.
bodleian-library: The first purpose-built library known at Oxford was founded in the 14th century under the will of Thomas Cobham, Bishop of Worcester (d. 1327): a small collection of chained books kept above the north side of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin. When Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, gave a great collection of manuscripts between 1435 and 1437 a larger room was needed, and one was built above the Divinity School and completed in 1488; it is still known as Duke Humfrey's Library.

In the later 16th century the library declined. Its furniture was sold, and only three of Duke Humphrey's original books remained. In 1598 Thomas Bodley, a former fellow of Merton College, wrote to the Vice Chancellor offering to restore it at his own cost. The room was refitted, Bodley gave some of his own books, and the library was formally reopened on 8 November 1602 with around 2,000 books.

In 1610 Bodley made an agreement with the Stationers' Company, suggested by the first librarian, Thomas James, that a copy of every book registered with the company would be placed in the library. The collection grew so fast that the building was extended between 1610 and 1612, and the Schools Quadrangle was built between 1613 and 1619. By 1620 there were 16,000 items. John Selden left his books and manuscripts to the library in 1654. Until the establishment of the British Museum in 1753 the Bodleian was effectively the national library of England.

The library took over the neighbouring Radcliffe Camera in 1860, and the Copyright Act of 1911 continued the Stationers' agreement by making it a library of legal deposit. Its holdings passed one million books in 1914. The New Bodleian, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, was completed in 1940; rebuilt behind its original façade, it reopened as the Weston Library on 21 March 2015.

The Bodleian works principally as a reference library, and documents may not be taken from the reading rooms. New readers must agree to a formal declaration not to remove, mark or damage anything in the library, nor to bring fire or flame into it. Its head is known as Bodley's Librarian; 25 people have held the office. Since 2000 it has been the largest member of a group of Oxford libraries, called the Bodleian Libraries since 2010. With over 13 million printed items it is the second-largest library in Britain after the British Library, and its principal store is at South Marston.
boeotia: Boeotia lies north of the eastern part of the Gulf of Corinth and has a short coastline on the Gulf of Euboea. It bordered Megaris in the south, Attica in the southeast, Euboea in the northeast, Opuntian Locris in the north and Phocis in the west. Mount Parnassus, Mount Helicon and Cithaeron form its main ranges, and the Cephissus is its longest river. Lake Copais, once a large lake at the centre, was drained in the 19th century. Boeotia gained political weight from its position and the strength of its frontiers, but it lacked good harbours, which hindered its development at sea.

The earliest inhabitants, linked with Orchomenus, were called Minyans. The Boeotians themselves are traditionally said to have come from Thessaly, from which they were expelled soon after the Trojan War, and Thessalian cults and place-names in Boeotia lead most scholars to accept this. They spoke Aeolic Greek. Thebes sought to absorb the other cities into one state, as Athens had annexed the Attic communities, but Orchomenus, Plataea and Thespiae resisted and allowed only a loose federation, at first merely religious. Boeotia hardly figures in history before the late 6th century BCE, when Athens defeated its levy in about 519 BCE and again in 507 BCE.

Thebes assisted the Persian invasion of 480 BCE and lost the presidency of the Boeotian League for a time. Athens ruled the country for ten years until the victory at Coronea in 447 BCE, and the Boeotians fought Athens in the Peloponnesian War, winning at Delium in 424 BCE. In 395 BCE the league comprised eleven groups of cities, each electing a Boeotarch and sending sixty delegates to a federal council at Thebes. Boeotian contingents fought with Epaminondas at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Alexander the Great destroyed Thebes in 335 BCE, and Rome dissolved the league in 171 BCE; it was revived under Augustus.

Boeotia is a regional unit in Central Greece. Its capital is Livadeia and its largest city is Thebes. Hesiod, Pindar, Epaminondas, Pelopidas and Plutarch came from the region. At Orchomenus, Heinrich Schliemann's excavations of 1880-86 revealed a Mycenaean tholos tomb that he called the Tomb of Minyas.
boers: The Boers descend from the proto-Afrikaans-speaking free burghers of the eastern Cape frontier. The Dutch East India Company sent an expedition under Jan van Riebeek in 1652, which built a fort and gardens at Table Bay. Company workers could ask to be discharged and become free burghers, and in 1657 van Riebeek set aside land near the Liesbeek River for the first nine. In 1688 and 1689 nearly two hundred French Huguenot refugees arrived and had assimilated by the middle of the 18th century. The word boer means farmer in Dutch and Afrikaans.

The United Kingdom incorporated the Cape into its empire in 1806, and many farmers disliked British rule. An ordinance of 1812 let magistrates bind Khoikhoi children as apprentices on terms little different from slavery, English became the language of the courts in 1827, Khoikhoi gained equal rights with whites in 1828, and the enslaved were emancipated in 1834. Farmers who thought the compensation inadequate resented it. From 1835 some 12,000 to 14,000 Boers left in the Great Trek, to the plains beyond the Orange River, Natal and the northern Transvaal. A Welsh clergyman who lived in the Transvaal reported that the Boers resisted abolition.

Out of the trek came the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. After the British annexed the Transvaal in 1877, Paul Kruger helped lead a resistance that expelled them. The Boers then fought the Second Boer War to keep the republics independent, but capitulated in 1902. A diaspora followed from 1903 to Patagonia in Argentina, to Brazil, to Kenya, and to Mexico and the south-western United States.

Trekgees, the desire to wander, was a notable trait of the Boers, seen in the Trekboers of the late 17th century and in the Great Trek. Frontier Boers were known for independence and self-sufficiency, and their political notions, which verged on anarchy, had begun to be influenced by republicanism. Most belonged to a Reformed church, and the Orange Free State was named for the House of Orange. Afrikaans developed from the Dutch of South Holland during the 18th century and was long called Cape Dutch.
boethius: Boethius was born in Rome to the Anicii, a wealthy and influential family that included the emperors Petronius Maximus and Olybrius, though it had lost much of its influence in the years before his birth. His grandfather of the same name died in 454 during the palace plot against Flavius Aetius, and his father, Manlius Boethius, consul in 487, died while he was still young. The patrician Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus adopted and raised him, introduced him to philosophy and literature, and later became his father-in-law.

Taking inspiration from Plato's Republic, Boethius left his scholarly pursuits to enter the service of Theodoric the Great, whom he had first met in 500 when the king stayed in Rome for six months. He became a senator by the age of 25 and a consul in 510. His earliest documented tasks were to investigate a charge that the paymaster of Theodoric's bodyguards had debased the coins of their pay, to produce a water clock as a gift for King Gundobad of the Burgundians and to recruit a lyre player for Clovis, King of the Franks.

Boethius set out to translate all the works of Aristotle and Plato from Greek into Latin and to reconcile their teaching with Christian theology. His completed translations of Aristotle's works on logic were the only significant portions of Aristotle available in Latin Christendom from the sixth century until the 12th. He also wrote commentaries, treatises on logic, handbooks on arithmetic and music, and theological treatises, among them one against Eutyches and Nestorius.

In 523 Boethius fell from power. At a meeting of the Royal Council in Verona the referendarius Cyprianus accused the former consul Caecina Decius Faustus Albinus of treasonous correspondence with Justin I, and Boethius defended him, declaring that if Albinus was guilty then so was the whole senate. Imprisoned at Pavia, he was executed in 524. In prison he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue with Philosophy personified as a woman, which King Alfred translated into Old English and Chaucer later into English.

Boethius was regarded as a Christian martyr by later generations; his feast day is 23 October, and his cult at Pavia was confirmed in 1883. Edward Kennard Rand called him the last of the Roman philosophers and the first of the scholastic theologians.
bogomilism: Bogomilism arose in the First Bulgarian Empire in the time of Tsar Peter I, who reigned from 927 to 969, most probably in the region of Macedonia. The name Bogomil means dear to God in free translation, and it is hard to say whether it came from the priest Bogomil or whether he took it from the sect. Social discontent fed the movement: services were first held in Greek, which only the elite knew, and taxes rose under Peter I.

Older dualist currents in the Bulgarian lands, Manichaeism and Paulicianism, also influenced it. The Paulicians had been driven out of Armenia, and in 970 the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes settled 200,000 of them near Philippopolis. Samuil of Bulgaria, who reigned from 976 to 1014, probably relied on popular support of the movement in his revolt against Byzantium, and no persecution is recorded in his reign.

The sources are imperfect and often hostile, and the Bogomils may have been Gnostics, adoptionists or dualists. Their dualism was at first moderate: God created and ruled the spiritual world and Satan the material one, with Satan inferior to God. Later they came to hold that God and Satan were eternal opponents. In one account God had two sons, Satanail, who rebelled and made the earth, and Michael, who was sent in human form and identified with Jesus Christ.

They rejected the church hierarchy, monasticism, the veneration of images, the cross, saints and relics, and held that the bread and wine of the eucharist were not physically changed. Communities chose their own teachers and each had twelve apostles, and women could become members of the elect. The priest Cosmas, writing against them, said they taught followers to scorn the rich and the tsars.

The Bogomils spread through the Balkans. At the end of the 12th century the Serbian grand prince Stefan Nemanja deemed it a heresy and expelled them, and many took refuge in Bosnia and Dalmatia. Hungarian rulers used the sheltering of heretics as a pretext for crusades against Bosnia. The Bosnian Church broke with Rome in 1254, but the original documents of its Krstjani show no trace of Bogomilism, and the dualist sect later reported by inquisitors was probably a different body. Bogomilism was eradicated in Bulgaria, Rascia and Byzantium in the 13th century, and survived in a few places in Bosnia and Hum until the Ottoman Empire gained control in 1463.

In the 12th and 13th centuries the Bogomils were known in the West as Cathars or Bulgari. Scholars debate whether the Cathars were an offshoot of the Bogomils or whether inquisitors conflated them, and several groups sometimes linked with them were unrelated or not dualist.
bogor: Bogor is a landlocked city in West Java. It spreads over a basin near the volcanoes of Salak and Mount Gede, at an average elevation of 265 metres. The soils are volcanic and the area is highly seismic. It has a tropical rainforest climate, more humid and rainy than much of West Java, which gives it the nickname Rain City. Temperatures are lower than on the coast, which made it a resting place for Dutch officials during the colonial period.

The first mention of a settlement at the site dates to the 5th century, when the area belonged to Tarumanagara. After defeats by Srivijaya it became the Sunda Kingdom, and in 669 its capital was built between the parallel rivers Ciliwung and Cisadane. It was named Pakuan Pajajaran and became one of the largest cities of medieval Indonesia, with a population reaching 48,000. Its chronicles were written in Sanskrit in Pallava script on rock steles called prasasti.

In the second half of the 17th century Pakuan was abandoned, and West Java, while formally under the Sultanate of Banten, passed under the Dutch East India Company, a transfer made formal on 17 April 1684. The company sent the Sundanese lieutenant Tanoejiwa in 1687 to develop the area. The eruption of Mount Salak on 4 and 5 January 1699 damaged the settlement but the fires cleared land for rice and coffee plantations, and in 1701 the villages were combined into a district headed by Tanoejiwa.

In the Dutch period the city was called Buitenzorg, meaning without worries in Dutch, and was the summer residence of the Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies. Its botanical garden, founded in 1817, drew naturalists from abroad. Japanese forces occupied it from 6 March 1942 and gave it the name Bogor to promote anti-Dutch feeling.

The Bogor Botanical Garden, one of the oldest and largest in the world, covers 87 hectares and holds more than 6,000 species of tropical plants. The former residence of the governor-general is now a palace of the President of Indonesia. The city is a scientific and educational centre, largely because of institutions founded in the Dutch period to improve colonial agriculture, and is home to IPB University. It had 1,043,070 people at the 2020 census.
bohdan-khmelnytsky: Zynoviy Bohdan Mykhailovych Khmelnytsky was a Ruthenian nobleman of the Abdank coat of arms. His date of birth is not firmly known. He was baptised Theodore, in Ukrainian Bohdan, and used Zynoviy on religious occasions but signed as Bohdan in daily life. After his studies he entered Cossack service in 1617. His father was killed at the Battle of Cecora on 17 September 1620, and Khmelnytsky was captured by the Turks and spent two years in captivity in Constantinople. In 1637, as military scribe of the Zaporozhian Host, he signed the rebels' capitulation at Borowica after a Cossack revolt.

In the Czapliński Affair the Chyhyryn starosta Daniel Czapliński was authorised to seize Khmelnytsky's Subotiv estate. This is generally regarded as the immediate cause of the uprising, though it was chiefly a catalyst for wider discontent among Orthodox Ruthenians over religion, ethnicity and economics. At the end of January 1648 a Cossack Rada unanimously elected him hetman, and he sought an alliance with the Khan of Crimea, İslâm III Giray. In 1648–1649 the Cossacks under his leadership massacred tens of thousands of Poles and Jews, and others were handed over as slaves to the Tatars.

The Treaty of Zboriv of 18 August 1649 was unfavourable to the Cossacks. At Berestechko on 18 June 1651 the Tatars betrayed him and held him captive, and the Cossacks suffered about 30,000 casualties. On 18 January 1654 the Cossack Rada concluded the Treaty of Pereiaslav, accepting the overlordship of Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich. Historians disagree whether he intended a military union, a suzerainty or full incorporation into Russia.

Khmelnytsky died on 6 August 1657. His rising permanently changed the balance of power in Europe, since Austria, Saxony, Prussia and Russia exploited the weakening of Poland–Lithuania. Opinions of him differ sharply. In Ukraine he is generally regarded as a national hero, and a city and a region bear his name. Poles called him the Scourge of God and blamed him for the decline of the Commonwealth. Jewish historiography judges him overwhelmingly negatively, since the uprising killed an estimated 18,000 to 100,000 Jews. Russian imperial and Soviet historiography presented him as the unifier of Ukraine with Russia.
bohemia: Bohemia is the westernmost and largest historical region of the Czech Republic, with an area of 52,065 square kilometres. The name derives from the Boii, a Celtic people; Roman authors refer to their former land as Boiohaemum, the earliest mention being in Tacitus. After the Boii left, Suebic peoples, among them the Marcomanni under their king Marobodus, became dominant there. Slavic tribes arrived from about the sixth century, and the Czech name Čechy comes from the Czechs who settled the area. Its borders were mostly marked by mountain ranges such as the Bohemian Forest, the Ore Mountains and the Giant Mountains.

In the 9th century Bohemia was part of Great Moravia under Svatopluk I, and when that state collapsed the Přemyslid dynasty ruled, entering semivassalage to the Frankish rulers. After the victory at Lechfeld in 955 Boleslaus I of Bohemia was granted Moravia by Otto the Great. The title of king became hereditary under Ottokar I in 1198, and Ottokar II conquered a short-lived empire containing modern Austria and Slovenia. Substantial German immigration began in the mid-13th century. The House of Luxembourg took the throne with John I in 1310, and his son Charles IV, king from 1346, founded Charles University in Prague two years later and was the first king of Bohemia elected Holy Roman Emperor.

Jan Hus was executed on 6 July 1415, despite a promise of protection from Emperor Sigismund, and the Hussite Wars followed, led first by Jan Žižka and then by Prokop the Great. The Utraquists defeated the Taborites at Lipany in 1434. After Louis II died at Mohács in 1526, Ferdinand I of Austria became king and Bohemia joined the Habsburg monarchy. The Bohemian Revolt of 1618 began the Thirty Years' War; after the defeat at White Mountain in 1620, 27 leaders of the estates and the rector Jan Jesenius were executed on 21 June 1621. A Czech National Revival began at the end of the 18th century.

After the First World War all of Bohemia became the core of Czechoslovakia. The Munich Agreement of 1938 gave the Sudetenland to Nazi Germany, and in 1939 the rest was occupied as the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia. After 1945 the vast majority of the Bohemian Germans were expelled. In 1949 the country was divided into administrative regions that did not follow the historical borders, and since the breakup of Czechoslovakia in 1993 Bohemia has lain in the Czech Republic. It has about 6.9 million of the republic's 10.9 million inhabitants, and the historical land names survive in municipal and geographical names.
bohemond-i-of-antioch: Bohemond was baptised Marc and nicknamed after a giant of legend. His parents, Robert Guiscard and Alberada of Buonalbergo, were related within the degrees forbidden by canon law, and Guiscard repudiated Alberada for Sikelgaita, sister of the Lombard prince of Salerno, which made Bohemond a bastard. His mother arranged a knightly education for him, and he was multilingual, speaking Norman and Greek. He commanded the advance guard of his father's invasion of the Byzantine Empire in 1081, took Valona, and fought on the left flank at the victory over Alexios I Komnenos at Dyrrhachium on 18 October 1081.

After Guiscard died on 17 July 1085, Bohemond contested the succession of his half-brother Roger Borsa, and under a compromise received Taranto, Oria, Otranto, Brindisi and Gallipoli, though the war was renewed in 1087. In 1097 crusaders passing through Italy drew him east. He brought a Norman army of about 500 knights and some thousands of infantry, took the oath of homage to Alexios at Constantinople in April 1097, and served as a go-between with the other leaders. At the siege of Antioch he was regarded as its actual leader. A commander of the wall, Firouz, let his troops in during May 1098, and he is credited with the plan that defeated Kerbogha's relief army.

Bohemond kept the city, arguing that Alexios had failed to come to the crusaders' aid, and Raymond of Toulouse gave up his claim in January 1099. In August 1100 he was ambushed by Turks near Melitene and held at Neo-Caesarea until 1103, when a ransom of 130,000 dinars was paid to Gazi Gümüshtigin. After a defeat at Harran he went to Europe in late 1104 to raise troops, married Constance, daughter of Philip I of France, and gathered an army of 34,000 men. With it he besieged Dyrrhachium in 1107–1108, but Alexios blockaded his camp.

Bohemond had to submit in 1108 to the Treaty of Deabolis, becoming Alexios's vassal with the title sebastos, promising to cede disputed territory and to admit a Greek patriarch to Antioch. He never returned to Antioch, which stayed in Norman hands under his nephew Tancred, and died in March 1111, being buried at Canosa in Apulia. His son by Constance was Bohemond II of Antioch. The anonymous Gesta Francorum was written by one of his followers, and the Byzantine princess Anna Komnene's Alexiad is a main source for his life; she wrote that the sight of him inspired admiration and the mention of his name terror.
bohol: Bohol lies in the Central Visayas, with Cebu to the west across the Cebu Strait, Leyte to the northeast and Mindanao to the south across the Bohol Sea. The province consists of the main island and about 70 smaller ones, of which Panglao Island is the largest. The main island has a land area of 4,821 km2. The terrain is rolling and hilly, about half the island is covered in limestone, and the interior is a large plateau. The name is derived from the local word bo-ol, a kind of tree that flourished on the island. Boholanos share a language with the Cebuano but keep a conscious distinction from them.

Southeastern Bohol, especially Cogtong Bay in Candijay and the Anda Peninsula, is called the cradle of civilisation of Bohol because of petroglyphs and burials in boat-shaped wooden coffins, estimated to be 6,000 years old. Miguel López de Legazpi arrived on 16 March 1565 seeking spices and gold. After convincing the datus that his men were not Portuguese, he made a peace pact with Datu Sikatuna, sealed with a sandugo, a blood compact. It is marked each year at the Sandugo Festival and appears on the provincial flag and seal.

American troops took over peacefully in March 1899, but in September 1900 Colonel Pedro Samson led 2,000 men in rebellion against their harsh treatment. American forces answered with a scorched-earth policy and burned 20 of Bohol's 35 towns. Japanese troops landed at Tagbilaran on 17 May 1942, and local guerrillas resisted until Filipino and American troops landed on 11 April 1945. Carlos P. Garcia, born in Talibon, became president of the Philippines in 1957, and Tagbilaran received its city charter on 18 June 1966.

Tagbilaran is the capital and largest city of the province, which has one component city, 47 municipalities and 1,109 barangays. Its population was 1,412,726 at the 2024 census. Most people speak Bohol Cebuano, and the Eskayans of the southeastern interior have an artificial language of their own, with its own alphabet. The Chocolate Hills, mounds of limestone, are the best-known attraction, and the Philippine tarsier, one of the world's smallest primates, is native to the island. Bohol became a UNESCO Global Geopark in 2023.
bohuslan: Bohuslän is a Swedish province in Götaland on the northernmost part of the country's west coast. It is bordered by Dalsland to the northeast, Västergötland to the southeast, the Skagerrak to the west and the Norwegian county of Østfold to the north. Its rocky coast fronts an archipelago of about 3,000 islands and 5,000 islets, which form the northern part of the Gothenburg archipelago, and its reefs and sunken rocks once caused many shipwrecks. Most of the coast is Bohus granite. The province takes its name from the medieval Norwegian castle of Bohus, or Båhus.

Rock carvings made in the Nordic Bronze Age, which lasted from about 1700 to 500 BCE, are found throughout the province. They show daily life, religious rituals, ships and animals, and those at Tanum are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the Viking Age the area was part of Viken. It has been claimed that King Harald Fairhair made it part of a unified Norway in about 872, but contemporary sources cast doubt on this, and the earliest attested information is from the 11th century. The fortress of Båhus was one of the kingdom's key defences.

When Norway was united with Denmark in 1537, the province declined in wealth, because Swedish forces often attacked the border zone, and its population contained a disproportionate number of soldier families. It belonged to Denmark-Norway until the Treaty of Roskilde of 1658 ceded it to Sweden. Sweden built the fortress of Carlsten at Marstrand, which for a time was a free port with free religious practice and the only synagogue in Sweden of its day.

Herring fishing increased in the 18th century, and the province flourished in the great herring period of 1747 to 1809, when small fishing communities grew up along the coast. Timber had been its largest export, but wood was increasingly used for houses, boats and the boilers that rendered herring oil, and deforestation in the 19th century helped to give the landscape its rugged, rocky look.

Swedish provinces have no administrative function. Bohuslän was long part of Gothenburg and Bohus County, which merged into Västra Götaland County in 1998. Its cities include Kungälv, Marstrand, Uddevalla and Strömstad, and the northwest of Gothenburg lies on the island of Hisingen. The dialect of Swedish spoken there keeps traces of Norwegian.
bokmal: Until about 1300 the written language of Norway, Old Norwegian, was essentially the same as the other Old Norse dialects. In 1380 Norway entered a personal union with Denmark, and by the early 16th century it had lost its separate political institutions. The Reformation, which prompted Christiern Pedersen's translation of the Bible into Danish, helped a Danish written language standardise, and it displaced the remnants of written Old Norse and Norwegian in virtually all administrative documents.

Danish was used in Norway mainly in writing, but urban elites also spoke it on formal occasions. By the time the ties with Denmark were cut in 1814, a Dano-Norwegian vernacular, often called the educated daily speech, had become the mother tongue of the elites in cities such as Bergen, Kristiania and Trondheim. It was Danish with regional Norwegian pronunciation, some Norwegian vocabulary and simplified grammar.

Bokmål, literally book-tongue, is one of the two official written standards of Norwegian, alongside Nynorsk. It is a Norwegianised variety of Danish and is adopted by around 90 percent of the population of Norway. There is no countrywide standard of pronunciation: the government does not regulate spoken Bokmål, and Urban East Norwegian is generally accepted as the de facto spoken standard in Eastern Norway.

The first Bokmål orthography was officially adopted in 1907 under the name Riksmål, after being under development since 1879; its architects were Marius Nygaard and Jacob Jonathan Aars. It adapted written Danish to the Dano-Norwegian koiné of the urban elite. The school reformer Knud Knudsen, whose work was important for the 1907 orthography and a reform in 1917, is often called the father of Bokmål.

Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson proposed the name Riksmål in 1899, and a movement under his leadership organised to resist the growing influence of Nynorsk. When Aftenposten adopted the 1907 orthography in 1923, Danish writing was practically out of use in Norway. The name Bokmål was adopted by parliament in 1929, after a proposal to call the language Dano-Norwegian lost by a single vote in the Lagting.

Official policy then aimed to merge the written standards into a common Samnorsk through spelling reforms. The 1938 reform, which made many forms mandatory, was harshly criticised by the Riksmål movement, and resistance under Arnulf Øverland culminated in the 1950s. The Norwegian Academy for Language and Literature, founded in 1953, regulates the more conservative standard still called Riksmål. After the Samnorsk policy was abandoned, Riksmål and Bokmål converged, and the Academy's online dictionary covers both.
boleslaw-i-the-brave: Bolesław was the only known child of Mieszko I and the Bohemian princess Dobrawa, and was named after his maternal grandfather, Boleslaus I, Duke of Bohemia. His epitaph calls his father faithless and his mother true-believing, which suggests that he was born before Mieszko's baptism. Dobrawa died in 977, and Mieszko then married Oda of Haldensleben. Around that time Bolesław became ruler of Lesser Poland, though historians differ on how: one holds that his father gave it to him, another that he seized it with the support of local lords, a third that his uncle Boleslav II of Bohemia granted it.

Mieszko I died on 25 May 992. The chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg recorded that Mieszko left his kingdom to be divided among many claimants, but that Bolesław united it with fox-like cunning, expelling his stepmother and half-brothers. He supported the missionaries Adalbert of Prague and Bruno of Querfurt, and after Adalbert's martyrdom in 997 he ransomed the bishop's remains, paying their weight in gold. At the Congress of Gniezno on 11 March 1000, Emperor Otto III permitted a Polish church structure with a metropolitan see at Gniezno, independent of Magdeburg, and Bolesław repudiated the payment of tribute to the Empire.

After Otto died in 1002 Bolesław took Lusatia and parts of Meissen, and in 1003 he entered Prague, where the Bohemian lords proclaimed him duke. A long series of wars with Otto's cousin and heir, Henry II, followed. The Peace of Bautzen of 30 January 1018 let Bolesław keep Lusatia and Meissen as part of Polish territory rather than as fiefs. Later that year, at the request of his son-in-law Sviatopolk I, he defeated Yaroslav the Wise at the river Bug and entered Kiev on 14 August. According to legend he notched his sword, later the Szczerbiec, on the Golden Gate of Kiev.

Historians dispute the date of his coronation, which scholars most often place on Easter Sunday 27 March 1025, though 1000 is also thought possible. German sources say that he crowned himself king after the death of Henry II in 1024. According to Cosmas of Prague, Bolesław died shortly after, on 17 June 1025. He was buried in Poznań, and his epitaph is one of the first sources to call him Brave, Chrobry. He established the Prince's Law, sponsored churches, monasteries and forts, introduced the grzywna as the first Polish monetary unit, and minted his own coins.
bolivia: Bolivia is a landlocked country of 1,098,581 square kilometres in central South America, the fifth largest in the continent. Its geography consists of an Andean region in the west and tropical lowlands in the east and north, and it includes the Altiplano plateau, temperate valleys, the Gran Chaco and part of the Amazon plain. Elevations range from 6,542 metres at Nevado Sajama to nearly 70 metres along the Paraguay River.

In the Andean southwest lie Lake Titicaca, the highest commercially navigable lake in the world and the largest lake in South America, and the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat in the world and an important source of lithium.

Tiwanaku, with its capital at Tiwanaku in western Bolivia, dates back as early as 1500 BCE, when it was a small agricultural village. It grew to urban proportions between 600 and 800 CE and, around 400 CE, began expanding its reach into the Yungas by creating colonies, fostering trade agreements and instituting state cults. As rainfall gradually decreased, food stores shrank and the elites lost power, and Tiwanaku disappeared around 1000 CE. Between 1438 and 1527 the Inca Empire expanded from Cusco into the region.

The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire began in 1524 and was mostly completed by 1533. The territory was known as Charcas, with local government from the Audiencia de Charcas at La Plata, modern Sucre. Potosí, founded in 1545 as a mining town, became the largest city in the New World, with a population exceeding 150,000. After an unsuccessful rebellion in Sucre on 25 May 1809, sixteen years of fighting preceded the establishment of the republic. Antonio José de Sucre chose to create a new state rather than join Peru or the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, and on 6 August 1825 named it in honour of Simón Bolívar.

The name Bolivia was approved on 3 October 1825. In the 19th and early 20th centuries the country lost peripheral territories, among them the Pacific coastal region seized by Chile in 1879. The Bolivian National Revolution of 1952 established universal suffrage and nationalised the tin mines.

La Paz is the seat of government and Sucre the constitutional capital, while Santa Cruz de la Sierra is the largest city. Bolivia is a constitutionally unitary state divided into nine departments, and since 2009 its official name has been the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Spanish is the official and predominant language, and 36 indigenous languages also have official status, of which Guaraní, Aymara and Quechua are most commonly spoken. Major archaeological ruins include Tiwanaku, El Fuerte de Samaipata, Inkallaqta and Iskanwaya.
bologna: Bologna lies on the edge of the Po Plain at the foot of the Apennine Mountains, where the valleys of the Reno and Savena rivers meet. Its two main watercourses flow directly to the sea, so the town stands outside the drainage basin of the River Po. It is the capital and largest city of the Emilia-Romagna region in northern Italy.

Traces of human habitation go back to the 3rd millennium BCE, with significant settlements from about the 9th century BCE, in the Villanovan culture. Etruscan influence reached the area in the 7th to 6th centuries BCE, and by the end of the 6th century the Etruscan city of Felsina stood on the site. By the 4th century BCE it was held by the Gaulish Boii, and in 196 BCE it became a Roman colony and municipium named Bonōnia. In the last years of the Western Roman Empire the Goths repeatedly sacked it. According to ancient chronicles, Bishop Petronius then rebuilt the ruined town and founded the basilica of Saint Stephen. He is still revered as the patron saint of Bologna.

In the Middle Ages Bologna was a free municipality and later a signoria, and was among the largest European cities by population. Papal rule lasted from 1506 to 1796, a period that historians have generally judged one of severe decline, though the 1500s brought major developments. Emperor Charles V was crowned there in 1530, the last emperor to be crowned by the pope. In 1564 the Archiginnasio, the main building of the university, was built, and the Bolognese School of painters, including Annibale Carracci, Domenichino and Guercino, arose in these years. The city then had ninety-six convents, more than any other Italian city.

Napoleon entered Bologna on 19 June 1796, and the city passed through the Cispadane Republic and the Cisalpine Republic to the Kingdom of Italy. The Congress of Vienna of 1815 restored it to the Papal States. Papal rule was contested in the uprisings of 1831, when the rebel provinces planned to unite with Bologna as their capital; Pope Gregory XVI asked for Austrian help, and Austrian forces defeated the rebellion by 26 April.

The University of Bologna, conventionally said to have been founded in 1088 by the glossators Irnerius and Pepo, is the oldest university in continuous operation. Its Studium began as a loosely organised system in which each master collected fees from students individually, and colleges were founded to support students of a particular nationality. It attracted scholars from Italy and across Europe and was an important centre of intellectual life in the Middle Ages. The city is known for its towers, churches and long porticoes, and in 2021 UNESCO recognised the porticoes as a World Heritage Site.
bolsena: Bolsena is a town and comune in the province of Viterbo in northern Lazio, on the eastern shore of Lake Bolsena. It lies 10 kilometres north-north-west of Montefiascone and 36 kilometres north-west of Viterbo. The ancient Via Cassia, today's highway SR143, follows the lakeshore for some distance and passes through the town. Bolsena calls itself the city of the Eucharistic miracle, from which the solemnity of Corpus Domini was extended to the whole Catholic Church.
